Mosque vandalized with swastikas, hate messages in Belgium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:08:53 UTC
22:08:53 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
A mosque in northern Belgium was vandalized with swastikas, hate messages and dog feces, local media reported Sunday.
The vandalism targeting the Tawfieq mosque in Schelle, in Belgium's Antwerp province, was discovered by mosque board members on Friday morning, according to Belgian public broadcaster VRT.
Hate messages and swastikas had been painted on the mosque's door and windows, while dog feces were scattered in front of its entrance.
“We were extremely shocked when we discovered the message, the swastikas and dog feces at our center,” the board said.
Officials photographed the vandalism before cleaning the building ahead of Friday prayers and filed a complaint with police against the unknown perpetrators.
The local Rupel police confirmed the incident, saying authorities were taking it seriously and had launched an investigation to identify those responsible.
Muslim Rights Watch Belgium described the incident as “Muslim hatred in its purest form.”
“This is not an isolated case of vandalism or an act of ‘troublemaking,’ but a disgusting and explicit expression of Muslim hatred,” the group's chairman, Mohamed Amin Chaib, said in the report.
The organization said it would also file a complaint and urged authorities to strengthen security around mosques.

Elements of Anchorage understandings will remain on agenda, Kremlin says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:05:38 UTC
22:05:38 KST

Kanyshai Butun
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Elements of the understandings reached in Anchorage “will always remain on the agenda,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Sunday.
In an interview with the Vesti media outlet, Peskov said that “certain understandings” were reached during the summit in Anchorage, Alaska, between the Russian president and US President Donald Trump in August last year, stressing: “It is difficult to say at this point how applicable they are from both the Ukrainian and US perspective.”
“But at least some elements of those understandings will always remain on the agenda,” he said.
He also said the meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner reflected an “atmosphere of trust.”
“The very fact that the meeting is taking place means that an atmosphere of trust does exist, at least through this channel of communication, and is strengthening,” Peskov said. “Usually, extended exchanges of such welcoming remarks appear when there are messages that the head of state considers necessary to send.”
Kushner and Witkoff arrived in Moscow Saturday to hold talks with Putin. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said the talks lasted three hours and 10 minutes and covered the Ukraine war as well as potential major Russian-US projects.
Ushakov described the meeting as “substantive, constructive and extremely frank.”
US envoys then traveled to Kyiv on Sunday for the first time since the Russia-Ukraine war began.
Moscow and Kyiv last held peace negotiations under US mediation earlier this year, holding three rounds of peace talks in January and February.
Negotiations have since been paused, with Moscow and Kyiv attributing the halt to the US war on Iran, which began in late February.

New Delhi building collapse kills 1, traps others
At least two people were hospitalised in critical condition, and the cause of the collapse was not immediately known
A building collapsed in New Delhi on Sunday, killing at least one person and trapping several others, officials said.
The five-storey building, which housed a boys’ hostel, collapsed in Satya Niketan, a densely populated neighbourhood known for its private student accommodation near a Delhi University campus.
Fire officer Abhilash Malik said about 30 to 40 people remained trapped in the rubble.
Lawmaker Anil Sharma said some people had been rescued and several others trapped inside were making phone calls for help while rescuers remained in contact with them.
Police, firefighters and crews from India’s disaster response agency searched the rubble as earth movers cleared debris to help rescuers reach those trapped inside.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,390 Troops, 33 Artillery Systems in One Day

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,390 Troops, 33 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,390 troops, 33 artillery systems, and three tanks over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on September 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the latest Ukrainian military figures, Russia’s total personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, have reached approximately 1,496,440.
Russian forces also lost five armored combat vehicles over the latest reporting period, bringing cumulative losses to 12,331 tanks and 25,278 armored combat vehicles.
Artillery losses climbed to 49,260 systems after another 33 were recorded over the past day. Ukraine also reported three additional Russian multiple-launch rocket systems lost, bringing the total to 2,096, while estimated air defense system losses rose by one to 1,605.
Russia’s estimated aviation losses remained unchanged at 441 aircraft and 355 helicopters. The General Staff reported another five unmanned ground systems lost over the past day, raising the cumulative figure in that category to 2,507.
Another 1,435 operational-tactical UAVs were recorded as lost during the latest 24-hour period, bringing Russia’s total to 501,244.
Russia’s other estimated losses stand at 5,070 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 144,435 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,644 pieces of special equipment. Another 392 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the past day.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 245 times across the front during the latest reporting period, with the Pokrovsk sector seeing the heaviest fighting. Russian forces launched 43 attacks there, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.
Over the past day, Russian forces also carried out 87 airstrikes, dropped 288 guided aerial bombs, deployed 8,340 attack drones, and conducted 2,389 shelling attacks against Ukrainian positions and settlements, including 32 using multiple-launch rocket systems.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces advanced in parts of the Kharkiv, Donetsk, and Dnipropetrovsk regions, while Russian troops failed to make confirmed gains across several key frontline sectors, according to ISW.

US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Kiyv after Putin talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:02:00 UTC
22:02:00 KST

US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Kiyv after Putin talks
September 6, 2026
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made their first official visit to Ukraine on Sunday as part of fresh efforts toward peace with Russia.
As Ukraine's airspace remains closed due to the conflict, the pair arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland, having spent more than three hours in talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier.
Putin had declared a three-day ceasefire to ensure the envoys' safety.
Zelenskyy: Ukraine's peace proposals are ready
Ahead of the visit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media that Kyiv is ready for a “constructive” discussion with its US counterparts.
“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer," he wrote. "Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared.”
Reuters news agency reported that national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France and Germany were also in Kyiv for talks with the US envoys, citing a source familiar with the matter.
Momentum by US President Donald Trump to end the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict has stalled in recent months after talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January failed to produce a result.
Ukraine's Budanov expects war to continue for many months
Despite hopes of a breakthrough with the Russian leader on Saturday, there were no announcements after the meeting.
Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow talks as constructive, frank, and useful but didn’t discuss specific outcomes.
Ushakov said the talks also focused on economic issues and potentially large Russia-US projects.
During previous talks, negotiators have struggled to bring both sides together on a range of key issues, including the future of the industrial Donbas region of eastern Ukraine.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and Washington are crucial to deterring Russia from further aggression.
Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, told the New York Times last weekend that he did not expect the fighting to end before spring 2027.
He also predicted further Russian strategic air strikes on Ukraine this winter.
The war has escalated in recent months, with Putin seeking the complete conquest of Dombas and Russian drones targeting the Ukrainian capital.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russia's energy sector. It has also targeted online retailers deep inside Russia to try and bring the war home to the public.

Survey reveals associations between Big Five personality traits and nightmare coping habits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:00:23 UTC
22:00:23 KST

New research indicates that a person’s personality traits might slightly influence how they deal with distressing dreams. People who are more outgoing tend to cope with nightmares by talking about them, while other personality traits show weaker links to specific coping behaviors. The findings were published in the Journal of Sleep Research.
Nightmares are vivid, frightening dreams that usually occur during rapid eye movement sleep. They often cause a person to wake up feeling intense fear that lingers even after they are fully conscious. If these bad dreams cause extreme distress or impair a person’s ability to function during the day, doctors might diagnose them with a nightmare disorder. However, occasional bad dreams are very common in the general population.
Despite the distress they cause, nightmares are rarely treated with specific medical interventions. This leaves many people to find their own ways to manage the experience in their daily lives. The “Big Five” is a well-established psychological model that groups human personality into five broad categories. These categories are openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.
Previous psychological research has shown that these traits affect how people manage daily stress. For instance, people with high levels of neuroticism, a trait associated with experiencing negative emotions, often use avoidant coping strategies. Researchers Julia Wiesenthal and Michael Schredl from Heidelberg University in Germany wanted to understand how the general public copes with nighttime distress. They designed a study to test if these personality traits play a role in selecting specific nightmare coping strategies.
To investigate this question, the researchers conducted an online survey of 411 adults. The participant pool consisted mostly of university psychology students, with an average age of 28. The participants completed standardized questionnaires that measured their personality traits, how often they experienced nightmares, and the level of distress those dreams caused. They also reported their experiences with lucid dreaming, a state where a person becomes aware that they are dreaming while the dream is still happening.
The survey included a section asking participants about eight specific coping strategies. These strategies included talking to someone, avoiding triggers, gathering information, using medication, and seeking professional help. The list also included cognitive techniques like trying to induce lucid dreams or practicing self-administered imagery rehearsal therapy. Imagery rehearsal therapy is a technique where a person writes down their bad dream and rewrites it with a positive ending while awake.
Participants indicated how often they used each strategy and rated how helpful they perceived each one to be. The researchers then used statistical models to look for associations between specific personality traits and coping behaviors. They adjusted their mathematical models to account for factors like the participants’ age, gender, and education levels. The team formulated three main predictions before they began analyzing the survey responses.
They expected that high openness to experience would predict seeking out information about nightmares. They also predicted that high extraversion would predict talking about the dreams, and high neuroticism would predict avoiding situations that might trigger a nightmare. Out of these three initial predictions, only one was supported by the survey data. The results showed a positive link between extraversion and discussing nightmares with others.
People scoring high in openness did not show a tendency to research their nightmares. Similarly, people with high levels of neuroticism were not more likely to avoid potential nightmare triggers. The study did reveal several secondary associations through exploratory data analysis. For example, people with higher neuroticism scores were slightly more likely to seek professional help for their dreams.
Participants who scored high in openness were somewhat more likely to practice self-administered imagery rehearsal therapy. They were also more likely to document their dreams by writing them down or drawing them. Agreeable individuals showed a slight preference for discussing their nightmares with friends or family. These agreeable participants were also less likely to practice lucid dreaming techniques to control their bad dreams.
Looking at overall habits across all personality types, discussing nightmares was the most common coping strategy. Participants also rated talking about their dreams as the most helpful approach. Avoiding potential triggers was the second most common method used by the respondents. Strategies like practicing lucid dreaming, seeking information, and rewriting the dream’s ending were used far less frequently.
Seeking professional help was quite rare among the participants in the survey. However, the small number of people who did consult a professional rated it as a highly helpful strategy. Using medication for nightmares was the least common approach reported. In line with the lack of medical evidence for treating regular nightmares with drugs, no participants rated medication as very helpful.
The researchers also noticed demographic differences in how people viewed the effectiveness of these strategies. Female participants tended to find talking about their nightmares more helpful than male participants did. Conversely, male participants rated lucid dreaming as a more effective coping tool than female participants did. Older participants generally found both discussing nightmares and rewriting dream endings to be less helpful than younger participants did.
The study relies on self-reported survey data collected at a single point in time. This type of research design means the results cannot prove that a specific personality trait causes a person to choose a certain coping mechanism. The data only shows that the personality traits and the coping behaviors are statistically related. People might also be biased in their survey responses, such as rating a strategy as highly effective simply because they use it often.
Because the participants were mostly university psychology students, their behavior might not represent how the broader public handles bad dreams. The study also measured perceived helpfulness rather than tracking actual changes in nightmare frequency over time. Future studies would need to track participants over a longer period to see if these coping strategies actually reduce the occurrence of nightmares.
Researchers might also assign specific coping techniques to different groups of people to better measure their true effectiveness. Assessing how coping mechanisms work in people formally diagnosed with nightmare disorders could also provide better guidance for medical treatments. Until then, these findings offer a preliminary look at how human personality shapes the way we handle nighttime fears.
The study, “Nightmare Coping Strategies and Their Association With Big Five Personality Traits,” was authored by Julia Wiesenthal and Michael Schredl.

35 universities join UK defence alliance
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:00:22 BST
22:00:22 KST

Thirty-five universities have joined a new Defence Universities Alliance intended to strengthen defence research, build specialist skills and improve links between academia, industry and the Armed Forces, the Ministry of Defence has said.
The alliance was launched by Defence Minister Luke Pollard at the University of Manchester after the founding members were selected from almost 100 applicants. It forms part of a wider £182 million defence skills package and follows an £80 million MOD investment supporting 2,500 student places across 24 universities and colleges.
The MOD said the Defence Universities Alliance will connect universities more closely with the defence sector, with particular emphasis on areas including cyber security, robotics, artificial intelligence, aerospace engineering and advanced manufacturing. The department said the programme is intended to improve routes from university into defence employment while supporting research that can be developed for military use.
Pollard said: “As we prepare for warfighting readiness, working with universities, students and innovators boosts skills and helps keep our country safe. The Defence Universities Alliance will create meaningful connections between students, academia and defence, boosting research, skills and defence expertise across the UK to strengthen industry. Universities play a key role in innovating and supporting defence, and the DUA helps marshal those efforts.”
He added: “In this new era of threat our £182 million defence skills package is helping to create opportunities for students, apprentices and young people, making sure our historic £298 billion defence investment is an engine for growth across the UK, and building on the more than 272,000 industry jobs supported by MOD spending.”
The alliance brings together the MOD, UK Armed Forces, the Office of the Chief Scientific Advisor for National Security and the higher education sector. According to the department, research conducted through the partnership could contribute both to battlefield capabilities and to medical advances supporting serving personnel, veterans and their families.
Professor Tim Dafforn, Chief Scientific Advisor at the Ministry of Defence, said: “The Defence Universities Alliance represents a genuinely transformative step forward in how Defence partners with the UK’s world-leading academic sector. By bringing together our shared expertise, ambition and innovation, the Alliance will help us tackle some of the most complex challenges facing Defence at a strategic level.”
He added: “I am incredibly excited about the opportunities this creates. The DUA will fundamentally change the way Defence, universities and industry work together – strengthening our national security, creating strategic advantage and supporting growth to deliver better outcomes for the UK.”
The initiative also sits alongside five Defence Technical Excellence Colleges backed by £50 million, which are intended to increase skills in advanced manufacturing, engineering and technology.
Professor Duncan Ivison, President and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Manchester, said: “The UK’s top universities have always played an important role in helping society respond to the challenges it faces. Today, that means working closely with government and industry to strengthen national security, develop new ideas and technologies, and deliver the skills needed in related industries.”
He continued: “The Defence Universities Alliance will deliver a more strategic approach to the contribution higher education makes. By working more closely together, we will better align with government and industry and create more opportunities for researchers and students, for the benefit of our region and the UK as a whole.”
The 35 founding members include Durham, Newcastle, Lancaster, Liverpool, Manchester, Sheffield, York, Birmingham, Warwick, Oxford, Bristol, Exeter and Plymouth, alongside King’s College London, University College London and Cranfield University. Scotland is represented by the universities of Edinburgh, Glasgow and Strathclyde, Wales by Cardiff and Swansea, and Northern Ireland by Queen’s University Belfast.
Vivienne Stern, Chief Executive of Universities UK, said: “The UK is changing rapidly and so is what the country needs from its universities. By equipping students with the skills needed for the defence sector jobs of tomorrow and carrying out cutting edge research, universities have an integral role in our national security.”
She added: “Universities are committed to backing the nation’s security, with almost 100 applying to be part of the DUA. The UK’s defence and university sectors have a proud history of working in partnership to strengthen Britain’s defence capability and keep communities safe. We look forward to the new opportunities that the DUA will bring for scaling up strategic partnerships to develop future talent, research and innovation.”

Punching above their weight: how China’s AI giants stretch each dollar in compute race
Lower costs and faster growth rates let China’s AI firms narrow the divide, raising the question: does the spending gap still matter?
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Howard Liuin Beijing
The massive gap in artificial intelligence spending between US and Chinese tech titans may not buy the advantage expected for American giants, as lower domestic costs and heavy state support allow Chinese firms to secure far more computing power per dollar, according to a new report by Moody’s Ratings.
While US hyperscalers outspent their Chinese counterparts by a staggering margin, the physical gap in computing capacity was nowhere near as wide as those mega-budgets suggested, the report said.
Lower buildout costs, targeted policy incentives and access to cheaper green energy meant Chinese tech firms were punching above their financial weight, narrowing the compute divide with American peers at a fraction of the price, Moody’s noted.
The US retained a clear overall lead in cutting-edge semiconductor chips, but the findings suggested headline capex numbers tell only part of the story. Here is what you need to know.
How wide is the spending gap between US and Chinese tech giants?
Capital expenditure by China’s major tech companies was set to more than double to around US$140 billion this year – up from US$65 billion in 2025 – and reach US$165 billion by 2027, according to Moody’s.

Jamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaican over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, the Caribbean nation’s culture minister has said.
The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.
“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.
“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so.”
First announced in June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to the Americas and sold into slavery.
Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery, that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.
“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.
“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.
“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.
He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.
There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.
In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbean launched a manifesto outlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmer resisted pressure from member states to include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.
Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.
On Sunday, the delegation will host a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum, to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.
She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.
“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”

Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ - but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich | Emma Beddington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

I’m sorry to break this to you, but you may be “Europoor”. This is, apparently, what proud American patriots (the kind who describe themselves in those terms on their flag-forward X profiles anyway) are calling us Europeans, mocking us for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport.
GB news presenter Tom Harwood declared this dig “entirely accurate”, but is it? Well, sort of. US post-pandemic GDP growth is more than double that of the eurozone (15.6% compared with 7.2%; the UK is even worse on 6.3%). As for wages, once you adjust for national differences in the cost of essentials such as housing, food and services, the US average is $86,977 compared with the UK’s $66,299, Germany’s $76,286 and France’s $60,483, according to the OECD. A Sunday Telegraph investigation of the “Europoor” question highlighted astronomically powerful growth of the US tech sector supercharged by AI, making it easy to raise and make big money unencumbered by “old world” regulation and taxation. “We don’t want to be like what Europe has become,” said the Republican pollster Brent Buchanan.
There are massive, obvious caveats. GDP is a wholly inadequate proxy for quality of life or even prosperity: the UN’s proposed alternative dashboard of 31 indicators includes the likes of “respect for the planet” and wealth inequalities, against which the US would surely take a beating. US mortality rates are higher than European ones and life expectancy is lower, so, when a medical diagnosis or accident could bankrupt you, how rich do you really feel?
But, actually, this Europoor stuff is hitting me where it hurts: my New York-based grad student son out-earns me, and his junior nurse girlfriend is paid six figures – that’s more than I made in a city law firm. Quite right – nurses should earn more than corporate lawyers – but it’s hard to imagine them ever choosing to live here in the UK (an NHS nurse’s starting salary is £32,073).
To console myself as I contemplate years of getting even Europoorer, flying long-haul to hug my son, I’ve been counting the ways we’re Eurorich. Sure, healthcare, social protections, holidays, blah blah – but what about the really important stuff?
Cheese
“The United States offers over 1,000+ cheese varieties and styles,” the Cheese from the USA website claims, to which I would counter: “But do any of them taste of anything?” I doubt a single Freedom Cheese can clear a train carriage like a ripe époisses.
Bikes
Apparently, Americans buy 130m bicycles a year, but I suspect that’s thanks to a handful of legmaxxing California billionaires. Anyway, 130m also feels like the number of bikes parked outside Amsterdam Centraal station on any given day (in 2019, 41% of Netherlanders said the bike was their main mode of transport).
Saints
The US has 11 saints – pathetic. I’ve seen the remains of more than 11 saints in a single European mini-break; Ireland alone has an estimated 1,000.
Wholesome food
Let’s take stock of this summer’s US food safety scares. Lettuce, blueberries, jalapenos, fruit bars, granola, eggs, alfalfa sprouts, mangoes, sourdough, tofu … basically anything healthier than Flamin’ Hot Cheetos is a gamble; Gwyneth Paltrow is probably claiming asylum in Puglia as I write.
Weird rulers
Sure, they have their stable genius, but nothing can match absolute monarchy and centuries of inbreeding for floridly unhinged leadership. Charles VI of France thought he was made of glass; the future Peter III of Russia court-martialled a rat for eating one of his toy soldiers.
Characterful teeth
The US has, I read, “entered the age of veneer regret”, with people rueing their decision to drop big money on massive, gleaming, Hollywood teeth. Not over here! We’ve still got teeth Breugel the Elder would recognise (in the UK it’s partly because we can’t access affordable dentistry, but sssh).
Disturbing folklore
Scratch the surface of any European country and some weird, sinister custom emerges. At Belgium’s Matî l’Ohê festival they mourn a bone by waving celery; Austria’s demon-chasing Perchten festival involves dressing like a horned haystack; in Wales’s Mari Lwyd, people take a horse skull on a pole from door to door singing for midwinter. In the name of carnival, we throw herring in northern France, execute a pretend mare in Czechia and hunt people dressed as bears all over the place. And really, what’s better – purchasing power or an annual opportunity to wave celery at a bone? I know my answer.

It also created the NIDAN database of narcotics offenders and a nationwide data-driven map of drug hotspots and trafficking patterns.
The government now uses a “bottom-to-top” and “top-to-bottom” reverse investigation model, tracing small drug seizures back to their source and large consignments forward to their intended users to uncover the wider network.Shah also highlighted the government’s claims on internal security, saying terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir was declining and the sentiment of separatism had weakened since the abrogation of Article 370.
He said those who had envisioned a Maoist “red corridor” from Tirupati to Pashupati had laid down arms and joined the mainstream, while more than 10,000 youths in the northeast had also surrendered their arms.Shah said Naxalism, which had persisted for five decades, had become a thing of the past. “We have eradicated Naxalism and will deal with menace of narcotics in the same manner,” he asserted.

Ayoub fell into the dry well on Wednesday while walking home in the village of Errokn, in the municipality of Ghassoul. He stepped on a wooden board covering the well opening, which gave way beneath him, and he plunged into the shaft, which was about 80 metres (262 feet) deep and 40cm (15.75 inches) in diameter.
Rescuers were unable to descend into the well, so they dug a parallel shaft to reach the boy through a horizontal passage, using machinery alongside technical experts, work that continued over several days. Loose soil and hard rock layers complicated the effort, officials said.
Authorities in el-Bayadh formed a crisis response unit under the provincial governor, Noureddine Belarbi, involving civil protection, security and military personnel.
Large crowds of residents gathered near the site over the following days to follow the operation and offer support to the family, while additional civil protection units were deployed as the rescue entered what officials described as a “decisive” phase on its fourth day.
Ayoub’s death has revived public debate in Algeria over the safety of unsecured wells in rural areas, with commentators questioning the lack of regulation covering such structures, particularly in isolated regions.
The case recalled the 2018 death of a young man who fell into a 100-metre (328-foot) well in Msila province, where a rescue operation lasted nine days before his body was recovered, and the widely followed 2022 case of Moroccan toddler Rayan, who died after falling into a 32-metre (105-foot) well and being trapped for more than 100 hours in an operation that drew global attention before he was pulled out and later confirmed dead.

In a post on social media before the envoys' arrival, Zelenskyy said he had held a preparatory meeting with his negotiating team and said Ukraine wanted an end to the war.
"Security guarantees are needed. A dignified post-war peace is needed. Our proposals have been drawn up," he said.
Temporary halt in strikes
A source familiar with the matter told Reuters the British, French and German national security advisers were also in Kyiv on Sunday. The source did not specify which meetings they would participate in.
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Moscow several times in their roles as peace envoys. But Sunday will be their first visit to Kiev in their capacity as US negotiators.
In previous talks, the sides have remained far apart on a range of key issues, including the future of the eastern Donbass region. Russia has demanded Ukraine's withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kiev has refused, reasoning that it can still hold on there for years.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the US are crucial to deterring Russia from attacking again.
Though the front lines of the ground war remain largely static, both Russian and Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks.
Russia has pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones for the past two weeks, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
Ukraine, on the other hand, has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and the warehouses of online retailer Wildberries.
The Kremlin has said it would pause strikes on Kiev until Monday, while Zelenskyy has said Ukraine would also halt strikes on Moscow.
Ukraine said on Sunday it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, around 480 km (300 miles) inside Russia, overnight, causing a fire.

Iran's Hormuz leverage wanes as US economic squeeze bites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:51:49 UTC
21:51:49 KST

Iran's Hormuz leverage wanes as US economic squeeze bites
ISTANBUL, Sept 6 - Six months after a conflict that rattled markets and pushed the Gulf to the brink of a wider war, the tide may be turning against Iran as Washington unleashes an unprecedented economic offensive to achieve what military force could not.
After years of surviving sanctions, Tehran is now confronting one of the harshest squeezes in the Islamic Republic's history, according to Iranian insiders and regional sources. A U.S. naval blockade and tougher sanctions are curbing oil exports, restricting access to foreign currency and exposing growing strains in the economy.
The campaign has led U.S. and regional officials to wager that mounting economic pressure can force Tehran to allow free passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which carries about a fifth of global oil and LNG supplies.
Their bet rests on a simple calculation: Iran is suffering more economic damage than it is inflicting. Efforts to choke off oil exports have cut state revenues, while attempts to disrupt shipping through Hormuz have not triggered the global economic shock Tehran hoped would force Washington to compromise. Energy markets have adjusted and alternative supplies have continued to flow.
"The balance of power has tilted against Iran a bit," said Iranian analyst Arash Azizi. Iran is losing some of the leverage it had over the Strait of Hormuz because it has been unable to close it fully, he said, adding that the U.S. naval blockade was "really hitting Iran."
Azizi said Tehran had expected disruption in the strait to trigger a major shock to the global economy and drive Washington back to the negotiating table. "It hasn't happened, really," he said. Other countries had adapted, exposing limits to Iran's ability to inflict economic pain on the region and beyond.
Whether the pressure will force concessions remains unclear, the regional sources said. Tehran has failed to impose the costs it hoped would break Washington's resolve but has shown little sign of abandoning demands for sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and recognition of its security role in Hormuz.
Still, a new formula for resolving the standoff is now under discussion between mediators and Iran, the sources said.
CAN TEHRAN OUTLAST THE SQUEEZE?
Three senior Iranian sources acknowledged that Washington's campaign is becoming increasingly difficult to withstand. The latest measures have sharply restricted Tehran's ability to access foreign currency, import goods and tap global financing networks that have helped keep the economy afloat.
Iranian leaders fear a worsening economy, marked by surging prices, weaker trade and pressure on household incomes, could reignite nationwide unrest that has repeatedly challenged the Islamic Republic.
Shortages of key imports, including fuel and wheat, are becoming an increasing concern, officials said.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the strategy as a "one-two punch" combining the blockade with "the toughest sanctions in history."
"It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this regime," he told CNBC.
For some U.S., Israeli and regional officials, such strains strengthen hopes that economic pressure could eventually carry political consequences inside Iran by triggering unrest, widening rifts within the leadership and weakening its grip on power.
Others remain sceptical that economic and military coercion will produce a political rupture, pointing to decades of failed efforts to destabilise the Islamic Republic and Tehran's willingness to suppress dissent. They argue Iran's rulers may again prove more resilient than their adversaries expect.
THE RESILIENCE TEST
Dennis Ross, a former U.S. negotiator, said Washington may be interpreting Iran's economic distress as evidence of strategic success when the reality is more complicated. Tehran remains determined to demonstrate it can control Hormuz, but appears to be calibrating its use of force while keeping further escalation in reserve.
The Revolutionary Guards may believe Iran can absorb the economic pain and outlast the pressure rather than compromise, Ross said.
"The Iranians have consistently surprised us in terms of their resiliency," he added, saying he doubted economic and military pressure alone would force a retreat. Hardliners, he said, may believe they can endure and ultimately secure what they want.
Resilience may depend as much on public tolerance as Tehran's ability to absorb economic hardship, said Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute.
"Of course, the economic squeeze raises the risk of public unrest, but for now, a wartime mentality appears to have a significant hold over the population," said Ozcelik. "Foreign military intervention, civilian casualties and the perception of a wider civilization confrontation with a U.S.-led order are sustaining a degree of 'Iran-first' patriotic support, tolerance or simply patience with the regime."
The result is a more stubborn impasse than Washington may have anticipated. Economic pressure is deepening the pain, but Tehran's powerful Revolutionary Guards may see endurance, backed by the threat of escalation, as leverage rather than a reason to concede.
The key question is not whether Iran is hurting, but whether it is hurting enough to compromise before either side slips toward another confrontation, the regional sources said.
Ross said the clearest path to a deal may lie in the dispute over shipping fees through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran could abandon any demand for a toll while retaining the right to charge for legitimate navigational, security or environmental services, he said.
Such an arrangement could give both sides a claim to victory, allowing Tehran to step back without appearing to capitulate.
"If you could announce that the Strait were reopened," Ross said, "I think Trump would do a deal." REUTERS

The next FIFA presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election next year.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the world football governing body said: "The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027. Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election.”
Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016, has been under huge pressure since FIFA announced a highly controversial - and since scrapped - private investment plan in late July, which would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).
The proposal drew fierce pushback from across the football community, with some accusing FIFA of looking to "sell" the sport.
A major divide quickly opened up in world football over Infantino's position as head of the governing body, with regional confederations and individual nations split over whether he should continue.
In August, European nations withdrew a threat to boycott FIFA competitions after UEFA said it had received "assurances" that the FFE plan had been “irrevocably and permanently withdrawn” and that it “will not re-appear in any other shape, construction, name or form."
UEFA has nevertheless continued to push for Infantino's removal.
The next FIFA presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.
Speaking at the 76th Congress in Vancouver, Canada earlier this year, Infantino vowed to re-run for the presidency.
“I want to tell you first – the 211 (FIFA) Member Associations – that I will be (a) candidate for the election of FIFA President next year,” he said to assembled delegates. “Thank you for your support over the last 10 years, your support today, your work, your progress, your love for the game, your commitment, and your passion.”

National security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany arrived in Kyiv on Sunday, Sept. 6, joining high-level diplomatic engagements alongside US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov confirmed the European presence while publishing footage welcoming the American delegation to the capital.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Glad to welcome the American delegation headed by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv. Ahead lies an eventful day and important negotiations,” Budanov stated. “Representatives of our European partners – France, Great Britain, and Germany – are also in Kyiv. Together, we are all working to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine.”
Reuters reported that national security advisers from the three European nations traveled to the Ukrainian capital concurrently with the US envoys. A diplomatic source cited by the agency did not specify the exact negotiation sessions or bilateral formats in which the European officials would participate.
President Volodymyr Zelensky subsequently clarified the format, explaining that consultations would proceed across several distinct stages rather than a single joint meeting, UA.News reported.
According to Zelensky, the Ukrainian negotiating team will first hold a dedicated bilateral discussion with Trump’s envoys before convening a second session with the European advisers.
US Envoys Witkoff and Kushner Arrive in Kyiv for First Visit
“One session is expected – our conversation, then another session will be with European NSAs,” Zelensky said ahead of the meetings, using the acronym for national security advisers from Britain, France, and Germany. “Several important sessions [are planned].”
The phased schedule is designed to allow Kyiv to address core bilateral issues with the American delegation before broadening discussions into a wider European multilateral format.
Witkoff and Kushner’s arrival
The European advisers’ visit coincides with direct negotiations launched earlier Sunday between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at St. Sophia Square.
“Started negotiations,” Zelensky announced in a concise statement marking the official start of the consultations.
The talks represent the first visit by Trump’s peace envoys to Ukraine since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The American delegation arrived overland by train after Russian drone and missile strikes disrupted initial plans to land by plane at operational Ukrainian airfields.
Upon arriving at Kyiv’s central railway station earlier Sunday, the US envoys were welcomed by Budanov, First Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Sergiy Kyslytsya, Head of the Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) Rustem Umerov, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia.
The diplomatic engagements in Kyiv follow a three-hour-and-10-minute Kremlin meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and the US envoys on Saturday evening, Sept. 5. During the Moscow talks, Russian officials discussed settlement concepts and bilateral economic projects, while Putin agreed to halt strikes on Kyiv for three days but rejected a wider frontline ceasefire.

‘Every student’s life is precious’: Rahul Gandhi flags student housing crisis after deadly Delhi collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:49:04 UTC
21:49:04 KST

Rescue operation underway after a five-storey building collapsed at Satya Niketan area, in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Sunday expressed grief over the building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan, urging the NDRF, Delhi Fire Service and other rescue teams to make every possible effort to reach those trapped under the debris. One person has died, two are in critical condition and several others are feared trapped following the collapse, officials said.Rahul Gandhi, in a post on X, said: " The news of the building collapse in Satya Niketan, Delhi, is extremely heartbreaking and alarming. Reports indicate that several people are trapped under the debris, including many students from Delhi University. My appeal is that NDRF, Delhi Fire Service, and all rescue teams reach every single student by making every possible effort, ensuring that the injured receive the best possible immediate treatment, so that no effort is spared in saving anyone."
"Congress and NSUI workers are present at the scene and are ready to provide every possible assistance. In this hour of difficulty, we all stand with the victims and their families. Students' lives were already filled with struggles—now the situation has turned life-threatening. Due to the lack of good hostels in colleges or universities, students are forced to live in PG accommodations, 40-40 at a time under one roof, in inhumane conditions.
Every student's life is precious, and their protection must be ensured under all circumstances," Rahul added.
A five-storey building being used as a boys' paying guest accommodation collapsed in the Satya Niketan area of South-West Delhi at around 1.30 pm on Sunday, triggering a major search and rescue operation in the densely populated neighbourhood near Delhi University's South Campus.Officials said one person was killed in the collapse, while two others were critically injured. Several people were initially feared trapped beneath the rubble as rescue personnel searched through the debris.JCB machines were deployed at the site to clear the collapsed structure and assist emergency teams in reaching those who may have been trapped.Delhi Police said the exact number of people trapped or injured was not immediately known. Multiple people were rescued and shifted to hospitals as the search operation continued.The building, located in an area lined with student accommodations, paying guest facilities and eateries, collapsed along narrow and densely populated lanes, making rescue operations challenging.
Building was being used as PG
According to Delhi Police, a local enquiry found that the structure was around 40 to 50 years old and comprised a basement and five upper floors. It was being used as a PG accommodation."From the local enquiry, it came to knowledge that this was a 40–50-year-old building, comprising a basement and five upper floors, and it was used as a PG accommodation. Repair work was underway in the basement when the incident occurred," the Delhi Police stated.The Delhi Fire Department received an alert about the collapse at around 1.30 pm, following which emergency personnel and rescue teams were rushed to the site.The rescue operation remained underway as teams continued to remove debris and search for survivors.Congress demands immediate actionCongress leader Abhishek Dutt described the incident as deeply distressing and called for immediate assistance to the victims and their families.“The issue far more significant than the election itself is the manner in which children are losing their lives here and how buildings in Delhi keep collapsing like this,” Dutt told ANI.He described the loss of lives as “deeply tragic” and called on the government to support the victims' families and take steps to prevent similar incidents.“Right now, the focus must be on helping the children and their families,” he said.
Kejriwal calls collapse alarming
AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal also described the incident as "extremely tragic and alarming" and urged the Delhi government to take large-scale measures to improve public safety."The incident of the building collapse in Satya Niketan, Delhi, is extremely tragic and alarming. I pray to God that the people trapped in the debris are rescued safely and quickly. Due to the government's negligence in Delhi, many such accidents have already occurred. The government must wake up from its slumber. There is a need to take large-scale action to ensure the safety of citizens."AAP MP Atishi demanded urgent relief operations and a high-level inquiry into the collapse."The news of the building collapse at Satya Niketan in Delhi's Moti Bagh is extremely heartbreaking and alarming. The apprehension that several people, including students, are trapped under the debris is deeply distressing. We appeal to the administration to carry out relief and rescue operations with utmost promptness and to safely extricate all those trapped under the rubble."She added, "The government must conduct a high-level investigation into this incident and ensure strict action against those responsible for negligence, so that such painful tragedies can be prevented in the future."AAP leader Saurabh Bharadwaj alleged that unchecked illegal construction and corruption had contributed to repeated building-related incidents in Delhi."Just a few days ago, you saw a four-story building collapse in Saket. It took the government and the MCD a whole week to admit it was a four-story building. Initially, they kept claiming it had only two floors... I am telling you about this case here as well. An illegal PG facility was operating in a four-story building... A basement was being illegally excavated there during the monsoon season," Bharadwaj told ANI.
He further alleged lapses involving multiple departments, saying, "Unless you go beyond the 'small fish' and target the 'big crocodiles'—the DC, the Commissioner, the one who was walking his dog in the stadium- this will keep happening... Previously, only the MCD was taking bribes. But for the past year, the MCD, the Fire Department, and the SDM/DM departments have all been taking bribes."AAP leader and former Delhi mayor Shelly Oberoi also criticised the Delhi government and the BJP-ruled Municipal Corporation of Delhi over alleged safety violations."Sometimes buildings are collapsing, sometimes fire incidents are shaking Delhi. The tragic accident in Satya Niketan is yet another proof of the BJP's dilapidated governance system and the failure of the BJP-ruled MCD. No action against illegal constructions, no adherence to safety rules, and no accountability either. Why should the people of Delhi pay the price for these accidents with their lives?"

Bennett reveals top-heavy technocratic Knesset slate ahead of election filing deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:59 UTC
21:47:59 KST

Former prime minister Naftali Bennett on Sunday unveiled the candidate slate for his Beyachad party, placing three women with senior public-sector management backgrounds directly behind him as parties race to finalize their lists ahead of the election filing deadline.
Keren Terner, former director-general of the Finance and Transportation ministries, will be No. 2. Liran Avisar Ben-Horin, former director-general of the Communications Ministry, will be No. 3, while Michal Negri, former director-general of the Ra’anana Municipality, will be No. 4. MK Eitan Ginzburg will take the fifth spot.
The rest of the top 10 includes party director-general Bruria Naim Arman, former Aharai CEO Amir Strugo, northern activist Nissan Ze’evi, Orly Harel and Yonatan Shalev, who will be placed at No. 10.
According to the party, nine members of the slate are active reservists who together served 2,825 days of reserve duty during the war.
The full list is:
1. Naftali Bennett
2. Keren Terner
3. Liran Avisar Ben-Horin
4. Michal Negri
5. Eitan Ginzburg
6. Yonatan Shalev
7. Bruria Naim Arman
8. Amir Strugo
9. Nissan Ze’evi
10. Orly Harel
11. Shahar Varon
12. Esti Ayalon Kobo
13. Jeremy Saltan
14. Tzvi Plotnitzky
15. Olesia Kantor
16. Mati Gill
17. Tomer Wiener
18. Tami Muziel
19. Yael Stern
20. Amit Barda
Bennett said the slate reflects the kind of team he wants to bring into government if his party is elected, emphasizing managerial experience and the ability to move quickly from the Knesset into government ministries.
“After hard work and a deep selection process, we are presenting today the best team for fixing the State of Israel,” he said.
He said the list was built around candidates with executive and implementation experience, describing them as people capable of entering the Knesset and government ministries and immediately beginning work.
Bennett also called the slate “the best and most effective” to run for the Knesset in the past generation, saying its members were chosen for their ability to work quickly and effectively.
The lineup underscores Bennett’s effort to present Beyachad as a managerial, execution-focused alternative built around former senior civil servants, experienced administrators and reservists, rather than a slate dominated by longtime politicians.

The government counts on the judges in Jerusalem to strike down their laws - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:35 UTC
21:47:35 KST

There are judges in Jerusalem. The government knew it.
The phrase, popularly associated with former prime minister Menachem Begin and the principle that governments must respect judicial rulings, is usually invoked as an expression of faith: However great the political pressure, the law will ultimately be upheld. In this case, however, it describes something considerably more cynical.
The coalition passed an amendment on July 14 after being warned, repeatedly and in the clearest possible terms, that it could not survive legal scrutiny. It then left the law effectively undefended in court. When nine justices unanimously struck it down, the politicians responsible attacked the court for producing the expected result.
The temporary amendment would have halted arrests, investigations, and other enforcement proceedings against qualifying ultra-Orthodox (haredi) yeshiva students who failed to report for military service. It did not exempt them from the draft; their legal obligation to serve remained, the state would simply have been prevented from enforcing it.
The law never took effect. Justice Ofer Grosskopf froze it the day after it passed, pending the petitions that produced Thursday’s judgment.
Grosskopf’s order was enacted against an already settled legal backdrop. After the statutory framework allowing yeshiva-student deferments expired in 2023, the High Court unanimously ruled in June 2024 that the government no longer had the authority to refrain from drafting eligible students. Subsequent rulings ordered the state to enforce that obligation meaningfully.
Its problems were not discovered after the vote by an overreaching court hunting for an excuse to intervene.
The Knesset’s own legal advisers warned lawmakers “once, twice, and three times,” as Deputy Supreme Court President Noam Sohlberg put it, that the legislation had departed entirely from the bill that passed its first reading.
That original bill was intended to increase haredi enlistment and national service, encourage employment, and reduce inequality. By the time the coalition had finished with it, it contained no enlistment targets, effective sanctions, or alternative enforcement system. Its principal achievement was to remove the consequences of refusing to report.
Knesset legal team warns High Court that legislative process fundamentally defective
The Knesset’s legal team eventually told the High Court that the legislative process was fundamentally defective. Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed the law on both procedural and constitutional grounds. IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir warned that it would encourage noncompliance and was “clearly and unequivocally inconsistent” with the military’s needs.
The government was permitted to obtain separate legal representation - and it still offered no substantive legal defense. Instead, it submitted a short position saying the result of the case was “known in advance.”
That sentence should follow every attack now being directed at the court.
This was not a law that unexpectedly encountered a newly invented judicial obstacle; the coalition was told, at every stage, that it was crossing the basic procedural boundaries that turn a proposal into law. It crossed them anyway.
Nine justices, along with the petitioners and state and Knesset attorneys, were then required to spend their time litigating what lawmakers had already been told before the legislation passed.
Now, if the law somehow survived, the coalition would obtain temporary immunity from enforcement for haredi draft evaders. If it was struck down - as almost everyone involved understood it would be - haredi politicians would obtain something else: another judgment around which to rally their voters and another opportunity to portray the court as the enemy of Torah.
The law failed, and Shas immediately called the justices “the greatest generators of chaos in the country,” accused them of trampling democracy, and claimed that they were intervening in the election on behalf of the Left.
Pass an indefensible law, force the court to intervene, and then present that intervention as proof that the court is persecuting the community the law purported to protect.
The fear within haredi society is real. The messaging to families, explicit and implicit, is that military enlistment threatens their children’s religious identity and standing within their community, and that enforcement of an obligation imposed by Israeli law amounts to persecution of Torah students.
But that fear was not created by the High Court. It is the product of decades in which political and religious leaders, with the state’s cooperation and frequent capitulation, allowed a separate understanding of citizenship to take hold: that the laws governing military service were ultimately negotiable for one community, even when they remained compulsory for everyone else.
The state bears deep responsibility for that failure. It failed to ensure that every Israeli child receives an education in the rights and obligations of citizenship, and allowed temporary arrangements to become an assumed way of life and repeatedly postponed the moment at which it would have to tell haredi citizens the truth.
Haredi leadership must take responsibility
But haredi leadership bears responsibility as well.
Citizenship cannot mean access to representation, budgets, benefits, and political power, while its obligations are framed as oppression whenever they become inconvenient.
This is why Sohlberg’s despair, which carries through very clearly in the decision, is so poignant.
Sohlberg is not a judge hostile to Torah study looking at haredi society from the outside. He is an observant Jew, a graduate of a hesder yeshiva, and a jurist whose opinions are steeped in Jewish law and religious texts.
At the July hearing, an attorney representing a haredi organization claimed that the Torah prohibited enlistment under the current conditions. Justice David Mintz, also observant, responded: “I simply cannot believe what I am hearing.”
In Thursday’s judgment, Sohlberg answered the claim at greater length.
“With the signing of another chapter - as bleak as those before it - in the saga of haredi enlistment, and precisely ‘out of recognition of the value of Torah study’ and the Torah’s values, I cannot refrain from what has nearly become a fixed ritual,” he wrote.
He would try once again, he said, to make clear “to anyone willing to listen, that this is not the way of Torah. Far from it.”
He cited Moses’s question to the tribes that sought to remain outside the coming battle: “Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?”
The court did not order the arrest of Torah students because they study Torah. As Sohlberg stressed, enforcement applies because they have not complied with a legal obligation to report for service.
Nor did the court create the haredi draft crisis; the Knesset preserved the duty to enlist and then attempted to switch off its enforcement for one group.

Lebanese Sunni MP Fouad Makhzoumi: Lebanon can sign Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:33 UTC
21:47:33 KST

Lebanon can join the Abraham Accords once Hezbollah is disarmed and can no longer use the country as a “launching pad” for attacks against Israel, Lebanese Sunni MP Fouad Makhzoumi told Middle East 24 last week.
Makhzoumi, who has previously urged the Lebanese military to demonstrate its willingness to confront Hezbollah’s arms trafficking by establishing a checkpoint in Beirut’s Dahieh neighborhood, said diplomatic relations and trade with Israel would be possible once “our side, as Lebanese, disarms the militias.”
As it stands, he said, Lebanon has a border that is outside the state’s control, allowing arms to be smuggled into and out of the country.
“I don't see any reason why we cannot sign peace with Israel,” Makhzoumi said, adding that it was possible for Lebanon to “achieve” membership in the Abraham Accords.
The CEO and executive chairman of Future Pipe Industries, a major international conglomerate, and the founder and leader of Lebanon’s National Dialogue Party, he framed Lebanon’s economic recovery and future growth as depending on the state’s ability to tackle corruption within the judicial system and dismantle Hezbollah’s “parallel state.”
Lebanon's central bank to conduct audit of transactions
Lebanon scored 23 out of 100 on Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 153 out of 182 countries.
Makhzoumi’s comments also came the same week that Lebanon’s central bank announced that France-based consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal would conduct an audit of transactions dating from October 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023.
For Makhzoumi, restoring investor confidence requires more than financial reforms. He argued that capital will not flow into Lebanon until there is a regulatory framework that is fairly applied to every investor, one military force representing the country and one law applied equally to all.
Achieving those conditions, he said, requires Lebanon to disarm Hezbollah, “make sure that there is no opportunity for somebody to take me to a war under ideological reasons,” establish a strong banking system that complies with international regulations, and “have peace with Israel.”
Such a shift could also open the door to greater investment from Lebanon’s regional partners. Notably, the United Arab Emirates, a signatory to the Abraham Accords, has become a major investor in Lebanon. UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi led a delegation of more than 80 prominent figures to Lebanon last month, where the two countries signed an intergovernmental memorandum of understanding aimed at strengthening bilateral relations.
Regional analysts who spoke with The Jerusalem Post suggested that increased UAE investment could help Beirut distance itself from Iran and Hezbollah.
Makhzoumi said he is already in discussions with individuals interested in investing in southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has created economic and social dependency by filling gaps in employment, healthcare and education.
Makhzoumi attempts to bring Lebanon's wealthy diaspora home
New investment, he argued, could encourage members of Lebanon’s wealthy diaspora to return.
“I myself operate in 50 countries, and wherever you go in the world, you find a Lebanese that has been successful, whether in a big corporation, or in a state, or in an advisory role,” he said. “So I am confident that the Lebanese will be willing to come and to build their country, but give me a state, give me a place that I can afford to bring my children back, and to make sure that they can live happily under the law, and not to be threatened by Hezbollah or by any other militia.”
The lack of economic and political stability has driven many young Lebanese to seek opportunities abroad, Makhzoumi said. Many leave the country after graduating because they cannot envision a future in a country where assassinations occur, the threat of war remains, and Hezbollah can threaten their security.
That emigration has accelerated amid Lebanon’s prolonged economic crisis, which began in 2019. According to figures published by the American University of Beirut, emigration increased by 450% in 2021 and 2022, with around 79,134 Lebanese citizens leaving the country in 2021 alone. The trend left a giant gap in numerous industries, especially in the healthcare sector.

Hapoel Tel Aviv dominates Beitar Jerusalem as Barda’s squad earns Premier League home victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:18 UTC
21:47:18 KST

Hapoel Tel Aviv cruised past Beitar Jerusalem 3-0 in Israel Premier League action as Roi Alkukin scored in the first half, while Douglas Owusu and Daniel Dappa added goals after the break to give Eliyaniv Barda’s squad a convincing victory in front of its home crowd at Bloomfield Stadium.
The match turned decisively in Hapoel’s favor when Beitar defender Luka Gadrani was sent off, leaving the yellow-and-black with a numerical disadvantage for the remainder of the contest.
Beitar owner Barak Abramov acknowledged that his club has endured a difficult opening to the season but said there would be no panic following the defeat.
“I’m here after a game, which I normally don’t do, but it’s important for me to be here during the tough times,” Abramov said. “We have a good squad and we are only in the second round of games, so I’m not going to even look at the issues that we are having. We are looking for the right player and we won’t bring in a player that doesn’t upgrade the club.
“We want to bring in a No. 6, a midfielder, and I’m sure we will find one as well. I’m not here to tell you any stories. We are just not playing well right now, and that is something that a football club goes through. There won’t be any type of earthquake prior to the next game against Bnei Sakhnin.”
Hapoel coach Barda was pleased with his team’s performance but warned that expectations have now risen.
“I don’t think that we can use the word ‘easy’ for this win, but the players were ready and we did things right in the first half,” Barda said. “After Beitar had a player sent off, it took us a bit of time to get into the swing of things, but we did and finished off the game back at Bloomfield Stadium in front of our fans for the first time in quite a while.
“The players were very happy about the win, but we now have to prepare for the game against Hapoel Ramat Gan. There are now much more expectations on our team, and we have an even higher standard that we have to meet.”
Hapoel Beersheba, Haifa played 2-2
Meanwhile, Hapoel Beersheba and Hapoel Haifa played to an entertaining 2-2 draw at Turner Stadium as Naor Sabag’s penalty deep into second-half stoppage time earned the Carmel Reds a share of the points.
Ron Kozuk’s Beersheba side started strongly, creating a number of chances in and around the box. Its pressure finally paid off in the 24th minute when Eliel Peretz scored from outside the box to give the hosts a 1-0 lead.
Hapoel Haifa, however, responded with a goal-of-the-season candidate from Alon Turgeman, who sent a spectacular volley past Ofir Marciano to level the score. Javon East then headed Beersheba back in front, but the hosts could not hold on.
In the dying moments, a handball by João Victor inside the box gave Haifa a penalty, which Sabag converted to secure a point for the visitors.
Kozuk was frustrated by the late concession but remained confident in his squad.
“Hapoel Beersheba are Hapoel Beersheba because of their philosophy, and if, in the final minutes, we sit back like cowards, that’s not who we are,” Kozuk said. “The first half was tremendous. We have to do what the coach asks. I attribute this to everyone who was on the pitch, including the coach.
“Against Maccabi Tel Aviv, we’ll need to do what we did for 94 minutes. We’ll have a squad that is good enough in terms of quality for the season in Europe, and we’ll try to keep this squad healthy.”
Maccabi Haifa also secured three points, slipping past Hapoel Petah Tikva 2-1 thanks to a late stunner from Bruninho.
After a goalless first half, Andrija Novakovich headed the Greens into the lead, but Boni Amian equalized for the visitors.
With the game winding down, Bruninho unleashed a powerful strike into the back of the net to give Maccabi Haifa the victory.
Still has work to do
Haifa’s Barak Bachar was pleased with the result but knows his team still has work to do.
“The most important thing is to win, and that’s what we did,” Bachar said. “It wasn’t perfect and we have plenty of work to do, but we did what we needed to. We controlled the game and came away with the result.
“We saw a lot of good things from a number of players, but we need to get more players involved. We saw Bruninho, who was great again, and that has to influence the others.”
Hapoel Jerusalem recorded its first victory of the season, defeating Ironi Kiryat Shmona 4-2 as Andrew Idoko scored twice in the second half to lead the capital-city Reds to the win.
Niv Gabbay gave Kiryat Shmona the lead after capitalizing on a brutal defensive error by Jerusalem captain Omer Agvadish. Christ Tiehi equalized early in the second half, but Ariel Sheratzky restored Kiryat Shmona’s advantage in the 56th minute.
Just seconds later, Idoko scored his first goal of the afternoon to make it 2-2. From there, Lior Zada’s side took control, with Abdulsalam Sani putting Jerusalem ahead before Idoko completed his brace to seal the victory.
“This game was a roller coaster, a scandal and a festival,” Zada said. “We came back well with a lot of character, and there are things we need to fix. The substitutes came on well, bringing a lot of energy and momentum.
“The quick goal in the second half helped us, and even when we conceded, we quickly came back to make it 2-2. Our attacking play was pretty good, but you can’t say the same about the defense.”
Ironi Tiberias also earned three points, defeating Maccabi Petah Tikva 2-1 despite playing with 10 men for more than an hour.
Nene Gbamble gave Tiberias an early lead, but Bar Cohen was sent off in the 27th minute following a reckless foul.
Maccabi Petah Tikva took advantage of the numerical advantage, with Jose Cortes equalizing for Ziv Arie’s side.
However, Ironi Tiberias refused to fold, and Chris Kouakou set up Ari Cohen, who fired home the winner to complete an impressive victory.
“It’s a weight lifted off our shoulders now that we’ve erased the point deficit that we began the season with,” Tiberias coach Alon Ziv said. “The players put in an incredible display of fighting spirit with 10 men. We played really good football, and there were stages when there was only one team on the pitch.”

Oscar hopes and Eurovision: Cultural challenges Israel faces next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
12:47:16 UTC
21:47:16 KST

In the latest episode of The Jerusalem Playlist, hosts Ezra Taylor and Hannah Brown discuss the biggest stories shaping Israeli culture, from Eurovision’s evolving rules to the films expected to make an impact during Israel’s awards season and at the Venice Film Festival.
The episode opens with Eurovision and the question of whether Bulgaria will be able to host the 2027 competition. Taylor and Brown discuss Netta Barzilai’s role in Israel’s Eurovision history, noting that she was the last Israeli artist to win the competition in 2018.
The hosts examine new Eurovision rules that state a country may become ineligible to host if it is involved in armed conflict, facing a sensitive geopolitical situation, or dealing with circumstances that could affect regional security and stability. While the rule was widely viewed as potentially affecting Israel, Taylor and Brown discuss whether Bulgaria could also face questions after Iran threatened the country over its decision to allow US aircraft to refuel there.
Shifting towards Israeli cinema
The conversation then shifts to Tell Me Everything, an Israeli film by director Moshe Rosenthal that follows a family during the 1980s and 1990s. Hannah Brown explains that the film centers on a young boy who discovers that his father is gay while preparing for his bar mitzvah, during the height of the AIDS epidemic, and explores the fear, confusion, and trauma that follow within the family.
The film has received 16 Ophir Award nominations, with Brown explaining the importance of the awards within Israel’s film industry. The Ophir Awards are considered Israel’s equivalent of the Oscars, and the Best Picture winner becomes Israel’s official submission for consideration in the Academy Awards’ Best International Feature category.
The episode concludes with a look at the Venice Film Festival and Israeli films making their mark on the international stage. Taylor and Brown discuss Nasa, a new film by two of the creators of No Other Land, as well as the broader history of Israeli cinema at Venice, where films have often explored questions of identity, politics and conflict.

Bus crash kills 25, mostly students in Cape Verde

Some 25 people died in a bus crash on Cape Verde's Fogo Island, with most of the victims being young people and teenagers, students from the Curral Grande and Ponta Verde areas on Saturday, according to local reports and officials.
