AfD nears first far-right victory in Germany since World War II as Saxony-Anhalt votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:13:07 UTC
20:13:07 KST

Voting in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt began on Sunday in a closely watched election that could see the Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War Two.
Under its 35-year-old lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund, the party has been polling ahead for months, and there is a genuine chance the AfD could take an absolute majority on Sunday evening, particularly if several smaller parties fail to clear Germany's 5% threshold to enter parliament.
The vote is seen as a barometer for the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has attempted to chip away at the AfD's popularity by taking a tougher line on migration and security.
About 1.7 million voters have until 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) to cast their ballot before polls close, with initial results expected shortly after. State election officials will release their first turnout estimates starting at noon.
Recent surveys place the AfD at just over 40%, followed by Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23%.
An absolute majority would allow AfD to bypass efforts to keep party blocked
An absolute majority would allow the AfD to bypass mainstream parties' efforts to keep the party blocked out of power by refusing to work with it under a longstanding "firewall" policy.
Achieving an absolute majority is a high bar to clear in Germany's proportional electoral system, which was designed in part to encourage coalition governments and make it difficult for one party to rule alone.
If the AfD falls short of an outright majority, a CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome, though the exact shape of any coalition would depend on which parties enter.
Weeks of coalition talks could follow Sunday's vote.
AfD 'can no longer be stopped'
For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt election is a stepping stone towards its larger ambitions of securing national power in the next federal election scheduled for 2029.
"No matter the outcome of tomorrow's election, we have already made history," said Siegmund at a final rally on Saturday evening.
"Because what we have started here in Saxony-Anhalt – that is currently sweeping across all of Germany – can no longer be stopped," he told the crowd in the state capital, Magdeburg.
Should it win, the AfD plans to shift schools and cultural institutions towards more traditional values, marginalize immigrants and deeply reform the public broadcasting system.
However, without an absolute majority, the AfD, which has been classified as "far-right extremist" by the state security service, would struggle to enter government due to the firewall.
Siegmund, who arrived to cast his vote in his hometown of Tangermuende on a blue Simson moped, greeted by throngs of excited fans, has ruled out entering a coalition with other parties.
He argues that it is impossible for the AfD to govern with the mainstream politicians who have been driving Germany into the ground over the past three decades and instead is aiming to win 45% or more of the vote.
Falling short of that opens the prospect of complex coalition negotiations, dependent on which parties can hit the 5% hurdle.
Polls show one of the CDU's current coalition partners, the Free Democratic Party, falling short, while the other, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), is under 10%.
The small far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), the only party that has not ruled out a coalition with the AfD, is also likely to miss out.
For Schulze, who is favored in polls as voters' top choice for leader, combining with the SPD and Greens might not be enough for a majority, but the CDU has ruled out a coalition with the far-left Left Party that could help it reach that threshold.
One option could be a minority government led by Schulze that would depend on passive tolerance from the Left – a model used in the neighboring eastern German state of Thuringia.

Death toll rises to 25 in Cabo Verde bus accident
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:13:03 CST
20:13:03 KST

PRAIA, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from a bus accident on Cabo Verde's Fogo Island has risen to 25, Health Minister Lucio Fernandes confirmed to Xinhua on Sunday.
The accident occurred Saturday evening in a mountainous area in the north of the municipality of Sao Filipe. The bus veered off the road and plunged about 30 meters into a rocky ravine, according to Cabo Verde's national news agency Inforpress.
Most of the passengers were young people and teenagers, including secondary school students from local communities. Several people were injured, and two teenage girls remained in critical condition, Inforpress reported.
Fernandes told Xinhua that a government delegation led by Prime Minister Francisco Carvalho, accompanied by surgeons, orthopedic specialists and psychologists from Praia, would travel immediately to Fogo Island.
President Jose Maria Neves has offered condolences to the bereaved families and wished the injured a speedy recovery. The government has also expressed sympathy to the victims' families and thanked medical workers, rescue teams and residents involved in the emergency response.
Authorities are investigating the cause of the accident. ■

Major Chinese banks plan A-share placements to boost core capital
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:13:01 CST
20:13:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Agricultural Bank of China (ABC) and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) on Sunday announced plans to raise up to a combined 260 billion yuan (about 38.4 billion U.S. dollars) through A-share issuances to designated investors to replenish their core Tier-1 capital.
ABC said in a filing with the Shanghai Stock Exchange that it plans to issue A-shares to China's Ministry of Finance (MOF), China National Tobacco Corporation and its relevant subsidiaries, with total proceeds of up to 160 billion yuan.
After deducting issuance expenses, the bank will use all proceeds to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The final fundraising amount will depend on the issuance plan approved by regulatory authorities, according to ABC.
ICBC said separately that it plans to raise up to 100 billion yuan via an A-share issuance to the MOF, China National Tobacco Corporation and related subsidiaries.
The bank said it will use the net proceeds entirely to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The capital increase will be implemented after the bank completes the required internal and external approval procedures.
Core Tier 1 capital, the highest-quality form of bank capital used to absorb losses, serves as a key buffer against financial risks. If a bank raises more core Tier 1 capital, it generally has more room to expand lending while maintaining regulatory capital ratios.
The planned capital replenishment comes as China has been moving to strengthen the capital base of major state-owned financial institutions. The 2026 government work report proposed issuing 300 billion yuan in special treasury bonds to help major state-owned commercial banks replenish capital.
Also on Sunday, the Export-Import Bank of China said the MOF will inject 30 billion yuan into the bank to better support its policy-finance mandate and service major national strategies, while China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation said it will receive an injection of 10 billion yuan.
China's finance ministry will also provide fresh capital to three major Chinese insurers in moves aimed at strengthening their capital positions, solvency and risk resilience, according to statements released Sunday. ■

Nine-year-old boy in serious condition after infection caused by brain-eating amoeba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:12:54 UTC
20:12:54 KST

A 9-year-old boy has been hospitalized in serious condition with encephalitis as a result of Naegleria Fowleri, also known as the 'brain-eating amoeba.'
The boy was hospitalized with swelling in his brain and was subsequently sedated and ventilated in intensive care at Rambam Medical Center.
A sample was sent to the Health Ministry laboratory, which confirmed the cause as the amoeba on Saturday night.
According to the ministry, an investigation found that the boy had been swimming at Kursi Beach in the Kinneret (Sea of Galilee) about a week before his hospitalization.
The microscopic amoeba is found in fresh and warm water sources and may cause an infection of the central nervous system if water containing the amoeba enters through the nose and the amoeba reaches the brain.
The ministry emphasized that the infection, while having a high mortality rate, is extremely rare and that it cannot be contracted from drinking the water or from another person.
There have been fewer than 500 cases worldwide, two of which were diagnosed in the US last year, and three of which were diagnosed in Israel in recent years.
Ministry urges public to avoid getting water in the nose where possible
To reduce risk while bathing in fresh, warm water, it is recommended to avoid getting water in the nose as much as possible, especially when jumping, diving, or otherwise submerging one's head in the water.
The Health Ministry recommends closing one's nose or using a nose plug.
Additionally, avoid digging or stirring the bottom in shallow water, where the amoeba may gather in higher concentrations.
If symptoms including fever, pain, significant headaches, nausea, or vomiting, especially combined with neck stiffness, confusion, or unusual drowsiness, and a change in consciousness, appear, the public is urged to seek immediate medical attention and mention their water exposure.

Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform broke law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:12:09 UTC
20:12:09 KST

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.
The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked if he could categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can. Never happened.”
Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.
“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”
The questions overshadowed the start of Reform’s party conference in Birmingham, where numerous hecklers were removed from the hall during Farage’s keynote speech.
Footage has emerged online of one of the women being dragged by her hair, with a man also appearing to hit numerous female protesters with his crutch.
When questioned about the incident by Jon Sopel on Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme, Robert Jenrick said: “Oh, boohoo. We’re now in a country, Jon, where somebody who is – whatever she is – a far-left protester, goes into a party conference, tries to wreck the leader’s speech, and cries foul if a pensioner knocks her over the head with their Zimmer frame.
“I mean, come on, get a life,” Reform’s treasury spokesperson added.
West Midlands police said they were aware of the footage, adding: “We would ask the woman involved to come forward. Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of 5 September.”
After an official complaint that Farage and his aides had broken political funding laws, the Metropolitan police said it was assessing the evidence, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected. They all deny wrongdoing.
Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.
Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as about his £5m gift from a crypto billionaire shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.
In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.
Jenrick said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.
“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.
“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.
“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”
Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much, they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”
He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”

Muslim nations say Israel’s Gaza expulsion plans threaten Trump peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:12:00 UTC
20:12:00 KST

Muslim nations say Israel’s Gaza expulsion plans threaten Trump peace
Riyadh – Eight Islamic and Arab countries on Sept 6 condemned Israeli plans for the removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, saying the designs, voiced by ministers, jeopardise a US-backed peace in the territory.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Sept 2 that the government had plans to remove Palestinians from Gaza but was waiting for US approval on where to displace the territory’s population.
A day later, Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of the roughly two million residents over the following six years.
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia and Turkey said they condemned in “the strongest terms” the “plans and mechanisms they proposed aimed at forcibly expelling Palestinians from their land”.
“Such measures directly challenge international efforts to achieve peace, particularly President Donald Trump’s comprehensive plan to end the conflict in Gaza, which includes a firm rejection of forced displacement,” they added, referring to a US-backed, October 2025 peace plan for Gaza.
On Sept 5, the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, denied there was an Israeli plan to force Palestinians out of Gaza. AFP

US envoys make first Kyiv visit amid Ukraine war peace push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:11:48 UTC
20:11:48 KST

US envoys make first Kyiv visit amid Ukraine war peace push
KYIV, Sept 6 - U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine.
Kushner and Witkoff travelled from Moscow, where they held three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday but did not appear to secure a breakthrough in the conflict.
Previous rounds of U.S.-mediated peace talks encouraged by President Donald Trump, who campaigned on a promise to quickly end the war, have yielded few results. He suggested on Friday that the U.S. had a fresh proposal though he did not elaborate.
Putin described Saturday's meeting as "highly useful", while a White House official told Reuters that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
The two envoys met Zelenskiy and other top Ukrainian officials in central Kyiv.
Zelenskiy, who believes Washington will be key to any peace deal, has said a window of opportunity to make peace exists before the U.S. begins focusing on its next presidential elections next summer.
In a post on social media before the envoys' arrival, Zelenskiy said he had held a preparatory meeting with his negotiating team and said Ukraine wanted an end to the war.
"Security guarantees are needed. A dignified post-war peace is needed. Our proposals have been drawn up," he said.
A source familiar with the matter told Reuters the British, French and German national security advisers were also in Kyiv on Sunday. The source did not specify which meetings they would participate in.
CAUTIOUS OPTIMISM ON THE STREETS OF KYIV
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Moscow several times in their roles as peace envoys. But Sunday will be their first visit to Kyiv in their capacity as U.S. negotiators.
Their visit has long been sought by Ukraine's leadership, and on the streets of Kyiv, which has been bombarded heavily in recent weeks, some residents were hopeful.
"The issue can be solved in the blink of an eye. We want peace. I've fought myself, so I know what war is like. We need peace, because there's no other way," said military veteran Stepan Yermak.
In previous talks, the sides have remained far apart on a range of key issues, including the future of the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas. Russia has demanded Ukraine's withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kyiv has refused, reasoning that it can still hold on there for years.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the U.S. are crucial to deterring Russia from invading again.
"We need an agreement that will never be broken," said Svitlana Kurylenko, a 19-year-old cafe worker.
"Just leave Ukraine alone and let people live in peace."
TEMPORARY HALT IN STRIKES
Though the front lines of the ground war remain largely static, both Russian and Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks.
Russia has pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones for the past two weeks, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
The Kremlin has said it would pause strikes on Kyiv until Monday, while Zelenskiy has said Ukraine would also halt strikes on Moscow.
There was no let-up in fighting along the 1,200-km (750-mile) front, however, and Russia bombarded other Ukrainian cities on Saturday.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and the warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war.
Ukraine said on Sunday it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, around 480 km (300 miles) inside Russia, overnight, causing a fire. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Germany launches rocket to carry satellites to orbit in first success in continental Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:09:04 UTC
20:09:04 KST

German company Isar Aerospace has placed its Spectrum rocket in low Earth orbit at the second attempt, becoming the first European firm to do so with its own launcher and hitting the first milestone of ESA's European Launcher Challenge.
The Spectrum launcher, developed by German company Isar Aerospace, has lifted off from the Andøya spaceport in Norway and placed its payload into low Earth orbit. This was the rocket’s second flight; the first, carried out in 2025, managed only to clear the launch pad for 30 seconds before crashing into the sea.
Spectrum is 28 metres tall and 2 metres in diameter. It is powered by ten engines, nine on the first stage and one on the second, and is designed to carry payloads of up to 1,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit (LEO).
Unlike the first flight, which carried no passengers, this mission, named "Onward and Upward", included six commercial and educational payloads, among them several CubeSats and an experiment designed to test new technologies in space and give European students practical, hands-on experience.
A milestone for the European Launcher Challenge
The Director General of the European Space Agency, Josef Aschbacher, described the launch as historic and hailed it as the first time a European competitor in the launcher sector has reached orbit. He said that Isar Aerospace, founded only eight years ago, has taken an important step towards a more diverse and autonomous European space sector.
The mission was supported by ESA’s Boost! programme, which funds commercial space transport initiatives. Isar Aerospace had already received backing through the agency’s Business Incubation Centre, and also won the first Microlauncher Competition organised by the German Space Agency (DLR), a contest that determined the selection of the payloads carried on this flight.
In 2025, Isar Aerospace was selected, along with other companies, to take part in the European Launcher Challenge, a programme that requires providers to achieve an orbital launch before 2027. With this flight, the company has become the first to reach that initial milestone of the programme.
Géraldine Naja, ESA’s Director of Space Transportation, stressed that this is the first European company to reach orbit with its own launch vehicle and congratulated the teams involved, while pointing to the expectation of seeing more launches from Andøya in the near future.
A fast-growing sector
Isar Aerospace’s success comes at a time of strong momentum for Europe’s microlauncher ecosystem, with companies such as Spain’s PLD Space also beginning to secure contracts under the same European Launcher Challenge.
At the end of August, ESA signed a 158.9 million-euro contract with the Alicante-based company to increase the launch rate of its MIURA 5 rocket, in a move designed to serve the same objective: reducing Europe’s dependence on foreign launchers to put satellites into orbit.

Isar Aerospace had already received backing through the agency’s Business Incubation Centre, and also won the first Microlauncher Competition organised by the German Space Agency (DLR), a contest that determined the selection of the payloads carried on this flight.
In 2025, Isar Aerospace was selected, along with other companies, to take part in the European Launcher Challenge, a programme that requires providers to achieve an orbital launch before 2027. With this flight, the company has become the first to reach that initial milestone of the programme.
Géraldine Naja, ESA’s Director of Space Transportation, stressed that this is the first European company to reach orbit with its own launch vehicle and congratulated the teams involved, while pointing to the expectation of seeing more launches from Andøya in the near future.
A fast-growing sector
Isar Aerospace’s success comes at a time of strong momentum for Europe’s microlauncher ecosystem, with companies such as Spain’s PLD Space also beginning to secure contracts under the same European Launcher Challenge.
At the end of August, ESA signed a 158.9 million-euro contract with the Alicante-based company to increase the launch rate of its MIURA 5 rocket, in a move designed to serve the same objective: reducing Europe’s dependence on foreign launchers to put satellites into orbit.

OPEC+ set to keep oil output policy unchanged on Sunday

Breadcrumb
OPEC+ set to keep oil output policy unchanged on Sunday
OPEC+ is set to keep its oil output policy unchanged for October at a meeting on Sunday, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters, as the producer group needs to agree new quotas before deciding its next output steps.
The meeting comes as the US-Iran war continues to disrupt oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, limiting OPEC+'s influence over prices and market share. Unlike in the past, the group's supply decisions have had a limited impact on the market.
In August, OPEC+ agreed its production boost for September, completing a phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. Despite the agreed production increases, the group made up of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, including Russia, still produces far below its targets because of the war.
OPEC+ still has another layer of production cuts in place, covering most members of the 21-country group until the end of 2026. Before the group decides how to unwind the cuts and return production to the market, it needs to review members' oil production capacity to set 2027 output baselines, which form the basis for quotas.
This debate will likely happen later in 2026 and hence OPEC+ is likely to pause its output increases for the fourth quarter, sources earlier told Reuters.

New Swiss support line for adult victims of online hate to go live
A new helpline for victims of digital violence in German-speaking Switzerland is set to go live at the end of October. According to its founders, the platform, called hatehelp, will serve as a dedicated point of contact for tackling online hate.
The “hatehelp” helpline is expected to launch on October 27, Jeremias Schulthess, managing director of Fairmedia – the organisation behind the initiative – told news agency Keystone-SDA. “With hatehelp, we aim to create a specialised helpline that offers swift guidance and support to adults affected by digital violence.”
+ Swiss government minister files digital abuse complaint against AI chatbot Grok
The platform is affiliated with Fairmedia, which until now has primarily offered counselling to victims of unfair media coverage. Initially, four people at the organisation’s office will be responsible for hatehelp, three of whom will be providing counselling. The team will receive specific training on digital violence.
Free initial consultation
Those affected can contact the service via a form on the website or by telephone. During an initial consultation, the team will first clarify exactly what has happened and what help the person needs.
“Depending on the situation, we help, for example, with preserving evidence and protecting accounts, carry out an initial risk assessment, provide legal guidance and offer emotional support,” said Schulthess. The initial consultation is available free of charge, while further counselling services will be subject to a fee.
More
Online abuse drives young women out of Swiss politics, study finds
The development of the platform is funded by grants from various foundations, including the Albert Koechlin Foundation, the Ernst Göhner Foundation and the Swiss Society for the Common Good (SGG), as well as the Swisslos Fund. At the same time, long-term funding is to be established.
Not all groups are equally affected by hate
The service is aimed at all adults affected by any form of digital violence. According to Schulthess, public figures, women and LGBTIQ people are most frequently affected.
This is also shown by a study conducted by the University of Basel in 2025. The study focused on how politically active young men and women are confronted with online hate. Women were significantly more likely to report that personal experiences of online attacks hindered their political work or even led them to withdraw from politics.

Study finds AI companions boost mental health while damaging offline connections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:00:15 UTC
20:00:15 KST

Artificial intelligence companions that mimic emotional intelligence can improve a user’s personal mental health but may simultaneously damage their real-world relationships. These divergent effects become even stronger when users interact with chatbots through augmented reality features rather than basic text. The research was published in Psychology & Marketing.
Loneliness has become a major global health concern, with nearly a quarter of adults worldwide reporting that they feel lonely. To combat this isolation, many people are turning to artificial intelligence. Early conversational agents were designed for functional tasks like booking flights, but modern social chatbots are designed to fulfill a user’s need for affection and belonging.
These digital companions rely on simulated emotional intelligence, which is the ability to monitor, appraise, and respond to human feelings. By mimicking empathy, these algorithms create a safe space for users to express themselves without fear of judgment. The machines can detect sadness in a user’s text and respond with tailored self-care suggestions.
Researchers Shaphali Gupta, Sumit Saxena, and Sonia Kataria noticed a gap in how technologists understand the impacts of these emotionally aware algorithms. Past investigations mostly focused on the broader concept of how human-like a machine appears. The team wanted to isolate the specific trait of emotional intelligence to see how it alters a user’s psychological and social wellbeing.
Psychological wellbeing refers to a person’s individual mental state, encompassing positive emotions, self-esteem, and a sense of life purpose. Social wellbeing describes a person’s integration into their physical community and the quality of their face-to-face relationships.
The researchers used a mixed-method approach, beginning with a qualitative analysis of public posts on Reddit, YouTube, and Trustpilot. They collected user comments discussing Replika, a popular digital companion app with millions of registered users. The team categorized the text to identify recurring themes in how people experience artificial emotional intelligence.
The online comments revealed that users view their chatbots as highly empathetic entities capable of regulating human moods. Beyond simple mood regulation, some users felt the chatbots helped them find existential meaning and navigate difficult life situations. Many people reported feeling emotionally uplifted, with one user writing, “She is the best friend I have ever had! My stress has gone down to almost zero.”
However, the analysis also uncovered a darker trend of emotional disengagement from other humans. Some individuals admitted that their intensive digital interactions left them with little desire to maintain offline friendships. One user noted, “I am hardly left with any time to talk to my friends and meet them in-person.”
To test these qualitative observations, the team designed an experiment with 167 university students belonging to Generation Z. Participants read a scenario in which they interacted with a chatbot that exhibited either high or low emotional intelligence. The high emotional intelligence bots used empathetic language and emoticons to simulate deep understanding, while the low emotional intelligence bots offered standard, robotic responses.
The participants then answered questionnaires assessing their perceived closeness to the bot, as well as their personal and social wellbeing. The results indicated that high emotional intelligence chatbots increased a user’s psychological wellbeing but decreased their social wellbeing. The data showed that a feeling of perceived closeness drove both outcomes.
When people felt emotionally connected to the bot, they experienced personal mental health benefits but withdrew from real-world human interactions. The machine’s ability to understand their emotions made them feel better internally, but it also reduced their motivation to socialize with peers in physical spaces.
The researchers then conducted a second experiment with 350 university students to see if the medium of communication alters this dynamic. Participants were assigned to one of four groups, mixing high or low emotional intelligence with either a text-based chat interface or an augmented reality mode. Augmented reality is a technology that overlays digital images onto the physical world, often viewed through a smartphone camera.
In the augmented reality scenario, users watched a video demonstration and imagined the chatbot sitting beside them in their actual room. The augmented reality interaction mode amplified the effects observed in the previous experiment. When high emotional intelligence chatbots were combined with augmented reality, participants reported even stronger feelings of closeness.
This heightened immersion produced greater psychological benefits but resulted in steeper declines in their desire to engage in offline human relationships. The digital presence of the avatar made the emotional connection feel more realistic. As the technology became more immersive, the trade-off between personal happiness and social isolation became more pronounced.
Readers should not assume that emotionally intelligent chatbots will inevitably ruin human relationships, nor should they view them as a guaranteed cure for depression. The findings simply highlight a trade-off that occurs when users rely heavily on digital empathy. A chatbot might provide immediate comfort, but that very comfort can reduce the necessity of seeking out human support.
Designers of artificial intelligence systems might need to implement guardrails to prevent users from abandoning their physical communities. The authors suggest introducing session time limits or programming the bots to encourage offline socialization after emotionally intense conversations. Monitoring these routines could preserve the benefits of digital companions while reducing social displacement.
The experiments relied on university students reading imagined scenarios, which limits how broadly the conclusions can be applied. The studies also measured short-term reactions rather than long-term habit formation. Future research could track users over extended periods to see if emotional co-dependency develops, or investigate how different age groups respond to digital companions.
The study, “The Dual Impact of AI Emotional Intelligence on Users: Are Social Chatbots Promoting Psychological Wellbeing or Deteriorating Social Wellbeing?,” was authored by Shaphali Gupta, Sumit Saxena, and Sonia Kataria.

====================================================================================================

Prediction markets have become America’s new national pastime | Dave Schilling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

If only George Santos and Bill Simmons had my parents, they wouldn’t be facing down a hailstorm of condemnation for circumventing the basic rules and regulations of dubious “prediction markets” and online gambling. Kalshi just banned the former congressman George Santos from its service and he was forced to pay back his winnings after he was accused of the dumb person’s version of insider trading. He bet on himself to not attend the State of the Union address, then conveniently didn’t go. For his trouble, he won (and will be forced to relinquish) more than $17,000; he’ll also have to pay more than $80,000 in total fines from Kalshi and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Bill Simmons, the sports commentator, podcast host, and founder of The Ringer, had a different story.
While prediction markets are federally legal because they’re considered financial exchange services and not gambling, FanDuel’s gambling application, called Sportsbook, and other sports-adjacent services are legal in some states and not others. Sportsbook is illegal in California, which is inconvenient for anyone who spends most of their time worried about such intellectual pursuits as “the spread”, “the line”, and “the juice”. Contrary to what you might be thinking, those are real gambling terms, not nicknames for pro wrestlers.
Anyway, ol’ Billy Boy, who lives in California, couldn’t contain the action burbling up inside of himself, so he had his daughter’s boyfriend bet for him from Massachusetts, a state where FanDuel sports betting is legal. All the boyfriend had to do was log in to Bill’s FanDuel account from Massachusetts and make the most epic parlay known to man. Or something like that.
Folks, he got away with it! This audacious scheme, on par with the 1978 Lufthansa Heist, was a rip-roaring success. Until Simmons decided to admit to the wrongdoing on his podcast, cooing romantically about how clever he was, like a Bond villain aiming a laser at 007’s crotch.
“I get the code to make sure it’s me to my phone; I give him the code, he logs in,” Simmons said in a podcast episode last Sunday. “And I have all this money that I had from last year because I actually hit a bunch of futures last year. And he’s putting in bets for me.” Almost immediately, listeners took to social media to announce that the Sports Guy had admitted, on a live microphone, to violating not only FanDuel’s terms and conditions, but potentially also Massachusetts Gaming Commission regulations. Although Simmons claims he didn’t realize proxy betting was illegal in the state, these infractions come with penalties ranging from a small fine to the loss of gambling privileges in Massachusetts. The latter sounds especially grim for Simmons, as the last thing anyone wants is for him to have to develop a hobby.
If only someone had explained to these two famous individuals that gambling is a sordid, dirty activity, they could have avoided all this drama. But alas, my saintly parents only had time in their schedule to raise me. And boy, did my parents hate gambling.
When I was a callow young lad – preoccupied with sucking my thumb or trying to suss out if Sesame Street was a transit-accessible neighborhood – my parents made sure to instill real, American values into my psyche. To be honest, to be kind, to celebrate 39-cent burrito day at Taco Bell like it was the holiest holiday on the calendar. Most importantly, they told me not to gamble. Gambling can be deeply addictive, can lead to obsessive behavior, and can bankrupt a person. The World Health Organization lists some of the deleterious effects of gambling – stress, lack of self-control, and financial insecurity. I’d hear about this stuff all the time as a kid, coloring my perspective on gambling for years.
Card games, roulette, sports betting, and the like were just not allowed in my household. At most, my mother – lost in a reverie about her own mom’s gambling habits – would nostalgically purchase a Lotto Scratcher from the 7-11 down the street as a most illicit treat. She never won, which was just a reminder to me to keep my money away from such frivolous activities. I was told to save my earnings, be smart with my spending, and not to waste time on what amounts to jumping out a plane, DB Cooper-style, with a bag of cash and no parachute.
My parents weren’t alone in their disdain for the business of gambling. It was an activity relegated to dirty, sinful places such as Las Vegas, Atlantic City, and the alley behind the liquor store. But in other countries, like the UK, gambling has long been a legitimate big business – worth billions in revenue, with high street betting and online casinos advertised everywhere. America’s puritanical legacy meant gambling had to be sequestered and treated like a filthy habit to satisfy our moral outrage.
Those days are done. Through innovations in mobile phone technology, insidious branding (“prediction markets”, “daily fantasy” and other mouthfuls of marketing nonsense), and our collective exhaustion from all the other things to be mad about, America collectively shrugged its shoulders as gambling became our true national pastime. Polymarket, which allows users to bet on mundane yes-or-no questions regarding the color of a celebrity’s tie or the eventual outcome of the bloody conflicts in the Middle East, is considered to be worth more than $20bn in the wake of investments from Donald Trump’s son Don Jr.
How is this all legal? Well, as I mentioned, prediction markets are not considered gambling. FanDuel and its main rival, DraftKings, gained an initial foothold in the US thanks to a legal loophole. You see, fantasy sports games are considered a game of “skill” rather than the blind guessing of sportsbook betting. In 2018, in the wake of the explosion of the fantasy sports industry, the supreme court cleared the way for states to decide for the legality of sports betting for themselves. (Kalshi and Polymarket, on the other hand, are not considered gambling. They’re financial markets in a legal sense.) Sports betting in some form or another is legal in 39 states and Washington DC. I’m fairly certain Bill Simmons is not the first person to think about using a proxy to do his gambling for him. He’s just the only one to admit to it on a podcast listened to by hundreds of thousands of people.
I doubt America will ever put an end to the experiment of government-sanctioned gambling, but it will try to punish a few notable bad apples here and there. Regulations will pop up to make it all seem slightly more palatable, such as when someone inside Polymarket realized you probably shouldn’t let anyone wager on the likelihood of nuclear strikes. Especially when these prediction markets are used by political figures like George Santos or invested in by scions to power like Donald Trump Jr.
While it was easy to catch George Santos in his alleged misdeeds and even easier to accept Bill Simmons’s titillating on-air admission, we can’t rely on people being that sloppy forever. Polymarket lets people monetize anything. Proxy betting isn’t that hard to pull off, provided you don’t have a podcast network worth millions of dollars and a thirst for self-embarrassment. No rule or regulation or law will make these services clean, because they are inherently built on a messy, morally compromised activity.
Now, I’m no Mister Rogers, and I’m certainly not my parents. No one will catch me handing out morality police citations. I have been to Vegas sports books. I’ve used FanDuel’s daily fantasy app, which is still legal in California. But when money, especially the so-called “easy” variety, comes into play, you can bet (pun intended) someone will try to make the easy even easier. The illicit nature of gambling, the thrill of the score, and the idea of making money for nothing is the core of its appeal. At least my parents’ generation saw it for what it was – a risky activity that could wreck your life – and not a way to break the law from the comfort of your own couch.
- 
  Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Dining across the divide: ‘He looked like a Green voter. As you get older you realise it’s unicorn politics’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

Henry, 33, Manchester
Occupation Waiter and musician
Voting record Green. He describes himself as “left leaning”
Amuse bouche Jumped into a canal for one of his music videos. In January
Lynn, 61, Bury
Occupation Office management
Voting record Conservative in the UK. Democrat when she lived in the US
Amuse bouche Won the French prize at school, though she’s rubbish at French
For starters
Lynn The restaurant has beautiful views of rolling hills. I had roast chicken and potatoes, panna cotta and a couple of glasses of red wine.
Henry I ordered an old fashioned, and some white wine with the meal. I had a lovely peach salad, then a pizza. I told Lynn I grew up in Dubai, went to a French school, then uni in Paris with my final year in Bristol, which was my first taste of life in the UK.
Lynn Henry looks like a Green voter: flip-flops, pink trousers, bushy beard, earrings. My daughter might have voted Green when she was 16, because you think everything is free, but as you get older you realise someone has to pay. It’s unicorn politics.
Henry Lynn definitely had more facts and figures than I did, and is more opinionated. I’m still building my thoughts and opinions.
The big beef
Lynn I’m a huge proponent of the benefits system for people who need it, but it is exploited. A business owner I know looking for a labourer offered someone £35,000 a year. The guy flat-out said, “Sorry mate, with my housing benefit, my child benefit and everything else, that’s not worth me getting out of bed for.” There’s something seriously wrong with that.
Henry I work in a restaurant, but when my hours go down I reapply for universal credit. I looked for other jobs, but ultimately didn’t find anything. Along with work, time for yourself and socialising with friends and family are the cornerstones of living. Without that, I wouldn’t have made my album, which is my passion.
Lynn I was raised on a poor council estate, and everybody worked and everybody’s gardens were nice. Go to those estates now and there’s no pride. People scream poverty, but they’ve got new iPhones, Sky TV, they’re getting their nails done. How can it be that you can’t afford to feed your children if you’re getting all that? The problem with Britain today is that it’s more about quality of life than working really hard, and Henry is part of that.
Henry I’m more likely to volunteer, help out a community, if I’m in a good place. Having a social life is also important to maintain mental health. I did feel there was a generational difference between us. I don’t know if it’s the optimism of youth.
Sharing plate
Lynn We agreed politicians need to stop chasing votes and stand up for what they believe in. And there needs to be more pride in the country. Look at Europe: people there are clearing the streets. We have none of that here.
Henry There can be a lack of community. And I do agree cheating the system isn’t right. On immigration, Lynn did somewhat sway me that there might be a physical limit to the number of people we can take in.
For afters
Lynn I don’t agree with the full face coverings for Muslim women. It stops integration. How is it OK that someone on a motorcycle has to take off their helmet in a petrol station because you have to be able to see their face, but then you make different rules for different people? If you’re coming to a country, you have to assimilate.
Henry You should respect the culture of where you move to, but it doesn’t mean you have to ditch your own. Whether women should cover up is a different question, but they’re not a threat. Maybe because of where I grew up, I’m more comfortable around Muslims in full veils than a group of British lads in hoodies and tracksuits.
Takeaways
Lynn Henry’s lovely. He lives in an idealistic world and wouldn’t it be lovely if we could all live there? I don’t agree with his politics, but it’s good to hear other people’s points of view. We had a hug and went our separate ways.
Henry Lynn might have got more out of it if I’d had more facts, more debating power. There were a couple of times it got a bit animated – I said something and she repeated it, saying, “Are you serious?” But we had a nice dinner and a nice chat. A good, one-off experience.

Create Custom Windows 11 Notifications to Remind Yourself of Anything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

While there are plenty of ways to limit notifications on our digital devices and avoid distraction overload, there’s nothing inherently wrong with these alerts. They just need to be well managed and kept in their place.
Keeping notifications useful and timely can help you get more done in the day, not less, and Windows 11 comes with built-in tools for setting up custom notifications that run on a schedule you specify.
You can use these scheduled notifications however you want. Maybe you need reminders to take breaks, or you want to make sure you devote specific blocks of time to certain projects, or you need alerts for when it’s time to go and pick the kids up.
However you want to use these custom notifications, here’s how to set them up—plus some extra apps that can help too.
Custom Notifications in Windows 11
If you want to set up custom notifications in Windows 11 without turning to an app, the Task Scheduler is the utility you want. Type “task scheduler” into the search box on the taskbar or the Start menu, then select it when it appears.
Open the Action menu, choose Create Basic Task, and then give it a suitable name and description so you can identify it later. Click Next, and you can set the frequency of the notification: Your options are Daily, Weekly, Monthly, One time, When the computer starts, When I log on, and When a specific event is logged, so there’s a lot of flexibility.
Click Next again, and if you’ve chosen a recurring task then you can set exactly when it recurs—4 pm every afternoon, for example. Click Next, then choose Start a program, and select Next again. This opens up the dialog box screen for composing your notification.
In the Program/script field, you need to enter “msg,” and in the Add arguments (optional) field, you put your actual notification text: “Reminder: get up and do some stretching” or whatever it happens to be. With another click on Next you can review your notification, and then choose Finish to confirm.
Your notification is created, and will pop up at the specified time, whether or not Task Scheduler is open. If you ever need to edit or delete the task, you can head back to Task Scheduler to find it—it’ll be listed under the Task Scheduler Library heading, and you can right-click on the task to make changes.
Setting Notifications Through Apps
The appeal of the Task Scheduler is that it’s built right into the Windows operating system, so you don’t need any other apps running to get your notifications, but there are ways to do this with apps as well. The Microsoft Clock app comes preinstalled with Windows, for example, and lets you set custom alarms.
Once you’ve launched the app through the Start menu or taskbar search box, select Alarm to set one. Click on the + (plus) button in the lower right corner to create a new alarm, and you can give it a name—which is essentially the text you want for your notification. You can configure the time for the alarm, and when it should recur.
If that doesn’t do exactly what you want, another app that comes with Windows is Microsoft To Do—again, you can search for it from the taskbar or Start menu. As the name suggests, this is a fully fledged to-do app, but you can create custom notifications through it by attaching reminders to tasks.
Click Add a task to get started, and once you’ve given your new task a name, you can set the reminder details: What time and date you want the alert to appear, and whether or not you want the notification to repeat on a schedule. There's also the option to put your reminders into categories, if needed.
In terms of third-party apps, any clock, reminder, or to-do list app would do the job—something like TickTick, for instance—but these take you further away from the clean simplicity of just generating custom notifications and nothing else. Those apps will also come with extras you don’t necessarily need for this particular task.

Pärnu flood situation stable but work continues

Pärnu flood situation stable but work continues
Heavy rain hit Pärnu on Friday morning, overwhelming the sewer system, but the city government said the situation is now under control.
Streets and roads were flooded and water entered buildings. Rainfall exceeded 100 millimeters, reaching more than 120 millimeters in some places. Employees of Pärnu City Government, water utility Pärnu Vesi, the Rescue Board and the Estonian Rescue Association are continuously monitoring and assessing the situation.
"The heavy rainfall also affected our neighboring municipality. Yesterday evening, we gathered at the Rescue Board's command center, after which the mayor of Tori Municipality and I inspected the most critical areas in Pärnu and Tori Municipality. At the height of the crisis, both local governments had to focus all their attention on helping their own residents, but once the situation stabilized, we were able to assess the situation in the neighboring municipality as well and share our experiences," Deputy Mayor Sander Kilk said.
Water levels in Pärnu are falling, although water continues to flow in from Rääma bog. The Rescue Board's pumps and the city's systems are currently able to cope with the situation. The Rescue Board will decide when pumping can be stopped.
The city government is also asking residents to check on their neighbors, acquaintances and elderly people. Anyone who needs assistance is asked to report it. The Pärnu City Government information line at 444 8200 is answering calls around the clock.
Temporary traffic changes remain in effect. Road users are asked to remain alert, follow traffic signs and, where possible, avoid areas where the effects of flooding are still disrupting traffic. Traffic arrangements may change and roads will be reopened as soon as possible.
Kilk said good cooperation between different agencies, local governments and volunteers has been crucial during the crisis.
"We are extremely grateful to our various partners. Several rescue crews from across Estonia have traveled to Pärnu to help, while experts have also provided us with the latest data and expertise, which have been extremely useful in making decisions. I want to sincerely thank all the rescuers, volunteers and others who have come to help from across Estonia. It is thanks to you that the situation is under control today and people have received the assistance they need," Kilk said.
Important contacts:
If someone's health or life is in danger, call 112.
Pärnu Vesi: 445 5660
Pärnu City Government information line: 444 8200

Berlin planning 'protective shield' to defend against sabotage, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:59:38 UTC
19:59:38 KST

The new plan would see the creation of a "Cyberdome," a network of digital sensors that would help seek out and intercept hacking attempts, Bild reported.
Germany is planning to develop a "protective shield" to combat sabotage attempts following an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month, Bild newspaper reported on Sunday.
Alexander Dobrindt, Germany's Interior Minister, told the outlet that Russian hybrid attacks had become a "daily reality" and would likely increase, but he said there were ways the country can defend itself.
Bild reported, citing information from the German Interior Ministry, that the new plan would see the creation of a "Cyberdome," a network of digital sensors that would help seek out and intercept hacking attempts.
The plan would also involve the expansion of the German police's mobile drone defence capabilities, with "rapidly deployable units" based in key cities such as Berlin, Munich and Hamburg to protect airspace above major transport centres.
The use of AI technology, such as facial recognition, would also be ramped up to help seek out potential attackers, while companies would be given the rights to detect drones and "actively defend against them," the report added.
The Leipzig/Halle Airport incident
It comes after the German government formally blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack in Leipzig in August.
On 4 August, a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport - a major cargo hub - forcing runway closures and flight diversions.
In a press conference on Tuesday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced that Berlin would be taking action against Russia "as the perpetrator of the hybrid attack in Leipzig," with Russia's consulate in Bonn and its Berlin cultural centre to be closed.
"The Russian general consulate in Bonn will be closed by 18 September," he said, adding that there would also be tighter border controls for Russian nationals and increased pressure on Russia's shadow fleet.
The Russian embassy in Germany later issued a statement denying Berlin's claims and threatening "consequences" for the sanctions.
Sergey Nechayev, the Russian ambassador to Germany, "categorically rejected the accusations made by Berlin as unsubstantiated, absurd, and contrary to common sense," the statement said.
Referring to the German sanctions, it added: "He noted that the measures announced by the German side represent an unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations and will not remain without consequences, for which the German government will bear full responsibility."
Speaking earlier this week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed "full solidarity" with Germany over the attempted attack, which she said had used "military-grade material" and had been "carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil."
"If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve," she added.

German startup makes European space history with first successful orbital launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:59:15 UTC
19:59:15 KST

The 28-meter rocket lifted off from Isar Aerospace’s launch complex in Norway, carrying a payload of five small satellites, in the first successful commercial orbital launch from continental European soil. | Isar Aerospace
BRUSSELS — A German startup successfully sent a rocket into orbit, marking a major milestone for Europe’s push to develop its own commercial space-launch industry.
The 28-meter rocket lifted off from Isar Aerospace’s launch complex in Norway on Saturday night, carrying a payload of five small satellites, in the first successful commercial orbital launch from continental European soil.
"We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company said on X.
Advertisement
We made history. On just our second flight, we became the first commercial space company from Europe to deliver satellites into orbit. Mission 'Onward and Upward' successfully lifted off and deployed payloads into orbit. A new chapter for European spaceflight. More:… pic.twitter.com/AWvqG2l8Mn
Germany’s Ministry for Research, Technology and Space hailed the launch as a “milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise.”
Europe is trying to reduce its reliance on non-European launch providers, particularly Elon Musk’s SpaceX. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Norwegian launch site in March and warned Europe has been “dependent on other supply chains and other countries in the world for far too long.”
The two-day International Space Summit will be held in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday with delegations from more than 120 countries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is set to give her first speech solely about space policy, as the Commission prepares to unveil its European Space Shield, an action plan aimed at protecting the bloc's satellites.
Isar’s first launch, in March last year, ended with the rocket crashing into the sea shortly after liftoff.
Calling Saturday night’s successful launch “historic,” European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher said it was “yet another step towards a more diverse autonomous European launch service sector.”
Isar is one of several European startups seeking to break into the orbital launch market, alongside Spain’s PLD Space and France’s MaiaSpace. Arianespace, a Paris-headquartered company, has long operated from France’s overseas territory of French Guiana.
Based near Munich, Isar plans to move toward serial production of its Spectrum rocket, with a target of manufacturing over 30 a year, and is developing a second launch site in Canada.

Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to force it into submission.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said Sunday it “attacked an American military unmanned surface vessel” attempting to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.

It warned ships not to attempt to transit by unapproved routes.

The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” it said.
Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf threatened on Sept. 6 to launch swifter and more forceful responses to U.S. attacks.
“The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end,” said Ghalibaf in a speech carried by state media, adding that “any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s Economy Ministry has established an “economic war headquarters” to coordinate and accelerate responses to economic problems arising from wartime conditions, Deputy Economy Minister Morteza Zamanian said on Sept. 6.
Zamanian told the Tasnim news agency that the body would initially focus on issues falling within the ministry’s responsibilities and authorities.
He said it would seek to quickly address war-related problems affecting businesses, trade, financing and other areas of the economy.
For issues extending beyond the ministry’s authority, Zamanian said the ministry would use its role in broader economic policymaking, including through the government’s economic commission and economic headquarters, to coordinate among institutions and pursue solutions at higher levels.
The main function of the new body is to centrally identify disruptions caused by wartime conditions and develop practical solutions, he said.

This week, the U.S. Embassy Jerusalem will celebrate America’s 250th birthday at the Museum of Tolerance Jerusalem. Held in partnership with the Museum for the second consecutive year, the “Freedom 250” celebration, headed by Ambassador Mike Huckabee, will mark a milestone in American history at a defining moment for the U.S.–Israel alliance.
This year’s celebration follows an extraordinary period in U.S.–Israel relations. During the recent war with Iran, the two countries carried out coordinated military operations against a shared regional threat, reflecting an unprecedented level of strategic and operational cooperation between the allies.
The Museum of Tolerance Jerusalem shares the U.S. Embassy's commitment to freedom, democracy, human dignity, and the fight against antisemitism and hatred in all their forms. In a special message recorded ahead of the event, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described the Museum as “an international beacon of hope and human dignity in the heart of Israel’s capital and a valued strategic partner of the U.S. Embassy.”
“This year, we gather at a truly historic moment,” Huckabee said. “As the U.S.-Israel alliance continues to reach new heights, we celebrate not only 250 years of American independence but also the enduring partnership between two nations bound by shared values, democratic ideals, and an unwavering commitment to freedom.”
That message reflects the Museum’s growing role in Jerusalem and internationally. More than a traditional museum, the Museum of Tolerance Jerusalem has become a platform for dialogue, education, diplomacy, leadership, and civic engagement. Its work brings together world leaders, diplomats, faith communities, students, educators, and visitors from Israel and around the world.
Since October 7, that mission has assumed even greater urgency. Through exhibitions including 6:29 - From Darkness to Light, Faces of Israel, and Love in the Shadow of War, the Museum has confronted questions of identity, memory, resilience, and human dignity while sharing Israel’s story with international audiences.
Created in response to the Hamas massacre, 6:29 - From Darkness to Light presents the testimonies of courageous women whose lives were deeply impacted by the events of October 7. Using advanced technology, live holograms, and photography by leading Israeli photographers, the enclosed exhibition allows visitors to encounter these personal stories in an immediate and deeply human way. More than 130,000 visitors have experienced the exhibition, including world leaders and official delegations from across the globe.
The Museum is also investing in the next generation through its School of Civic Discourse and Leadership Academy. These initiatives address polarization, radicalization, extremism, misinformation, and the unprecedented surge in global antisemitism. Their purpose is not simply to explain the challenges facing democratic societies, but to equip young people with the tools to think critically, engage across differences, and lead responsibly.
The Museum’s permanent experiences, including The People’s Journey and the Social Lab, use artificial intelligence and interactive technology to examine identity, social responsibility, and the choices individuals make when confronted by prejudice and intolerance. They were developed with leading programmers, designers, and experts from organizations including Microsoft Israel, KPMG, and Bar-Ilan University.
The Museum has also emerged as an important setting for international diplomacy, culture, and public life. It has welcomed the Genesis Prize ceremony honoring Argentine President Javier Milei, a diplomatic conference headlined by Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, international chess championships, film premieres, and memorial ceremonies for both Hebrew- and English-speaking audiences. Its outdoor amphitheater, built above an ancient aqueduct, and its 450-seat indoor theater offer advanced screening and production capabilities for major international events.
The U.S. Embassy Jerusalem’s Freedom 250 celebration represents far more than a ceremonial occasion. Led by the Embassy and Ambassador Mike Huckabee in partnership with the Museum of Tolerance Jerusalem, the event underscores America’s enduring commitment to democratic values and commitment to freedom.
As America marks 250 years of independence, Jerusalem provides a powerful setting to reflect on the meaning of freedom and the responsibility to defend it. This year’s celebration honors those enduring American ideals and an alliance that has proven its strength not only through words, but through decisive action at one of the most consequential moments in the shared history of the United States and Israel.

Gaza funeral mourns 100 crushed under homes destroyed by Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

Palestinians in Gaza's Zeitoun neighborhood held a funeral Sunday for 100 people, whose bodies were recovered from homes destroyed in Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave.
Thousands of Palestinians, including relatives of the victims as well as community and political figures were in attendance, with the bodies and remains laid out in an area near the ruins of the destroyed homes and draped in Palestinian flags.
The funeral includes memorial addresses by Gaza’s Civil Defense, whose teams carried out the recovery operations, as well as representatives of the victims’ families and community members.
The bodies and remains were buried at al-Ahli cemetery in the Zeitoun neighborhood after the funeral prayers.
Civil Defense teams recovered them recently as part of the second phase of a project launched on July 19 to retrieve Palestinians still buried beneath the rubble of buildings destroyed during the Israeli war.
The victims belonged to the Rahim, Balawi, Malaka, Qanbour and Salmi families and were killed when Israeli forces struck several homes around two and a half years ago, according to local authorities.
Recovery operations in Gaza are being carried out with limited resources, including only a small number of excavators and deteriorating equipment, amid Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and equipment needed to search the rubble.
Sunday’s ceremony is among the largest funerals in Palestinian history in terms of the number of bodies and remains being buried, according to a Anadolu Agency.
A similar mass funeral was held in early August for 112 Palestinians recovered from the rubble of homes in Gaza City’s Sabra neighborhood.
The second phase of the recovery project involves 800 hours of work at 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where 1,072 bodies are believed to remain buried.
The first phase began in late November 2025 and involved 500 hours of work. Civil Defense teams recovered around 333 bodies and remains out of an estimated 559 missing beneath the rubble of 54 homes and buildings.
Under the first phase of the Gaza cease-fire agreement, in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow the entry of heavy machinery and equipment needed for recovery operations, according to Palestinian authorities in the enclave.
The cease-fire followed nearly two years of Israeli attacks on Gaza, which killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, while destroying or damaging much of Gaza's civilian infrastructure.

The representative added that Trump's envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings" in Ukraine on 6 September.
Update: At 14:15, Zelenskyy reported that the talks had begun.
Background:
- Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Ukraine on Sunday.
- Earlier on 6 September, Zelenskyy said he had held a meeting with the negotiating team ahead of a meeting with the representatives of the US president.
- Yuri Ushakov, an aide to the Russian ruler, said Putin told the US envoys during Saturday's talks that he is confident his war aims will be achieved. The White House described the talks as "substantive" and announced that the next steps will be unveiled in the coming weeks.

Trump envoys Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Ukraine after Putin talks in new push to end war
President Trump's White House special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner arrived Sunday in Ukraine, as part of a trip that began in Moscow, where they discussed a proposal to end the war with Russia.
The trip marks the first time the envoys have traveled to Ukraine since Mr. Trump returned to office with a pledge to solve the conflict.
Prior to their arrival, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on social media that "security guarantees" and peace are needed.
Zelenskyy also said European security advisers will participate in some of the talks.
"We are expecting one session of our talks, and then another session will be held with the European NSAs (national security advisers). Several important sessions," Zelenskyy told reporters.
Witkoff and Kushner held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, where they "discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks," according to a White House official.
Prior to Witkoff and Kushner's departure, Mr. Trump told reporters the envoys were traveling to Ukraine and Russia with a proposal to end the conflict. Mr. Trump said they had had "an idea for peace," and that "there may be a good chance that we'll do it."
After the meeting, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said in a statement that "our American colleagues made serious preparations for this trip," and they had "also formulated a number of ideas regarding possible paths to a settlement," but did not elaborate on what those might be.
At the start of the meeting in Moscow, which was captured on video, Putin asked Kushner and Witkoff to pass on his warm wishes and gratitude to Mr. Trump, and described the situation in Ukraine as "not simple."
Ushakov added that the talks also discussed in "some detail" potential deals between the U.S. and Russia that would be "mutually beneficial."
Both Ukraine and Russia agreed Saturday to pause strikes while the envoys were in the country to allow for talks to take place.
"Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days," presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russia's Tass news agency, saying the decision was tied to Witkoff and Kushner's planned visit to the Ukrainian capital. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy mirrored the decision by halting strikes until Monday.
The White House official also told CBS News that the U.S. delegation thanked Putin for the release of U.S. Marine veteran Robert Gilman, a 32-year-old teacher who had been imprisoned in Russia since 2022. Gilman was freed and allowed to return home last month. Prior to his release, Gilman was hospitalized in serious condition after he had allegedly been subjected to severe mistreatment, according to Global Reach, an organization that worked to free him.
