US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:49:22 UTC
19:49:22 KST

US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
The US and Iran attack tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, as the two sides try to exert control over the strategic waterway.
The United States and Iran have escalated tit-for-tat attacks in the past 24 hours, with Washington targeting three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hitting tankers and firing a ballistic missile towards US warships patrolling near the Strait of Hormuz.
Experts have dubbed Iran’s targeting of the two US aircraft carriers a “calculated escalation”, as the months-long fighting is increasingly playing out at sea, with both sides trying to exert control over the strategic strait – a global chokepoint used by Tehran as leverage in the war.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
- list 2 of 3At least four civilians killed in Houthi missile strike near Yemen’s Taiz
- list 3 of 3Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
The attacks on tankers come as the US claims that an increasing volume of oil has started to flow through the strait, though the exact figures are still debatable, while the naval blockade of Iranian ports continues.
The latest exchanges further dim hopes for a de-escalation through diplomacy as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy supplies and slowed economic growth around the world.
So, what do we know about the latest tanker wars, and where is the conflict headed?
What do we know about the latest attacks on tankers?
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces struck three Iranian vessels, including a tanker off Kharg Island, the hub through which Iran exported 90 percent of its crude before the war.
Another tanker was struck near Jask, and an unladen vessel was hit in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was told to abandon ship.
CENTCOM said the attacks followed Iranian ballistic missile launches against a US aircraft carrier and navy destroyer, which it said successfully evaded the strikes. No US personnel were injured.
“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it launched “several ballistic missiles” at the aircraft carrier and destroyer, accusing them of “harassing Iranian ships” and taking part in a naval blockade.
“The Iranians did not only target two ordinary warships – they targeted a missile destroyer and, remarkably, an aircraft carrier … the backbone of the American campaign against Iran,” defence analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera.
“This is a very, very significant development, and it doesn’t come as a surprise that the Americans retaliated.”
Iran then said its forces also targeted three oil tankers travelling through what it called an “unauthorised route” in the Strait of Hormuz and three US-linked vessels elsewhere.
In a statement carried by Iranian broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC navy warned all vessels in the Gulf or near the Strait of Hormuz not to be “deceived” by the US military and to “refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at transiting unauthorised waterways”.
“Otherwise, you will be targeted,” it said.
On Sunday, Iran claimed it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Why are they attacking tankers?
Washington claimed the Iranian tankers it struck were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network financing the IRGC and its regional allies.
Iran has long relied partly on a shadow fleet to circumvent sanctions and sell oil, a source of revenue that has become more important since the US began blockading Iranian ports in April.
Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil supplies flowed, in retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks that began on February 28. Some 20 million barrels of oil flowed daily before the war began.
Hassan Ghashghavi, a lawmaker and spokesman for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security Commission, said the attacks on US warships were part of “an existential war with America”, arguing that Washington’s naval blockade “should never have existed” in the first place.
“Naturally, they have acted militarily in violation of all international laws,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that “because America is far from us, it does not see this war as existential”.
Meanwhile, the US has continued to build pressure on Iran to open the key waterway, both militarily and economically.
Last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a raft of economic measures to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.
Bessent said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran.
This comes despite US assertions of normalcy in the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington insisting the waterway is open and that dozens of ships carrying millions of barrels of oil transit it each day.
Last week, Bessent claimed that some 17 million barrels of crude oil a day had been shipped out recently, according to a report in the United Kingdom’s The Times newspaper. Al Jazeera, however, could not independently verify the claims in the report.
President Donald Trump claimed last month that the US was in “total control” of the strait.
Yet figures from marine analytics firm Kpler show only six vessels crossed the strait on Wednesday, 11 on Tuesday and five on Monday, with a 10-day average of just 13 vessels per day.
What is the latest with oil prices?
The attacks are adding to concerns about global energy supplies.
Brent crude futures closed on Friday at $96.28 a barrel, their highest level since July 24, up from roughly $70 before the war.
Predictably, US oil and gas prices have also skyrocketed, coming at a crucial time for Trump as Americans head to the polls for midterm elections in November.
Diesel hit a new record price in the US on Friday, soaring to an average of $5.85 a gallon ($1.55 per litre) for the first time ever. Polls have repeatedly suggested a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has also plunged Trump’s popularity.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted in late August found that only 31 percent of Americans back the war, while 63 percent are against it.
The same polling suggested Trump’s approval rating has dropped to 33 percent, down from 40 percent since the fighting began.
Where is the conflict headed?
The renewed exchanges of strikes between Iran and the US mark an escalation in the six-month-long conflict, according to the director of the Middle East studies programme at George Washington University, Sina Azodi.
Azodi told Al Jazeera that neither side will “cave in” because it “will not look good on them, so the only option is to escalate”.
He said unless there is a political settlement, the war will continue.
“There’s going to be more clashes between the Iranians and the Americans. There can be miscalculations. There can be more civilian casualties”, especially on the Iranian side, Azodi said.
“The [US] secretary of defence can send more troops to the region, but I don’t think the Iranians are going to back down. They’re going to resist that blockade and impose further costs on the United States.”
He said the goal of the US and Iran is to force the other to back down. “The winner is going to be the one that can accept more costs and punishment,” Azodi said.
Commenting on Iran’s strategy, Ali Akbar Dareini, an analyst at the Center for Strategic Studies in Tehran, echoed Azodi, saying the US attacks on Iranian oil tankers are a “big issue” that Iran cannot afford to let “go unanswered”.
“Does it make Iran surrender? No, it compels Iran. It incentivises Iran to lash out and retaliate” more harshly, Dareini told Al Jazeera.
He said the US naval blockade, coupled with sanctions, is inflicting severe pain on Iran, but added the latter has plans to counter it. Iran cannot tolerate this naval blockade to continue, so Iran is already making preparations to break the siege.
“At the same time, Iran definitely has its own plans to make sure that oil prices will shoot up over $100 per barrel,” Dareini said.

Father of child hurt in electric scooter accident: It's better to see a sulking kid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

Father of child hurt in electric scooter accident: It's better to see a sulking kid
In May, 12-year-old Elisabet was seriously injured in an electric scooter accident. Her father believes the use of powerful electric scooters by children should be subject to stricter restrictions.
Twelve-year-old Elisabet was seriously injured in May when she crashed an electric scooter borrowed from a friend in Järveküla, leaving her in a coma for several days. At the time of the accident, the scooter was traveling at more than 55 kilometers per hour and the girl was not wearing a helmet.
Elisabet has since recovered from the accident. Her father, Pert Lomp, told ETV's "Hommik Anuga" morning show that she has almost fully recovered, with only her sense of smell and taste and hearing in one ear still causing some concern.
"But fortunately, she is still growing and is a girl who is about to turn 13. The doctors have said she will grow out of all of this and everything will be fine."
Elisabet herself does not remember the accident. She only remembers the morning of the day it happened. It later emerged that she had borrowed the scooter from a friend to go and get some pastries.
"Her view of it is still that it was a terrible thing, something she could never have imagined might happen to her."
There were reportedly no difficult traffic conditions at the scene of the accident. The road was straight and visibility was good. Most likely, the scooter's handlebars began to wobble at high speed and the girl lost control of the vehicle. A woman witnessed the accident and immediately called an ambulance for the child. Pert Lomp learned what had happened from the school principal.
"At that moment, my world completely stopped," he said.
Elisabet's father, mother and sister arrived at the scene as she was being lifted into the ambulance. Her father said he could immediately see that the situation was very serious.
"I ran over to the ambulance to try to make contact with my daughter and then I realized that something was very badly wrong: her eyes had rolled back and she was making some sounds, but they were the kind of sounds that left me at a loss for words. Fortunately, the doctors were there and quickly explained what had happened and told me the situation was serious," Lomp recalled.
Lomp said electric scooters were not unfamiliar to the family before the accident. The family had scooters that the children could ride, but their top speed was around 25 kilometers per hour and the children wore helmets while riding them. The younger children, however, wanted their parents to buy them more powerful models.
"We had long discussions about it. She really wanted one. As her father, I had almost given in, but I told my daughter: finish the school year first and then we'll see what your report card looks like and how everything else is going. Then we'll revisit the issue. Now it's off the table for good."
He also urged other parents not to give in to their children's every wish.
"It's better to see your child sulking for two or three days than not to see them at all anymore. This is where we, as parents, have to consciously make those decisions ourselves. Sometimes you have to be a strict mother or a strict father to prevent something that could lead to a situation like the one our family went through," he said.
After his daughter's accident, Lomp published a post on social media describing what had happened and warning other parents. He received messages of support from other parents in response, with many saying they had decided against buying their child a high-speed electric scooter.
"I'm also extremely and sincerely grateful today that you invited me on the show to talk about this because if we can save even one child and their parents from this kind of tragedy, then coming here will have been entirely worthwhile."
At the same time, Lomp does not believe electric scooters should be banned altogether. However, he said proper regulation is crucial to prevent people from racing along sidewalks at speeds of more than 60 kilometers per hour.
"If it's regulated, then in a sense it's also a green way of thinking. It also gives people a certain freedom to get from point A to point B. But the rules have to be very clear," Lomp stressed.
Police: Situation serious
In Estonia, an electric scooter is classified as a personal light electric vehicle if its maximum design speed does not exceed 25 kilometers per hour and its motor has a maximum power output of one kilowatt. A faster or more powerful vehicle no longer qualifies as a personal light electric vehicle permitted in traffic. Riders aged 10 and older must have a bicycle license, while those under 16 are required to wear a helmet.
Mari-Liis Mölder, a unit head at the East Harju Police Department, said the situation involving electric scooters speeding along the streets is quite serious. Police also carried out thorough checks of scooters on the streets this week. The checks identified around 10 scooters that did not meet legal requirements. Some were capable of speeds of around 56 kilometers per hour, while others could exceed 70 kilometers per hour.
"Most of the riders were schoolchildren, generally in grades one through nine. Some said they weren't aware of the rules, while others said their parents allowed it. Many had scooters fitted with speed limiters, but when you check them, the limiters can be removed very easily," auxiliary police officer Taavi Valgmäe explained.
Mölder said importers and retailers of electric scooters have generally taken responsibility by not selling scooters capable of traveling faster than 25 kilometers per hour. However, scooters are also ordered from abroad where such controls may not be in place or where the speed restriction can be disabled at the push of a button. If parents have bought their child a scooter online, they can have a speed limiter installed by a retailer in Estonia.
Above all, however, Mölder recommends not buying electric scooters for children.
"This kind of vehicle shouldn't be in the hands of a child under 15 or 16 at all. Once a young person reaches 15 or 16, their behavior in traffic and their awareness of road safety have certainly developed. But younger children are very reckless and very unaware of the dangers," she said.

Black-clad Dover protesters condemned for ‘dressing up in costumes’ by minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:47:25 UTC
19:47:25 KST

A cabinet minister has condemned the blocking of Dover roads by dozens of masked and black-clad people on Saturday.
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said that although peaceful protest was an “essential part of British life”, this differed from “dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives”.
He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “So I would condemn it, but I’d condemn the disruption it caused for local people as well.”
Adding that the situation had been resolved, he said: “Clearly, that’s not something we would want or expect to see on the [streets] of Britain.”
He declined to comment “on the security and policing side of it”, but when pressed on the apparent unpreparedness of the police, he said he thought that “on the whole, the police handled it very well”.
Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by Patriot Platform, an anti-immigration group with links to the far right which styles itself as having a “fierce love for our homeland”.
Kent police attended and engaged with the protest on Saturday, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. Protesters had dispersed by lunchtime, and no arrests were made during the incident.
Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 45 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways. Videos shared online showed masked people in black marching on the road in a group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars. The number of people involved was not immediately clear, and police did not give an official estimate. One livestreamer estimated that he was marching with hundreds of people.
Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20, chanting “stop the boats” and “England till I die”.
Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, posted on X: “A clearly coordinated protest is not ‘spontaneous’ as described by Police. We can and must do better.”
He noted that Kent police appeared to have had “little advance warning”, and questioned whether intelligence had been missed. “I will be asking why,” he wrote.
“Concerns around illegal migration are not racist. I’ve said that many times. But what we saw today in Dover is against our laws and not fair on residents.”
In a piece for the Mirror, Tapp suggested that he would like additional officers, including mutual aid from forces such as the Met, mobilised quickly if Dover is targeted again.
He wrote: “The Port of Dover is not just another road junction. It is critical national infrastructure, handling around a third of UK trade in goods with the EU and huge volumes of roll-on, roll-off freight. When Dover stops, Britain feels it.
“And the law matters. Wilfully obstructing a highway can be a criminal offence. New legislation also means police can designate protest areas where concealing your identity with a balaclava or other face covering becomes an offence.”
A government spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.”

U.S. Marine Corps sends F-35B jets to Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:46:10 UTC
19:46:10 KST

- VMFA-533, the Hawks, arrived at MCAS Iwakuni, Japan, on September 5, replacing VMFA-232 under the Unit Deployment Program.
- The squadron deployed with F-35B Lightning II jets for the first time under this program, after receiving its first F-35B in October 2024.
An F-35B fighter squadron from South Carolina has taken over rotational duty in Japan, replacing a Hornet squadron under a U.S. Marine Corps program that keeps U.S.-based units cycling through the Pacific.
Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 533, known as the Hawks, arrived at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni on September 5 under the Unit Deployment Program. The squadron is based at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort, South Carolina, and now joins Marine Aircraft Group 12, part of the 1st Marine Aircraft Wing, in the Indo-Pacific region.
VMFA-533 replaces VMFA-232, the Red Devils, which had held the rotational slot since arriving from Marine Corps Air Station Miramar, California, in September 2025.
The Unit Deployment Program sends Marine Corps units based in the continental United States to Japan on a rotating basis, giving them experience operating in the Indo-Pacific without permanently moving personnel and families overseas. The Marine Corps has run the program since 1980, when VMFA-533’s own predecessor squadron became the first unit to deploy under it.
This marks the Hawks’ first Unit Deployment Program rotation flying the F-35B. The squadron received its first F-35B Lightning II at Beaufort on October 11, 2024, after decades flying the F/A-18D Hornet. VMFA-533 has deployed to Iwakuni under the program multiple times before, most recently with Hornets in 2018, but arrives this time with the short takeoff and vertical landing jet that has become standard across Marine Corps fighter squadrons.
Iwakuni already hosts other F-35B squadrons alongside F/A-18D Hornets and KC-130J refueling aircraft. The base also supports elements of the U.S. Navy’s Carrier Air Wing 5.
The Marine Corps said the deployment supports the U.S.-Japan Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security and gives the 1st Marine Aircraft Wing additional combat-ready aviation forces able to operate from naval and expeditionary sites. The Marine Corps did not disclose how many aircraft or personnel deployed with VMFA-533 or how long the rotation is expected to last.

IIT Mandi orders inquiry after poster says Shudras should ‘serve higher classes’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

19:42:51 KST

Controversial caste poster at IIT Mandi sparks row, institute orders inquiry into display
NEW DELHI: IIT Mandi has set up an inquiry after a Bhagavad Gita-themed poster displayed on its campus during Janmashtami celebrations described Shudras as being meant to "serve higher classes", triggering controversy over caste discrimination.Institute Director Laxmidhar Behera said the poster was part of a student-led event and had not been approved by the institute. He said he was "shocked" when he learnt about the display and stressed that IIT Mandi does not support caste-based discrimination.
Director distances institute from poster
In an email to the IIT Mandi community on Sunday, Behera described the development as an "Outright condemnation of recent poster display within campus". He said the poster, displayed on September 4, had not been endorsed by the institute "in any manner"."I have personally fought against caste-based discrimination in any form in every forum. I have instituted an enquiry committee in this matter such that the institute campus is never used for any such violation of social harmony. I fully empathise with members of our community who have been hurt by this incident," he wrote.Behera said IIT Mandi was committed to "the values of equality, social justice, scientific temper" and the principles laid down in the Constitution.
"The institute strongly condemns any form of caste based discrimination," he said, urging members of the campus community to "stand together against such biases/discrimination in any form".Speaking to PTI, Behera said the poster had been prepared for a student event. He said the inquiry committee included faculty members and representatives from different social categories, including members of the Scheduled Castes and Other Backward Classes.
What the controversial poster said
The poster, titled "Bhagavad Gita - The Timeless Wisdom", was put up outside the institute's auditorium during Janmashtami celebrations.It divided society into four groups mentioned in the Bhagavad Gita, namely Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. It described Brahmanas as those who "spread God's message", Kshatriyas as those who "protect society and spirituality" and Vaishyas as those who "drive economy, support others".For Shudras, however, the poster listed their role as "serve higher classes", which became the focus of the controversy.The poster also quoted a Bhagavad Gita verse stating that the four divisions of human society were created according to the "three modes of material nature and the work associated with them".Behera said he had been away from IIT Mandi and returned on Saturday. He said he learnt about the controversy on Sunday morning."I have not seen the poster. I don't want to take a side here and let the panel decide," he told PTI.
Behera's Gita and ISKCON links
The controversy has also drawn attention to Behera's long association with the Bhagavad Gita and ISKCON.According to his official IIT Mandi profile, Behera has spent 27 years teaching what he describes as the "universal principles of peace through Bhagavad Gita". He is also known as "HG Lila Purushottam Das" and is the founder of the proposed Bhaktivedanta University, whose website describes it as an ISKCON initiative.Behera currently teaches a three-credit course on the Bhagavad Gita at IIT Mandi.He defended ISKCON's position on caste, saying the organisation opposes discrimination and promotes equality."ISKCON is the only organisation that strictly and strongly speaks against caste-based discrimination. In ISKCON, pujaris are also from the Shudra community. Muslims are also pujaris," he claimed."We are against casteism in all forms. All occupational duties are according to guna and karma," he added.Behera also highlighted what he said was increased representation of marginalised communities at IIT Mandi during his tenure. According to him, the institute had no OBC, SC or ST faculty members when he joined, while their numbers have since risen substantially. The IIT director has previously faced criticism over his public views.
In 2023, he asked students to take a pledge against eating meat and linked landslides and cloudbursts in Himachal Pradesh to cruelty towards animals. In 2022, shortly after becoming IIT Mandi director, a video surfaced in which he claimed to have helped a friend's family get rid of "evil spirits" through chanting holy mantras.More recently, IIT Mandi's Indian Knowledge System and Mental Health Applications Centre held a conference in June that included sessions on the Bhagavad Gita, Ayurveda and reincarnation. Behera was among its general chairs and co-organised a session titled "Reincarnation, OBEs and afterlife communication".The institute's inquiry committee will now examine how the poster was prepared, displayed and presented during the student-led event.

A fire broke out aboard the diesel-electric icebreaker Admiral Makarov at the Kronstadt Marine Plant, where the vessel is undergoing repairs.
The Telegram channel 112 reported the incident.
According to the channel, the fire started in the steering-gear compartment, which houses components controlling the rudder drive. The area affected by the fire was initially estimated at 100 square meters.
A total of 52 emergency responders and 10 pieces of equipment were involved in extinguishing the fire. Within two hours, firefighters contained the blaze and extinguished the open flames. According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties.
— dimdim (@dimdim518484) September 5, 2026
The cause of the fire and the extent of damage to the icebreaker are currently unknown.
Admiral Makarov is a large Project R-1039 diesel-electric icebreaker built in 1975 at the Wärtsilä shipyard in Helsinki.
The vessel belongs to the Ermak-class series of icebreakers built in Finland for the Soviet Union. Its primary purpose is to escort transport vessels through challenging ice conditions.
Key technical specifications of the Admiral Makarov:
For many years, Admiral Makarov operated in the Russian Far East and was later deployed for operations in the Arctic. In late 2025, the vessel was transferred to the North-Western Basin Branch of Rosmorport.
Following completion of its repairs, the icebreaker was planned to escort vessels to Russian ports in the eastern part of the Gulf of Finland during the winter navigation season.
In spring 2025, the vessel was placed in dry dock for repairs to its hull, propellers, and three propeller shafts. Separately, repairs to the icebreaker’s main engines are also underway, with completion planned by the end of 2026.
On the morning of June 3, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Project 20380 Boikiy-class missile corvette at Kronstadt Naval Base. The attack sparked a large-scale fire aboard the vessel. According to assessments, the nature and extent of the damage indicate that the ship is beyond repair.

Palestinians in Gaza bury remains of 100 people recovered from rubble
Unknown

Palestinians in Gaza bury remains of 100 people recovered from rubble
The remains of thousands more people are believed to be buried in buildings destroyed and damaged in Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, authorities say.
Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood.
The remains were carried on Sunday by family members from Zeitoun to al-Ma’madani cemetery in central Gaza City for burial, according to Al Jazeera’s correspondent at the scene, Ghazi al-Aloul.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Gaza teams recover remains of 55 people nearly 3 years after Israeli strike
- list 2 of 3US rejects Israeli suggestions of removing Palestinians from Gaza
- list 3 of 3Did Israel’s destruction of Gaza worsen its water crisis?
Civil defence crews and family members had spent weeks digging through the ruins of homes hit during Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
Many of the victims were part of the extended Malaka family, which alone lost 55 members.
Al-Aloul said families had waited a long time to be able to bury their loved ones in “known, proper cemeteries”. He said that the chance to bury the remains of family members was “not available to every family”, noting that Israeli forces had destroyed and dug up cemeteries elsewhere in Gaza during the war.
Al-Aloul said the remains, though wrapped in shrouds resembling intact bodies, were often only fragments.
“These are bone remains and remnants of belongings that may have been found on the bodies, especially the children’s,” he said, adding that no complete bodies had been recovered from the site because “the Israeli occupation has prolonged this process, and continues to prolong it and prevent it from being completed quickly”.
Raed al-Dahshan, head of Gaza’s civil defence service, told Al Jazeera his teams had formulated plans to carry out recovery operations for thousands more missing bodies, but said the work was being held back by a shortage of heavy machinery.
“We don’t have equipment, we don’t have protective equipment” for rescue workers, he told Al Jazeera.
Dahshan said the recovery of an estimated 8,000 bodies still believed to be under rubble could be completed in about 90 days with proper equipment, but “if that equipment is barred from entering Gaza … this work will continue for years”.
He said his agency had submitted a detailed list of needed equipment to international institutions and was willing to have that machinery remain under international control rather than with the civil defence directly.
He said crews needed large excavators, personal protective equipment and search equipment to locate remains urgently.
On identifying remains, he said crews rely on survivors and neighbouring families to establish who was in a building and where they were at the time of the strike, supported by a team of engineers who sort and document findings in the field. He said Israeli forces’ failure to warn residents before strikes meant “dozens, even hundreds” of homes still required excavation.
Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territories, told Al Jazeera that the scenes were a reminder of “the brutality of this conflict”, noting some of the remains dated back to November 2023.
“Thousands of people are still languishing under this rubble … We’re talking about areas that may be under Israeli military control, 70 percent of Gaza – there’s difficulty accessing these areas to extract these bodies.”
“Accountability must happen … It’s essential that we preserve the evidence we’ve been able to obtain during this sensitive period.”
Gaza’s Health Ministry says at least 73,651 Palestinians have been killed and 174,592 wounded since October 2023.
Similar recovery operations in recent weeks have retrieved more than 100 bodies of people from the Abu Shariah and Hassaniya families who were killed in a single strike, as well as more than 500 bodies from the Al-Taj tower site, officials and activists said.

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday, Sept. 6, marking their first visit to Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The US delegation arrived by train at Kyiv’s central railway station for direct negotiations with Ukraine’s leadership.

A senior Ukrainian delegation met the envoys upon arrival, including Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, First Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Sergiy Kyslytsya, Head of the Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) Rustem Umerov, and “Servant of the People” parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia.
“Welcome to Kyiv, representatives of the President of the United States Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner,” Umerov wrote in a statement. “We continue close coordination on further steps to end the war.”
Strategy session and preceding Kremlin talks
The arrival of the US envoys follows a preparatory strategy meeting convened by Zelensky earlier Sunday with members of Ukraine’s negotiating delegation to finalize Kyiv’s diplomatic positions.
The Kyiv talks follow a three-hour-and-10-minute meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and the US delegation at the Kremlin on Saturday evening, Sept. 5.
Following those discussions, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov claimed that Witkoff and Kushner agreed to factor Putin’s battlefield assessments into their dialogue in Kyiv.
Kurkov: The War Could Transform Ukraine’s Political Culture
Russian officials characterized the Moscow session – which also included an informal working dinner – as “meaningful,” “frank,” and conducted in an atmosphere of mutual trust, noting that potential large-scale US-Russian commercial projects were raised alongside conflict settlement concepts.
The broader Washington delegation visiting the region included officials from the National Security Council, the State Department, and the Treasury Department.
Gene Lange, acting head of the US Treasury’s sanctions division, traveled to Moscow and held a preparatory session with Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special representative for economic cooperation.
While Lange did not attend the direct session with Putin, his presence underscored that sanctions policy formed part of the dialogue, despite recent assertions by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ruling out economic concessions without an end to the war.
At the onset of the Moscow talks, Putin confirmed that Russian forces had paused aerial strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight on Sept. 5, but rejected Ukraine’s proposal for a wider three-day frontline ceasefire.
In reciprocal coordination to safeguard the diplomatic process, Zelensky previously pledged that Ukrainian forces would refrain from striking Moscow through Monday as the US envoys conduct their meetings.

Russian Ballistic Strike Shuts Down Ukraine’s Kamet Steel Plant, Killing Five Workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:36:25 UTC
19:36:25 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Ballistic Strike Shuts Down Ukraine’s Kamet Steel Plant, Killing Five Workers
A Russian ballistic missile strike on the Kamet Steel plant in Kamianske, Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region, killed five people, wounded four others, and forced the major steelmaking facility to suspend production.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Metinvest, the plant’s parent company, on September 5, the attack occurred overnight and damaged Kamet Steel’s sinter and blast furnace operations, as well as energy and transport infrastructure across the industrial site.
Four Kamet Steel employees and one worker from a contractor were killed in the strike. Another four employees sustained injuries of varying severity and remain under medical supervision.
Only several minutes passed between the declaration of an air raid alert and the missile strike, Metinvest said, leaving some workers unable to reach shelters in time.
Oleksandr Myronenko, Metinvest’s chief operating officer, said there were no military facilities, equipment, or military production at the plant.
“Only civilians worked here, smelting iron and steel exclusively for civilian purposes,” Myronenko said.
Emergency and recovery operations are underway at the site. Specialists will be able to conduct a full assessment of the damaged equipment and infrastructure after debris removal is completed, according to the company.
Metinvest has not provided a timeline for restarting production. Kamet Steel is one of Ukraine’s major metallurgical facilities and produces pig iron, steel, and rolled products. The plant is part of Metinvest, one of the country’s largest industrial groups.
The September 5 attack marks the second time in recent weeks that a major Metinvest steel facility has halted operations following a Russian ballistic missile strike.
In August, Zaporizhstal suspended operations after a ballistic attack struck the facility shortly after an air raid alert was issued. Seven plant employees were killed and another 21 were injured in that attack.
Kamianske declared September 5 a day of mourning for those killed in the latest strike, while flags were lowered at Metinvest facilities.
The strike on Kamet Steel came during a broader Russian overnight attack on Ukraine on September 5. Russia also targeted Kyiv and Boryspil airports with Shahed-type drones, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy linked to preparations for a possible US delegation arriving in Ukraine by air.

Germany Unveils Anti-Sabotage Plan After Leipzig Airport Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

Germany is preparing a comprehensive package of domestic security measures to counter Russian sabotage, cyberattacks, and hybrid threats following an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, Bild reported.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced that Berlin is planning robust countermeasures covering drone defense, the protection of critical infrastructure, cyber resilience, and enhanced surveillance to detect spies and potential terrorists.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia’s hybrid attacks using explosive drones against airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks, and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality,” Dobrindt said. “These attacks will intensify, but we can fight back and defend ourselves.”
Under the proposal, Germany will expand the Federal Police’s mobile anti-drone capabilities. Rapid-reaction units equipped with specialized vehicles and helicopters will be stationed across nine key cities: Frankfurt am Main, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
Their operational remit will cover the protection of airspace over key transit hubs, airports, major railway stations, and the government quarter in Berlin, with the technical ability to intercept and neutralize explosive-laden drones.
The plan also grants critical infrastructure operators – including water utilities, energy companies, and defense manufacturing plants – expanded legal authority to actively counter and neutralize unauthorized drones without waiting for state law enforcement to arrive.
US Sanctions Chief Joins Moscow Talks as Putin Cites War Goals
Additionally, Berlin intends to deploy artificial intelligence tools, biometric facial recognition, and automated video surveillance at transport hubs to detect weapons, identify suspicious conduct, and track individuals suspected of espionage.
To guard against digital intrusion, Germany plans to establish a national “Cyberdome,” a distributed digital sensor network designed to detect and block coordinated cyberattacks.
Baltic shadow fleet pressure and rising sabotage wave
The domestic security initiative coincides with broader efforts by Berlin to apply economic and regulatory pressure against Moscow following the Aug. 4 drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Dobrindt publicly attributed responsibility for the airport attack directly to the Russian state, a stance endorsed across governing coalition parties. Siemtje Möller, foreign policy spokesperson for the Social Democratic Party (SPD) parliamentary group, affirmed that directly naming Russia was the correct course of action.
According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), German authorities are evaluating punitive measures targeting Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet” in the Baltic Sea. Officials are exploring stricter administrative, inspection, and legal mechanisms to impede or halt the transit of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent international sanctions.
The heightened security alerts follow a confidential assessment by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), which recorded 165 suspected sabotage cases, 24 espionage investigations, and 747 suspicious drone flights nationwide during the first eight months of 2026.

Satellite images verify new strikes on two Russian airbases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:35:28 UTC
19:35:28 KST

- Satellite images confirmed Ukrainian FP-1 drones destroyed an ammunition depot and maintenance facility and damaged two radars at Russia's Millerovo airbase on August 30.
- Separate imagery from a September 4 strike showed a destroyed Ka-52 and Mi-28 helicopter and a damaged Mi-8 at Sochi's airport.
Satellite imagery has confirmed damage to two radar systems, a maintenance facility and an ammunition depot at Russia’s Millerovo airbase in Rostov Oblast, following a Ukrainian drone strike on the night of August 30, according to images published by the Dnipro OSINT.
Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported that Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out the attack using FP-1 long-range strike drones, also striking Yeysk airbase the same night. At Millerovo, the satellite images show the ammunition depot and the base’s technical and maintenance facility, known by its Ukrainian abbreviation TECh, were completely destroyed, while an RSP-27 precision approach radar and a Nebo-SV early warning radar were both damaged.
Millerovo has been struck repeatedly since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. The base sits about four kilometers northwest of Millerovo city and has hosted Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment, which flies Su-30SM fighters, along with earlier deployments of Su-25 attack aircraft. Ukrainian officials have described the base as a key staging point for Russian frontline aviation supporting operations in eastern and southern Ukraine, and it was previously hit in drone attacks in December 2023 and July 2025.
The FP-1 is built by the Ukrainian company Fire Point and has become one of Ukraine’s primary tools for long-range strikes inside Russia. The drone carries a warhead of 60 to 120 kilograms depending on configuration, with a documented range of 1,600 kilometers, and Fire Point has said an upgraded model unveiled this year can reach as far as 2,700 kilometers. Ukraine’s military has credited FP-1 strikes with more than half of its long-range drone missions against Russian targets, including ammunition depots, oil refineries, radar stations and air defense systems.
Separately, satellite and visual evidence reviewed following a strike on September 4 identified damage to Russian military aircraft parked at Sochi’s airport in Krasnodar Krai, according to the same reporting.
A Ka-52 attack helicopter and a Mi-28 attack helicopter were destroyed, and a Mi-8 transport helicopter was damaged, at the facility’s military helicopter parking area. Sochi’s airport has been targeted in prior Ukrainian strikes, including an October 2023 attack that Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence directorate said hit a parking area for Russian helicopters in the airport’s Adler district, and an August 2025 strike that set fire to a nearby oil depot.
Russian authorities have not issued a public statement on either the Millerovo or Sochi strikes described in this report.

Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko stated that he had nothing to do with covering up illegal call centers, had not given instructions to facilitate such activities, and had not used the powers of the Prosecutor General for that purpose. He wrote this on Telegram, reports UNN.
Details
Regarding the Office of the Prosecutor General employee who appears in the investigation, decisions have already been made. He has been suspended from performing his official duties. I instructed that a personnel decision on his dismissal be prepared in accordance with the procedure established by law. Guilt is determined by a court. I am responsible for management decisions in the system I head

He instructed that the work of the Department of International Cooperation, where the employee in question worked, and the cybercrime countermeasures unit be reviewed. Justice Minister Akın Gürlek has announced that an operation targeting illegal betting had been carried out ahead of the derby between Fenerbahçe and Beşiktaş.
In a post on his social media, the minister said that the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office coordinated a comprehensive operation to disrupt the flow of funds to illegal betting sites ahead of the match.
As a result of operations conducted by the cybercrime branch of the Istanbul Gendarmerie, 245 illegal betting sites, 110 different payment methods, 1,200 IBANs, and approximately 98,000 websites linked to illegal betting were identified.
A court order was issued to block access to the websites and the IBANs belonging to more than 1000 individuals and legal entities found to have been used in illegal betting activities and the laundering of criminal proceeds were seized.
Gürlek noted that an investigation had been launched against the individuals in question on charges of “violation of law no. 7258,” which is the primary legislation enacted to regulate and penalize illegal gambling and games of chance, and “laundering of assets acquired from an offence.”
Thanking the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Istanbul Gendarmerie and the public officials involved in the operation process, the minister emphasized zero toleration for turning the excitement of sports into illegal profits.
“We will resolutely continue our fight against illegal betting networks and criminal proceeds,” Gürlek added.

These Cyborg Cockroaches Could Save Your Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Small robots and drones have increasingly been used to help respond to disasters, reaching locations that are too hard or too dangerous to send humans, such as collapsed buildings. Many of these efforts have been focused on search and rescue. But new research shows how bugs—with their ability to crawl through even narrower gaps in rubbled—outfitted with electrodes could be used as the next generation of first responders.
A research team from the University of Queensland (UQ) and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) have developed the “Paraborg” to not only help with searching for victims, but also administer first aid. While the idea of receiving medical care from a cockroach might be a little skin-crawling, the new cyborg bug could one day help buy human rescuers valuable time in a disaster zone.
“Cyborg insects have been designed for ‘search and explore’ missions for the past couple of decades,” Tan Vo Doan, a bio-robotics researcher at UQ, says in a press release. “We wanted to take the next step.”
The team relied on a giant burrowing cockroach that inhabits northern Queensland to develop the Paraborg, which they documented in a recent paper published the journal Advanced Science. The armored cockroach is up to 87 millimeters (3.5 inches) in length and weighs up to 40 grams (1.4 ounces).
Taking advantage of this large size, the research team developed two types of Paraborgs with different functions: one equipped with a camera to film the condition of disaster victims, and another with an automatic injection mechanism to administer medication. Cockroaches can carry up to 1.5 times its body weight. In practice, a cockroach equipped with the injection mechanism saw its total height increase by about 15 millimeters and its weight by about 17 grams, which the study found did not significantly impair its normal movements. To create the cyborg cockroaches, the team anesthetized them when the electrodes and microchips were attached, and they lived as normal cockroaches once the equipment was removed.
By applying electrical stimuli to electrodes embedded in the cockroach’s antennae and cerci—a pair of protruding sensory organs at the rear of the abdomen—researchers were able to remotely control the bug’s direction of travel and walking speed.
They were able to steer the roach by stimulating each antenna independently, while stimulating both cerci controlled the pace. The scientists administered different frequencies between 10 and 40 hertz after finding that anything over 50 hertz became ineffective over time.
The injection mechanism is a small device that deploys a syringe using a spring system. That triggers a process that breaks the seal between a chamber containing citric acid and another containing baking soda. The resulting chemical reaction—basically the same one you might’ve done as a kid to make a volcano with baking soda and vinegar—creates enough carbon dioxide to push the plunger on the syringe and administer medication.
For the study, the research team remotely controlled a cockroach to travel from its starting point through three checkpoints and administer an injection to a simulated target.
The results showed that the success rate for injections made at close range—within 150 millimeters of the target—topped out at approximately 95 percent. The success rate for the entire sequence of tasks—from departure to completion of the injection—was 72 percent.
The researchers also successfully demonstrated teamwork, where one cockroach uses a camera to locate a simulated target while another serves as the injector.
Although the research team has previously developed cyborg beetles capable of climbing vertical walls, they note that larger cockroaches are better-suited for carrying specialized rescue and medical equipment.
While the results of the new research are promising, the experiment didn’t replicate the complex environmental conditions found at actual disaster sites, such as debris, uneven terrain, and shifting landscapes.
Vo Doan expressed hope that, if resources can be secured to speed up research and field testing, a rescue team of cyborg insects could be deployed at actual disaster sites within five to 10 years.
“Rather than building one robot to do everything, we can harness the natural strengths of different insects and equip them for different missions,” Vo-Doan says.
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

My Brief Summer Fling With Siri AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

When I first tested the developer beta of Apple's Siri AI by taking it as my tour guide around San Francisco, I was convinced the overhauled smartphone assistant would be an “everything tool” on the iPhone. The answers felt reliable enough and more helpful than previous versions of Siri. Also, the chatbot-style app for Siri felt very sleek, very Apple-y.
Over the next month, I kept experimenting with the Siri AI in the iOS 27 beta. The tool was quite powerful, especially with the personal context brought in by indexing the contents of my phone. Finding an ancient text message or photo has never been easier. Even so, my usage of the smartphone assistant slowly started tapering off.
It’s not that Siri AI isn’t better now. It is! This new version is quite the step change, which makes my reaction even more devastating. Siri AI isn’t revolutionizing how I interact with my phone the way I'd initially hoped, especially as an AI assistant built directly into the device and factoring in that Apple gives more thought to preserving my privacy than many other AI companies.
Even though I wasn't going out of my way to interact with Siri AI, I didn’t mind how it was now, essentially, the search bar for the smartphone. As the summer months faded, I wasn’t souring on Siri AI. Instead, I just grew more neutral.
Old habits die hard. Soon I was back to my regularly scheduled doomscrolling on Instagram and aimless Yelp expeditions. I was manually typing and swiping for myself rather than relying on a smartphone assistant for help. And I was already low-key locked in with another chatbot, Anthropic’s Claude, and already used that app fairly often on my phone.
Even though some AI power users may not go all in on this new Siri, analysts say this won’t matter, since everyday users are often fine with Apple’s default software. “Will Siri bear the weight of criticism for not being as good as some of its peers? Sure,” says Dipanjan Chatterjee, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester, a research and consultancy company. “Will it make a difference to the vast installed base of iPhone users and cause them to look elsewhere? Not a chance.” Some iPhone users trust Apple with their data in ways they don't with any other company. Siri AI may reap those same benefits.
Tech analysts see Apple’s long-cultivated consumer trust in data privacy as potentially a compelling distinction. Ramon Llamas, a research director analyzing the mobile device market at the International Data Corporation, believes users deep in the Apple ecosystem, who previously had qualms about the safety of other AI tools, may be open to trying the new Siri.
My experience with Siri AI—loving it and then leaving it for dust—may be an outlier. Many other beta testers are still rocking with the smartphone assistant.
“In the past, I was unwilling to trust that Siri could do anything useful,” says Avi Greengart, founder and lead analyst at Techsponential. “But with the latest beta software, I'm finding myself not only using it more, but for more things: Siri is now able to find information buried on my phone faster and more efficiently than any other method, its world knowledge is vastly better than before, and even dictation works better.”
That said, the cultural backlash to generative AI has been brewing. Another solid segment of iPhone owners may choose to avoid the new Siri altogether because of the AI attached to its name. Whether it’s a moral objection or broader distrust of AI tools, these holdouts are unlikely to be won over by Siri’s feature improvements.
Ultimately, my own summer fling with Siri AI was short-lived. But I promise, it’s not you. It’s me.

19 lakh lives impacted as Ganga breaches flood mark in Patna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:29:53 UTC
19:29:53 KST

The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016.
NEW DELHI: More than 19.57 lakh people have been affected by floods across 11 districts of Bihar as of Sunday, with authorities putting downstream areas on high alert. This comes after the Ganga, following heavy rain, crossed its previous highest flood level at Gandhi Ghat in Patna.The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016. While the trend was stable at Gandhi Ghat, authorities warned that Hathidah and subsequent gauge stations could be affected over the next one to three days.The rising water levels have prompted heightened vigilance across several downstream districts, with officials monitoring river levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas and keeping rescue machinery ready.
19.57 lakh people affected across 11 districts
According to officials, flooding has affected around 19.57 lakh people in 330 gram panchayats across Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Vaishali, Bhagalpur, Begusarai, Buxar, Samastipur, Munger, Katihar and Araria.The latest figures indicate a worsening impact compared with earlier assessments, when around 16.85 lakh people across 61 blocks and 300 gram panchayats had been reported affected.With several rivers continuing to flow above danger levels, authorities have intensified relief and rescue operations in the affected districts.
The Water Resources Department has warned that the Ganga at Hathidah may also cross its previous HFL, increasing the risk for Begusarai, Lakhisarai, Munger, Bhagalpur and Katihar.“Officials and field-level authorities have been directed to remain alert and continuously monitor water levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas, while taking precautionary measures as required.“Engineers have been asked to keep flood-control resources and machinery ready. People in affected areas have been advised to avoid going near the river and remain cautious,” the advisory stated.Local administrations have also been asked to keep a close watch on boat operations, prevent overloading and ensure residents receive regular updates about the flood situation.
Ganga breaches danger levels at several locations
The Ganga is above the danger mark at several locations in Bihar.At Buxar, the river was 0.08 metres above the danger mark, although its level was declining. At Dighaghat in Patna, it was 1.54 metres above the danger mark, while at Gandhi Ghat it stood 1.96 metres above it.At Hathidah, the Ganga was 1.74 metres above the danger mark and continued to rise. Munger recorded a level 0.51 metres above the danger mark, with the river showing a rising trend.The river was also 2.01 metres above the danger mark at Sultanganj and 0.65 metres above it at Bhagalpur. The Ganga remained above the danger mark at Kahalgaon as well.At Pandarak in Patna, the river was flowing at 43.92 metres at 6 am, 0.19 metres above its previous HFL of 43.73 metres recorded on August 16, 2021.In contrast, the Ganga remained below the warning level in Prayagraj and Varanasi. Its level was rising in Prayagraj but declining in Varanasi.
Several rivers remain above danger levels
The flood threat is not confined to the Ganga. Several other rivers in Bihar are also flowing above their respective danger levels.The Gandak is above the danger mark at Dumariaghat and Hajipur, while the Kosi has crossed the mark at Baltara and Kursela. The Budhi Gandak is above the danger level at Khagaria.The Punpun is above the danger mark at Sripalpur, while the Bagmati has crossed it at Benibad. The Ghaghra is also flowing above the danger level at Darauli.The combination of rising river levels and further rainfall has kept authorities on alert, particularly in downstream and low-lying areas.
Relief operations expanded across flood-hit districts
The administration has deployed significant resources to assist people affected by the floods.A total of 110 community kitchens are currently operating in various districts to provide food to affected residents. Earlier official figures had put the number of operational community kitchens at 80, with around 1.21 lakh people receiving meals through them.One relief camp is also operational, providing accommodation, food, medical assistance and other essential facilities to 326 flood-affected people.Authorities have distributed around 45,900 polythene sheets and 11,700 dry ration packets as part of relief efforts.Boats are being used extensively to evacuate residents and maintain movement in areas affected by rising waters. The latest deployment stands at 1,345 boats across the state, compared with 1,158 reported earlier.
SDRF, NDRF teams deployed
With the possibility of further flooding, 27 State Disaster Response Force teams and 10 National Disaster Response Force teams have been deployed across different districts.The teams have been tasked with undertaking rapid relief and rescue operations, while district administrations continue to monitor vulnerable areas and river embankments.Officials have also been instructed to ensure that flood-control equipment and machinery remain ready for deployment as required.
Rain forecast raises concern over further rise
The flood situation could remain challenging over the coming days as the Bihar Meteorological Service Centre has forecast light to moderate rainfall at several places across the state over the next two days.Heavy rainfall is also possible at some locations.Authorities are therefore preparing for the possibility of further increases in river levels, particularly in areas already affected by flooding. The state government and district administrations are continuing to monitor the situation and deploy relief materials, boats and rescue teams according to local requirements.
Rail services affected on Patna-Gaya section
The flooding has also disrupted railway operations in parts of the state.The East Central Railway said on Sunday that some trains had been cancelled or diverted because of the “alarmingly high water level at bridge number 21" connecting Punpun and Parsa Bazar stations on the Patna-Gaya section.The development adds to the disruption caused by rising waters as authorities continue to focus on evacuation, relief and the safety of residents in flood-affected areas.
Barrage discharge data recorded at 9 am on Sunday showed that the Sone Barrage at Indrapuri was releasing 2,27,739 cusecs of water, although the flow was declining.The Kosi Barrage at Birpur was releasing 1,68,400 cusecs, with the discharge remaining stable. The Gandak Barrage at Valmikinagar was releasing 1,29,000 cusecs, also with a stable trend.With multiple rivers remaining above danger levels, further rainfall forecast over the next two days and the Ganga already having crossed its previous HFL at Gandhi Ghat, authorities have urged residents in vulnerable areas to remain cautious and avoid approaching swollen rivers.

Making Aliyah? ynet Global summit tackles banking, healthcare, jobs and your first days in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:28:43 UTC
19:28:43 KST

The decision to make Aliyah can take years. Sometimes it develops over months, and sometimes it follows a single moment that changes everything. But once the ticket is booked and the suitcases begin to close, the big questions about Zionism, identity and belonging quickly give way to much more practical ones.
What do you do on your first day? Where do you register? How do you receive your documents? Which health fund should you choose? When do you open a bank account? What happens to money left overseas? How do you find a job without starting your career from scratch? And if something happens in the middle of the night, who do you call?
On September 8, ynet Global will hold the Global Aliyah Live Summit, a special international day of broadcasts devoted to Aliyah and the life that comes after it.
The summit will be broadcast in Hebrew, English, Russian and French, bringing together senior public officials, Aliyah and absorption organizations, and experts in healthcare, banking, employment and housing with the people currently experiencing the process themselves: new immigrants.
The first 24 hours: you landed. What now?
One of the summit’s central panels will focus on the moment when months or years of preparation suddenly become reality: the first 24 hours in Israel.
After the flight, the welcome and the first photo in the country comes Israeli bureaucracy, which can feel like an entirely new system that newcomers have to learn from scratch.
Which documents do you receive when you arrive? What has to be done immediately and what can wait? How do you begin dealing with government offices? When should you register with a health fund? How do you open a bank account? What benefits are available to new immigrants, and how do you access them?
The panel will bring those different steps together and help make sense of the stage when everything is unfamiliar, from the country and language to the systems and unwritten rules of daily life.
What to do before you board the plane
Some of the mistakes new immigrants make begin before they ever land in Israel.
The summit will therefore also focus on the days and weeks before Aliyah: which documents to bring, what to arrange with banks in the country of origin, what to do with savings and assets abroad, when to start looking for work in Israel and which arrangements can be completed before departure.
But those final days are not only about lists and documents. New immigrants participating in the summit will also talk about the moment Aliyah stops being an idea and becomes real: saying goodbye to family and friends, leaving a job, packing up a home, dealing with uncertainty and realizing that within days they will need to build a new routine in another country.
The money stays the same. The rules change
Opening a bank account in Israel may sound like a technical step, but for new immigrants it can raise an entire set of questions.
A special financial panel, featuring experts and representatives including Bank Leumi and mortgage advisers, will explain how financial life in Israel works for newcomers.
How do you transfer money from abroad? What happens when some income or assets remain overseas? How does Israel’s credit system work? What should you know about foreign currency, fees and international transfers?
The discussion will also move to a question many olim face later: whether and when to buy a home in Israel.
Mortgage advisers will explain what purchasing property looks like from a new immigrant’s perspective and what should be checked before making one of the biggest financial decisions of a lifetime.
You made Aliyah. Your career does not have to stay behind
A doctor, engineer, tech professional, teacher, executive or entrepreneur can arrive in Israel with 10 or 20 years of experience and discover that the first challenge is explaining to the local job market who they are.
That is why one of the summit’s major topics will be how to bring your career with you.
Employment specialists, including representatives of centers that work with new immigrants, will address questions facing almost every working-age oleh: When should you begin searching? How should a résumé be adapted for the Israeli market? How do you build a professional network from scratch? Which professions require Israeli licensing? And what happens when substantial overseas experience does not automatically translate into an equivalent position in Israel?
The discussions will also cover entrepreneurship, retraining and the options available to those who want to start a business.
The goal is not simply to help newcomers find work, but to help them bring to Israel the knowledge, experience and skills they have already spent years building.
Health funds, family doctors and one number to remember
Israel’s healthcare system can also take time to understand, particularly for people arriving from countries where medical care works very differently.
Representatives from Clalit Health Services will explain how to register with a health fund, choose a doctor, make appointments and access services available to new immigrants from the beginning of their lives in Israel.
The summit will also address a question nobody wants to face but everyone needs to know how to answer: what happens in a medical emergency?
A dedicated segment will explain how to contact Magen David Adom, what happens after dialing 101, what information dispatchers need and what new immigrants should know about Israel’s emergency medical system.
Among all the new phone numbers, passwords and apps that come with moving countries, 101 is one number worth knowing from day one.
Not just talking about olim, but talking with them
Alongside officials, experts and organizations, the summit will also feature new immigrants at different stages of their lives in Israel, and they will not be there only to tell success stories.
They will talk about what surprised them, what was harder than expected, where bureaucracy caught them unprepared, what their first weeks looked like, how they found a job or apartment and what they know now that they wish they had known before boarding the plane.
That combination of official information and firsthand experience will be one of the summit’s central themes.
Sometimes the best answer to a question from someone planning Aliyah comes from someone who made it a month ago.
From the Ministry of Aliyah to the Jewish Agency
The Global Aliyah Live Summit will feature senior officials and representatives from many of the central organizations involved in Aliyah and integration in Israel, including the Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, the World Zionist Organization, Keren Hayesod, Ofek Israeli, Nefesh B’Nefesh, Clalit Health Services, Bank Leumi, the Jerusalem Municipality, Masa Israel Journey and Magen David Adom, along with employment organizations, advisers and other professionals.
Participants will also include the Minister of Aliyah and Integration and the chairman of the Jewish Agency, who will address the broader picture: Who is making Aliyah today? What has changed in recent waves of immigration? What barriers still confront newcomers? And what does Israel need to do not only to bring Jews to the country, but to help them stay and succeed?
Broadcast schedule, Israel time
13:00-14:00 — Live broadcast in Russian, in cooperation with Vesti
14:00-17:00 — Live broadcast in English on ynet Global and ynet
17:00-18:00 — Live broadcast in French on ynet Global
Four languages, one country
The September 8 broadcast will be held in Hebrew, English, Russian and French and is intended both for people already in Israel and for Jews around the world at different stages of planning Aliyah.
Throughout the day, the discussions will cover nearly every part of starting a new life in Israel: healthcare, money, work, housing, mortgages, rights, bureaucracy, community and everyday life.
Behind all of those practical questions is one larger one: How do you turn the dream of Aliyah into a life that actually works?
ynet Global’s Global Aliyah project has been following olim and prospective immigrants throughout the year with guides, articles, personal stories and practical information about life in Israel. On September 8, that conversation moves live.
For those who have already booked a ticket, those planning to arrive within the next year and those still sitting in Paris, London, New York, Toronto or Moscow wondering whether the time has come, the summit is designed to offer answers to the large and small questions that come with the decision.
Because Aliyah does not end when you land at Ben Gurion Airport.
That is where it really begins.

The Higher Education Board (YÖK) has launched an investigation into 23 foundation universities for exceeding the 25 percent tuition hike cap set for the 2026–2027 academic year.

As part of the investigation launched following the claims from students and parents received by YÖK, the tuition fees set by these universities will be compared with the actual rate of increase charged to students.

In an earlier statement, YÖK had announced that applications, reports and complaints deemed to have resulted in adverse consequences for students would be reviewed daily and with utmost urgency.

Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:25:00 UTC
19:25:00 KST

Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
September 6, 2026
It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.
The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.
The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.
Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.
Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.
Seeking German cooperation
Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.
One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.
Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.
A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."
"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.
Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.
Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.
"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.
Patients require intensive care, isolation
He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.
Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.
"If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.
Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.
Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.
The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.
Successful tick tactics
Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.
Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.
In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.
Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.
Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.
"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."
This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.
This article was originally written in German.
