Netanyahu races to finalize Likud election slate amid growing party tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:58:45 UTC
14:58:45 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is racing to finalize Likud’s Knesset slate before Tuesday night’s filing deadline, as internal pressure mounts over his remaining appointments and uncertainty persists over possible last-minute recruits and political alliances.
Likud Secretariat members were informed Saturday night that Netanyahu wants to convene the body Tuesday, just hours before the 10 p.m. deadline for submitting candidate lists for the 26th Knesset. The meeting is expected to approve any remaining candidates Netanyahu chooses to add to the slate.
The timing has heightened tensions inside Likud. Ministers, lawmakers, activists and local party officials are pressing Netanyahu not to make additional appointments unless they offer a clear electoral advantage, with some candidates already pushed significantly lower on the list following the party’s primaries.
Netanyahu has so far secured places for Defense Minister Israel Katz and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar near the top of the slate, as well as for Likud Central Committee chairman Haim Katz and businessman Oren Dobronsky. Several additional places remain available for potential recruits or political deals before the deadline.
One name recently floated is Dr. Keren Assayag, a lecturer and breast cancer researcher who recently met Netanyahu. After initially expressing reservations about entering politics, party figures now believe she may be willing to join Likud, though it remains unclear whether she would receive a realistic position on the slate or simply endorse the party publicly.
Netanyahu has also sought to use the remaining flexibility to encourage broader cooperation on the right. He had hoped to bring retired Brig. Gen. Ofer Winter into an alliance involving Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Moshe Feiglin’s Identity party, which have already joined forces.
Winter, however, has repeatedly rejected merger proposals and, according to several reports, also turned down offers of reserved places on the Likud slate. If those efforts fail, Netanyahu is expected to unveil new candidates instead, a move that could reignite tensions inside a party still unsettled by its contentious primaries.
The dispute is particularly sensitive because reserved appointments can push candidates elected in the primaries into significantly lower positions. Some who initially finished near the start of the second group of 10 candidates have already fallen into the third after reserved places were inserted.
That has prompted lawmakers and ministers to mobilize activists, branch chiefs and local officials in an effort to persuade Netanyahu not to use every appointment available to him. Netanyahu is aware of the pressure, but the decision to convene the Secretariat indicates he intends to keep all options open until the final hours.
The scramble inside Likud is part of a broader rush across Israel’s political system as parties prepare their final election slates.
Naftali Bennett is expected to present the list of his Beyachad alliance Sunday night while continuing efforts to recruit Chili Tropper. The emerging slate, which includes figures from Yesh Atid, currently contains more candidates than polling suggests will win seats.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman is also expected to unveil his party’s list Sunday. The party has been polling at around 10 seats, while Lieberman has recruited several new candidates in recent weeks, particularly figures associated with liberal religious Zionism and active military reservists.
Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar! party has emerged in polls as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, is due to present his slate Monday. “I’m talking to everyone,” Eisenkot said over the weekend. “We’re preparing more surprises for the next three or four days.”
A possible alliance between Eisenkot and Bennett also remains in play. Neither has confirmed that talks are advancing, but both stopped short of ruling out such a move when questioned at a Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth conference last week.
Tropper remains another potential piece in the final round of maneuvering, with the possibility that his Zionist Home-Reservists faction could join either Bennett or Eisenkot before Tuesday night’s deadline.

Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:54:00 UTC
14:54:00 KST

Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
September 6, 2026
Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.
Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.
Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.
Orban, allies lived lives of luxury
Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.
The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.
Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.
Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.
It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.
At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.
Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.
This time, things are meant to be different.
The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.
The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.
Controversy around new anti-corruption body
But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.
Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.
Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.
Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.
Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.
No justice in next 6 years?
Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.
Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.
The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.
"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.
In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.
Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.
This article was originally written in German.

Germany's far-right AfD eyes historic state victory in Saxony-Anhalt election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:52:06 UTC
14:52:06 KST

Germany's far-right AfD eyes historic state victory in Saxony-Anhalt election
Germany's anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany party is aiming to become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II as voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt head to the polls Sunday. However, a failure to secure an absolute majority may see the politically isolated party struggle to form a government.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will go to the polls on Sunday in a closely watched election that could see the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II.
Under the smiling and telegenic 35-year-old leader Ulrich Siegmund, the party has been polling comfortably ahead for months, and there is a genuine chance the AfD could take an absolute majority on Sunday evening – particularly if several smaller parties fail to clear Germany's 5 percent threshold to enter parliament.
Polls opened at 8am local time (06:00 GMT) and some 1.7 million voters have until 6pm (16:00 GMT) to cast their ballots, with first projections expected shortly after.
The AfD's key campaign promises include a "remigration and deportation offensive", a ban on LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools and an end to new wind farms.
Read moreGermany: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the ideologist behind the AFD’s plans in Saxony-Anhalt
Germany's domestic intelligence agency considers the AfD chapter Siegmund represents as "right-wing extremist" with links to ethno-nationalist groups and think-tanks.
Siegmund was present at a 2023 secret meeting near Berlin where extreme right-wing activists discussed a radical "remigration" plan to forcibly expel millions of people with a migration background from the country.
Sunday's vote is being closely watched as a barometer for the government of the deeply unpopular Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has attempted to chip away at the AfD's popularity by taking a tougher line on irregular migration and security.
Recent surveys place the AfD at just over 40 percent, followed by Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23 percent.
An absolute majority would allow the AfD to bypass mainstream parties' efforts to keep the party blocked out of power by refusing to work with it under a longstanding "firewall" policy.
Achieving an absolute majority is a high bar to clear in Germany's proportional electoral system, which was designed in part to encourage coalition governments and make it difficult for one party to rule alone.
If the AfD falls short of an outright majority, a CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome, though the exact shape of any coalition would depend on which parties enter.
Weeks of coalition talks could follow Sunday's vote.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'What we have started here can no longer be stopped'
For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt election is a stepping stone towards its larger ambitions of securing national power in the next federal election scheduled for 2029.
"No matter the outcome of tomorrow's election, we have already made history," said Siegmund at a final rally on Saturday evening.
"Because what we have started here in Saxony-Anhalt – what is currently sweeping across all of Germany – can no longer be stopped," he told the crowd in Saxony-Anhalt's capital, Magdeburg.
The AfD has long tapped into lingering resentment in Germany's East about an enduring wealth gap with the West decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
Many state-owned enterprises were shuttered following the absorption of the communist German Democratic Republic by the West, sparking large-scale unemployment and population flight, especially by young women.
Decades on, wages and savings remain lower on average, most big business is still based in the west, and eastern Germans – one fifth of the population – are under-represented in politics.
Even if the AfD emerges as the frontrunner on Sunday, though, the party would struggle to enter government due to the firewall.
Such a result opens the prospect of complex coalition negotiations, dependent on which parties can hit the 5 percent hurdle.
Polls show one of the CDU's current coalition partners, the liberal FDP, falling short, while the other, the centre-left SPD, is under 10 percent.
The small far-left anti-immigration BSW, the only party that has not ruled out a coalition with the AfD, is also likely to miss out.
For Schulze, who is favoured in polls as voters' top choice for leader, combining with the SPD and Greens might not be enough for a majority, but the CDU has ruled out a coalition with the far-left Left Party that could help it reach that threshold.
One option could be a minority government led by Schulze that would depend on passive tolerance from the Left – a model used in the neighbouring eastern German state of Thuringia.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

Serbia Is Not a Russian Province, and Lavrov Has No Right to Decide Its Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:52:00 UTC
14:52:00 KST

On Sept. 3, at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Sergey Lavrov said: “Out of inertia, countries continue; our Serbian friends and now our Armenian colleagues are seeking to join the EU.” He added that he was confident “this desire will disappear very soon.”
There is neither friendship nor respect for Serbia in those words. What they reveal instead is an old Kremlin reflex: treating countries it deems close to Russia as places where Moscow is somehow entitled to interpret their interests, judge how serious their decisions are and predict when they will abandon them. Lavrov was not commenting on a passing decision by a Serbian government. He reduced Serbia’s entire strategic course to a temporary weakness from which, in his view, the country will eventually recover, and such contempt deserves an answer stripped of diplomatic euphemism.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sergey Lavrov has no right whatsoever to decide what Serbia should want, how long it is permitted to want it or where Serbia belongs. Vladimir Putin has no such right either, nor does a state that has demonstrated its understanding of sovereignty by sending tanks across the internationally recognized borders of another country.
Serbia is not a Russian province, not Moscow’s political property, and not a country over which the Kremlin possesses some historical, moral, or political title. Nobody in Moscow has been given a mandate to treat Serbia as part of a Russian sphere of influence, to dismiss its foreign-policy choices as a temporary mistake, or to decide how much independence Serbia may exercise before Russian interests take precedence. Serbia owes Russia neither its future nor its foreign policy, neither its alliances nor its right to decide where it belongs. Any attempt by the Kremlin to behave as though Serbian independence ends where Russian interests begin is not friendship, but imperial arrogance.
British Journalist: In Ukraine, the Nation, Not Its Leaders, Drives History
If Serbia wants to negotiate membership in the European Union, that is Serbia’s decision. If Serbia one day decides to abandon that course, that decision must also belong to Serbia. A Russian foreign minister cannot announce in advance that a sovereign country will soon “get over” its own policy, as though Serbia were merely passing through a phase that Moscow expects eventually to cure. That is not the language of an equal relationship between sovereign states, but of political guardianship that Serbia has granted to no one.
The arrogance is all the more grotesque because it comes from today’s Russia, a rogue state that attacked Ukraine, seized parts of its territory and attempted to alter internationally recognized borders by force. Russian armed forces and authorities have committed war crimes in Ukraine. The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry has documented willful killings, attacks on civilians, unlawful confinement, torture, rape, and the unlawful transfer and deportation of children. The UN has also documented the widespread and systematic torture of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees held under Russian control, as well as executions of captured Ukrainian soldiers. Russian attacks continued to strike Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure throughout 2026, and in July the monthly number of civilians killed reached its highest level since May 2022.
None of this is incidental background to Lavrov’s remarks about Serbia. It is the record of the state he represents and of the aggression he has spent years defending before the world.
Ukraine has already lived through the consequences of the doctrine behind Lavrov’s contempt for Serbia’s choices. Moscow spent years insisting that it understood Ukraine better than Ukrainians themselves, that it knew where Ukraine belonged, which alliances it was entitled to pursue, and how real its independence could be if its chosen direction conflicted with Russian interests.
When political pressure failed to secure obedience, the Kremlin resorted to force. Russian troops entered Ukraine, occupied its territory, destroyed its cities, and, through annexation, attempted to turn the spoils of war into Russian land. In occupied areas, Russian authorities imposed Russian citizenship, Russian law, and the Russian education system, while people considered disloyal were subjected to intimidation, detention, torture, deportation, and forced displacement.
This is the ultimate destination of a policy that begins with the belief that a neighboring or “friendly” country does not possess the full right to choose against Moscow’s wishes.
Among the most repugnant elements of Russia’s occupation policy has been its treatment of Ukrainian children. Russian authorities have transferred children from Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine to the Russian Federation and to other areas under Russian control, in numerous cases separating them from the families and communities to which they belong. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s Commissioner for Children’s Rights, for the war crime of unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children. Putin is therefore the president of a state waging a war of aggression and a man subject to an international arrest warrant over crimes involving children taken from the occupied territory of another country. Against that record, Lavrov’s presumption that he can pronounce upon Serbia’s future is not merely offensive; it is obscene.
Lavrov is no peripheral figure in this regime, and there is no reason to indulge the fiction that he is simply a professional diplomat carrying out somebody else’s policy. He has been Russia’s foreign minister since 2004 and is one of the longest-serving senior figures in Putin’s system. He was foreign minister when Russia went to war with Georgia, when it annexed Crimea, when it tore into Ukrainian sovereignty in Donbas and when, in 2022, it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Throughout those years, his role has been to give diplomatic vocabulary to what Russian power does on the ground: aggression recast as defense, occupation dressed up as historical correction, and another country’s freedom of choice portrayed as a threat to Russian security. Lavrov understands perfectly well what the UN Charter means, what internationally recognized borders mean and what the prohibition of aggression means. That knowledge does not diminish his responsibility; it makes his role more damning. He has spent years consciously representing and defending a policy that has brought war, occupation and war crimes back to Europe.
In 2022, the European Parliament recognized Russia as a state sponsor of terrorism and as a state that uses terrorist methods, citing deliberate attacks and atrocities against Ukrainian civilians, the destruction of civilian infrastructure and other grave violations of international and humanitarian law amounting to war crimes. Describing today’s Russia as a rogue state is not rhetorical inflation. It is an entirely fitting description of a government that has trampled the fundamental rules of the international order while demanding the protection of those same rules for itself. The Kremlin insists that Russia’s borders are inviolable while changing Ukraine’s borders by force, invokes sovereignty whenever it wants to keep others out of Russian affairs and discards the sovereignty of its neighbors when their policies cease to suit Moscow. That double standard has left dead civilians, devastated cities, and occupied land in its wake, and Lavrov consequently has no political or moral standing from which to prescribe the limits of any other European country’s freedom of choice.
His phrase “our Serbian friends” sounds all the more cynical for that reason. Serbia is useful to the Kremlin as a “friend” only for as long as it refuses to impose sanctions on Russia, allows space for Russian political influence and keeps European Union membership sufficiently distant for Moscow to treat it as unfinished and ultimately unattainable business. Whenever Serbia reaffirms EU membership as a strategic goal or supports the territorial integrity of Ukraine, Moscow explains those decisions away as the product of Western pressure, a failure by Serbia to understand its own interests or, as Lavrov now puts it, mere “inertia” that will soon pass. That has nothing to do with a relationship between equals. It is an expectation of political obedience.
Serbia has been a candidate for European Union membership since 2012 and has conducted accession negotiations since 2014. The process has lasted far too long and has been burdened by mistakes in Belgrade, slow reforms and the indecision of the European Union itself, but all that belongs in a debate between Serbia and the EU. Lavrov has no place in that debate. Serbia may change its policy, alter the pace of negotiations or even change its ultimate objective, but it can do so only through its own sovereign decision. There is no Russian veto over Serbia’s European future, however much the Kremlin might wish otherwise.
The deepest insult in Lavrov’s statement is not his contempt for the European Union, but his assumption that Serbia still belongs to a category of countries to which Moscow feels entitled to explain what they really want. The Kremlin has never received a mandate from Serbian citizens to determine the strategic direction of their country. No episode of diplomatic alignment between Moscow and Belgrade gives Russia any claim over Serbian sovereignty. Russia holds no title deed to Serbian foreign policy and possesses no historical license to invalidate Serbia’s decisions whenever they displease the Kremlin. If Moscow understands friendship as an entitlement to Serbian obedience, the problem is not some supposed Serbian failure to appreciate Russia, but Russia’s refusal to accept Serbia as a fully independent state.
Putin’s Russia possesses neither the political nor the moral authority to lecture Serbia about its future. The boundary the Kremlin must accept could hardly be clearer: Russian state power ends at the borders of the Russian Federation, beyond which lie other countries, other peoples and decisions that belong to neither Putin nor Lavrov. That includes Serbia’s right to decide for itself whether it will one day become a member of the European Union. Serbia does not have to prove the depth of its European commitment in order to state the obvious fact that Moscow will have no say in that decision. It need only behave as a sovereign country and answer Sergey Lavrov’s prediction in the only terms appropriate for a man speaking on behalf of a rogue state that has already written its claim to decide the future of other nations in Ukrainian blood: the Kremlin must keep its hands off Serbia.

Archaeologists in Ghent may have uncovered the remains of a medieval city gate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:50:00 UTC
14:50:00 KST

In Ghent, capital of East Flanders, archaeologists may have found traces of a medieval city gate. These are believed to be the foundations of the Ketelpoort. The excavations are being carried out in phases as part of the redevelopment of Flanders’s busiest tram line, between Gent-Sint-Pieters Station and the commercial hub of the Veldstraat. The works will continue until 2029 and cost 23 million euros.
Archaeologists in Ghent may have uncovered the remains of a medieval city gate
The Ketelpoort or Kettle Gate stood on the Ketelvest—a defensive moat or water channel dug to connect the Rivers Scheldt and Leie. The Ketelvest waterway is said to have bubbled or churned like a boiling cauldron or 'ketel' in Dutch, where the waters met.
Following a summer break, archaeologists have now resumed excavations in the centre of Ghent. This is where Flanders’s busiest tram line is being rebuilt. Archaeologists are first carrying out excavations to find new traces of medieval Ghent before they are buried beneath the new tram line. The reconstruction began this spring and will take at least three years.
So far, the excavations have mainly yielded small finds, which confirm that the city began to expand systematically in this area around the 11th century. The ground has been disturbed by previous sewerage works, meaning that large structures are less well preserved. However, some were discovered at the Ketel Bridge.
Foundations made of Tournai limestone
Archaeologists found older masonry sewers, part of a cobbled surface and the foundations of a late medieval building, constructed from bricks nearly 30 centimetres long. Beneath these, they discovered what may be the remains of the city gate.
‘There was a foundation made of Tournai limestone. That material was used between the 11th and 13th centuries,’ says Robrecht Vanoverbeke of archaeology firm BAAC. ‘This may have been part of the Ketelpoort, a medieval gateway into the city.’
This theory is supported by an earlier report from 1990. At that time, city archaeologists carried out an inspection a few metres away, prior to the start of sewerage works. They noted the remains of a brick wall, which they linked to the Ketelpoort, based on a painting from 1534.
A place where two districts grew together
The Ketelpoort was one of the medieval gates in the first city wall. It consisted of an inner and an outer gate, connected by a bridge. The gate was demolished in 1780. The present-day Ketel Bridge stands on the same site.
In the early Middle Ages, Ghent consisted of separate settlements that gradually merged to form a single city. This also happened at the Ketelpoort. There, the settlements of the Sint-Pieters Village (centred around the abbey of the same name) and the area around the medieval harbour (the Graslei and the Korenlei) eventually merged. The fields and farmland in between gave way to built-up areas. Names such as ‘Veldstraat’ (Field Street) still bear witness to this.
Meanwhile, in the Zonnestraat, archaeologists have also uncovered remains of the façade of a stone medieval town house. Excavations are now continuing here. The ground has been much less disturbed than elsewhere, which raises hopes of even better finds.
The foundations of the Ketelpoort are now once again underground.

UK’s largest carmaker to axe thousands of jobs – media

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

UK’s largest carmaker to axe thousands of jobs – media
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed plans to cut jobs as Britain’s largest carmaker struggles with rising costs, falling sales, and the impact of US tariffs, with The Times reporting that up to 4,000 positions could be eliminated.
JLR has faced mounting pressure from US tariffs, which have made its British-built vehicles more expensive to sell in the US despite London securing a reduced 10% rate. The impact has been particularly significant given that North America is the company’s largest market. Its troubles were compounded by a major cyberattack last year that forced it to halt production for several weeks.
JLR’s revenue fell by nearly 10% in the quarter ending in June, while pre-tax profit plunged by more than two-thirds to £109 million ($147 million). According to The Times, chief executive PB Balaji is under pressure from JLR’s Indian owner, Tata Motors, to cut costs.
In a statement to media, JLR said it “must adapt to evolving global market conditions” while seeking approximately £1.7 billion ($2.3 billion) in savings over the next two years and lowering its annual break-even point to 300,000 vehicles.
JLR said it is “opening a voluntary redundancy program” for salaried and management staff.
Employees were reportedly informed on Friday. The Times reported that up to 4,000 positions could be eliminated over the next two years, although JLR has not confirmed the number.
JLR directly employs around 34,000 people at sites in the West Midlands and Merseyside and supports an estimated 120,000 jobs across Britain’s automotive supply chain.
European carmakers have been reducing their workforces amid weak demand, rising costs, and growing competition from lower-cost Chinese manufacturers. Volkswagen this week approved another 50,000 job cuts by 2030, bringing its planned global workforce reduction to approximately 100,000. Its Porsche subsidiary is set to eliminate another 5,000 positions by 2035.
Germany’s car-manufacturing crisis has also been compounded by high energy costs since the country lost access to much of the cheap Russian pipeline gas on which its industrial economy had long relied following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume has separately cited US tariffs and intensifying Chinese competition among the pressures weighing on the company’s competitiveness.

Trump's approval rating falls to record low — Financial Times poll
Unknown

14:44:14 KST

LONDON, September 6. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump's approval rating has dropped to a record low in a survey conducted by the British company Focaldata for the Financial Times, with only a third of US voters approving of his performance at the White House.
According to the study, only 33% of respondents supported Trump's current political course, compared to 35% a month earlier. At the same time, his support among Republican voters fell to 72%, which is also an anti-record in FT polls.
It is noted that the overwhelming majority of respondents rejected Washington's trade policy and the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration, linking them to the rising cost of living for US citizens. Two-thirds of voters believe the US economy is moving in the wrong direction, with another 57% saying that Trump's administration policies have negatively affected their financial well-being. Furthermore, 56% of survey participants expressed dissatisfaction with the latest trade tariffs on Canada, voicing concern over a possible further increase in prices for consumers.
FT also noted a decline in Trump's level of support as a political ally, as 46% of respondents believe that the current president is making the upcoming midterm congressional elections more difficult for the Republican Party. Another 47% stated their unwillingness to support a candidate publicly endorsed by Trump.
The poll was conducted from August 28 to September 1 among 1,914 registered voters, with a margin of error of approximately 2.6 percentage points.

The US rejected a claim by Malaysia’s opposition Islamist party that Washington once sought to influence the country’s choice of political leadership, calling the allegation false.
“The United States has never sought to decide Malaysia’s political leadership,” US embassy in Malaysia Charge d’Affaires David H. Gamble Jnr said in a statement on social media on Sunday. “Any account to the contrary is false.”
Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) president Abdul Hadi Awang said at the Islamist party’s annual congress on Saturday that a US ambassador once asked the party whom it would propose as prime minister if it took power.

Colombia vows crackdown after deadly drone swarm attack (VIDEOS)
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has vowed to step up operations against armed groups after a drone swarm attack on a military compound killed three soldiers and injured four others.
The assault comes as Colombia is grappling with what has been described as its worst wave of violence in a decade. In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 officers and killed a police dog. Earlier this week, a car bomb outside another police station in the northeast killed one civilian and injured 11 others.
The latest attack occurred on Friday night at the El Trapiche military post in Ocana, in the northeastern department of Norte de Santander, according to Colombian authorities.
At least 20 UAVs were used in the assault, AFP reported. Explosives dropped from the drones struck barracks and other parts of the base before a firefight broke out. Two soldiers died at the scene and a third passed away after receiving medical attention. A Colombian Air Force helicopter was also hit by shrapnel.

Ukraine’s drone forces say they hit 58,465 Russian targets in August, nearly 1,900 a day. Three named campaigns did the strategic damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:31:45 UTC
14:31:45 KST

Ukraine's drone forces say they struck 58,465 Russian targets in August, an average of nearly 1,900 a day. The tally is up almost 9 percent on July and more than double January's, and it included 54 vessels of Russia's shadow fleet, 33 air-defense systems, and 168 energy nodes, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Madiar" Brovdi reported on his Telegram channel.
The volume matters less than where some of it lands. Cutting power to occupied Crimea and the south is meant to blind Russian air defense, much of which runs on the grid. Meanwhile, the strikes on Russia's sanctions-evading shadow fleet squeeze both Crimea's fuel supply and Moscow's oil exports.
Ukraine's drone forces claim 11,010 Russian troop casualties in August
Brovdi also said the strikes killed or wounded 11,010 Russian soldiers over the month, about 355 a day — a figure that counts only losses the drone force attributes to its own strikes, not Russia's total casualties.
That daily rate was slightly below July's 374, down about 5 percent, even as the number of targets rose. Compared with January, the force said Russian personnel losses were up 17.3 percent.
Three campaigns inside the count
Most of the headline volume is small front-line targets, but three named operations account for the strategic hits. Under Operation "Milk", the force said it struck 54 shadow-fleet vessels in August, bringing the total to 260 since the campaign began on 6 July. Operation "PPOpad" — a play on the Ukrainian for air defense — hit 33 Russian air-defense elements in August and 263 across 2026.
The third, Operation "Crimean Switch Off", struck 168 energy nodes in August, bringing the total to 349 since early July. That campaign has been running for months, blacking out swaths of occupied Crimea.
Brovdi has argued that cutting power to stationary radars and other air-defense elements opens the airspace for deeper Ukrainian strikes. Months of these strikes have left occupied Crimea rationing fuel and living with rolling blackouts, and cut the Kerch ferry crossing's capacity by about three-quarters. All of the figures are the force's own, and Ukraine's military claims of Russian losses are not independently verified.

GAZA CITY, Palestine / ISTANBUL
For more than two years, their families could not reach them.
On Saturday, the bodies and remains of around 100 Palestinians finally lay before their relatives in Gaza City, recovered from beneath homes destroyed in Israeli attacks and gathered for a long-delayed farewell.
Near the Imam al-Shafi’i Mosque in the southeastern Zeitoun neighborhood, rows of remains were draped in Palestinian flags as families lit candles, laid flowers and moved among photographs and the names of children, women, men and elderly victims.
Some searched for relatives they had not seen since their homes were bombed. Others stood over remains that bore little resemblance to the people they remembered beyond what had allowed them to be identified.
The remains were recovered in recent days by Gaza’s Civil Defense from homes belonging to the Rahim, Balawi, Malaka and Qanbour families as part of a project to retrieve Palestinians still buried beneath buildings destroyed during Israel’s war on the enclave.
Civil Defense crews are working with only a handful of excavators and worn-out equipment because of Israeli restrictions on the entry of machinery needed for recovery operations.
‘My whole life is gone’
Among the mourners was Maryam Hassan al-Balawi, standing before members of the family she had waited years to recover. Malak, her only surviving daughter, stood beside her.
“My husband and my children were killed. I have no one left except my only surviving daughter, Malak,” Balawi told Anadolu.
“My whole life is gone. My husband and my children are gone. I have no life left,” she said, adding that Malak still cries every day for her father and siblings.
Balawi also recalled a final request from her husband before he was killed.
“If I die, shroud me with your own hands and bury me with your own hands,” she recalled him telling her.
For more than two years, she could not fulfill that wish.
“What am I supposed to do? My home is gone, my children are gone, my life is gone,” she said.
Yet recovering the remains brought a measure of relief after years in which Balawi repeatedly returned to the ruins where her family remained buried.
“When they brought them out, I felt some relief in my heart, as though my soul came out with them,” she said. “I used to go there every day and say: ‘God, let them come out so I can see them.’ Today, after they were recovered, I feel a little peace.”
Only survivor
For Balawi, much of that pain rests with Malak.
“What did my daughter do to deserve this?” she asked. “She cries every day. She wants her father and her brothers and sisters.”
“She says: ‘What did I do, Dad? Why did they bomb them? They did nothing.’”
Jadallah Rahim stood nearby beside the remains of 32 relatives killed when their home was struck Feb. 19, 2024. More than 15 were children and around 10 were women, he said.
“Their only ‘fault’ was that they stayed in their homes,” said Rahim. “They were suddenly bombed and they were all killed in an instant.”
Thirty-three people had been inside, said Rahim, pointing to a girl standing nearby.
“She was number 33. She was the only survivor.”
The others remained beneath the destroyed home for around two-and-a-half years before Civil Defense crews were finally able to reach them after days of digging with limited equipment.
Looking toward the names placed beside the remains, Rahim stressed that those before him were not merely casualty figures.
“These are not numbers,” he said. “Look at their names. Men, women, children, elderly people.”
‘The grief came back’
Recovery ended one wait but reopened another wound.
“This is not joy,” said Rahim. “The grief came back. The pain came back. The tears came back.”
He pointed to a young girl moving among the remains of her family, saying she lost her father, mother, sisters and brothers.
“Today she walks among them crying for her grandfather, her father, her mother, her brother, her sister and her grandmother.”
For Rahim, however, recovering the dead also meant finally giving them a burial after years beneath the rubble.
As darkness settled above Zeitoun, candles continued to burn beside the rows of remains, surrounded by flowers, Palestinian flags and families who had waited years for this moment.
On Sunday morning, they are expected to carry their loved ones in a mass funeral procession.
The second phase of the Civil Defense recovery project covers 147 destroyed homes in Gaza City and the northern and central Gaza Strip, where an estimated 1,072 bodies are beneath the rubble.
During the first phase, launched in November 2025, crews recovered around 333 bodies and sets of remains from 54 destroyed homes and buildings.
Since October 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 73,651 Palestinians and injured 174,575, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
For the families in Zeitoun, however, the numbers tell only part of the story.
After more than two years beneath the rubble, their dead had finally come home.

====================================================================================================

Far-right surge challenges Germany’s postwar taboo as AfD closes in on historic state victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:18:48 UTC
14:18:48 KST

Germany’s political attention is fixed Sunday on the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where an election in a region of just 2.1 million people could become one of the most consequential moments in German politics since World War II. For the first time since 1945, a far-right party could win enough power to govern a German state.
Alternative for Germany, or AfD, enters the vote with a commanding lead. The latest ZDF poll put the party at 41%, compared with 23% for the Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, of incumbent state premier Sven Schulze. Another poll placed the AfD as high as 43%. That would represent close to a doubling of its 20.8% result in the previous Saxony-Anhalt election in 2021. The party has also surged nationally: in Germany’s 2025 federal election it doubled its support from 10.4% to 20.8%, becoming the largest opposition party in the Bundestag.
But winning the most votes does not necessarily mean taking power. Germany’s major parties have so far refused to enter coalitions with the AfD, maintaining the political “firewall” designed to isolate it. The party’s 35-year-old candidate for state premier, Ulrich Siegmund, has said he is not interested in coalition partners either and would seek the premiership only if the AfD wins an absolute majority and can govern alone.
That makes Germany’s 5% electoral threshold one of the biggest variables in Sunday’s vote. Parties that fail to cross it are excluded from the distribution of parliamentary seats, meaning the AfD would not necessarily need 50% of the popular vote to control more than half the legislature. The more votes cast for parties that fail to enter parliament, the greater the AfD’s relative share of seats could become.
The Social Democrats, or SPD, and the Greens are projected by some polls to clear the threshold, though the Greens remain close to the danger zone at around 5% to 6%. The Free Democratic Party, or FDP, and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, BSW, are expected to fall short.
The prospect of an AfD majority has even triggered a campaign for tactical voting, urging opponents of the party to back the SPD or Greens even if they would not normally support them, simply to ensure those parties cross the threshold and reduce the AfD’s share of seats. As a result, one of the central questions Sunday is not only who finishes first, but how many parties make it into parliament at all.
“No matter what tomorrow’s result is, we have already made history,” Siegmund told an AfD closing rally in Magdeburg on Saturday night. “What we started here in Saxony-Anhalt, and what is now sweeping across all of Germany, can no longer be stopped.”
Immigration, schools and Pride flags
An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would have consequences far beyond symbolism. Germany’s states wield broad powers over education, culture and internal security, while also holding seats in the Bundesrat, the upper house of the federal parliament. Saxony-Anhalt controls four of its 69 votes.
In its “Vision 2026” platform, the AfD lays out how it would use that authority. The party pledges to launch a deportation drive and establish a task force to accelerate removals, reduce reliance on foreign workers it describes as coming from “culturally foreign backgrounds,” and challenge the status of Ukrainian refugees.
In schools, the AfD proposes placing refugee children in separate classes, returning students with disabilities to special education frameworks, banning Pride flags and requiring the German flag to be flown daily. It also wants to reshape school curricula in what it describes as a more patriotic direction, restrict Islamic practices including the Muslim call to prayer, dismantle the state’s current public broadcasting structure and withdraw funding from certain cultural institutions.
Ahead of the election, ynet spoke with two Jewish figures who have extensive experience with both antisemitism and Germany’s far right: Max Privorozki, chairman of the Jewish community in Halle, where a neo-Nazi gunman tried to storm a synagogue on Yom Kippur in 2019 before murdering two people outside; and Stephan Kramer, a German Jew who has headed the domestic intelligence agency in neighboring Thuringia since December 2015.
“Alternative must be under surveillance,” Kramer said. “There are strong indications that influential parts of the party are acting against human dignity and the German Constitution and are working against the democratic order.” He noted that the AfD has been classified as a confirmed far-right extremist organization by local domestic intelligence authorities in Thuringia and, since 2023, in Saxony-Anhalt.
At the federal level, the legal picture is more complicated. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, announced in May 2025 that it was classifying the AfD as a confirmed far-right extremist organization, but later temporarily suspended use of that designation pending a legal challenge by the party. The Saxony-Anhalt branch itself remains classified by the state intelligence service as confirmed far-right extremist.
“The party’s appeal comes from a mixture of protest, distrust of the traditional parties, concern about immigration and social change, and the sense that it is talking about problems the other parties ignore,” Kramer said. “In that sense, some of the attraction is also a symptom of the failure of the other parties to reach these voters. There are even Jews who support it because of its positions on Israel, Islam, security and immigration, despite the fact that it is an extremist party.”
Kramer cautioned against confusing control of one German state with control of the country as a whole. “You have to put things in proportion. In the upper house, it would have only four votes out of 69,” he said. “But if it forms a government, it will have power, access to sensitive information and the ability to appoint people in the police, intelligence services, security forces and the Interior Ministry. Using the machinery of government could also give the party momentum at the federal level.”
‘Jews don’t have the luxury of choosing whom to fear’
For Germany’s Jewish community, Kramer said, the contradiction surrounding the AfD is particularly stark. “Alternative presents itself as supporting Jewish life and Israel,” he said. “But it opposes kosher slaughter, it has leaders who use conspiracy theories and antisemitic language, and senior figures who want to challenge the way Germany deals with its historical responsibility and focus less on the darkest years of German history.”
“The problem is not that every Alternative voter is an antisemite,” he added. “The problem is that parts of the party promote ethno-nationalist ideas of belonging and want to weaken institutions that were built specifically after 1945 to protect democracy and minorities. At that point, the question is no longer whether Alternative is good for Jews, but whether liberal democracy is capable of protecting Jewish life and other minorities, whose rights can exist only if everyone is equal before the law.”
German law bans the public use of Nazi symbols and slogans, as well as Holocaust denial and the trivialization of Nazi crimes. Kramer said several senior AfD figures have repeatedly tested those limits. “There are leaders in the party who have clearly crossed the forbidden lines,” he said. “Björn Höcke, the party leader in Thuringia, was convicted of using the Nazi slogan ‘Everything for Germany.’ There are other examples of him using similar language. He is a trained history teacher. He knows what he is talking about. But in general, their language is much more sophisticated: coded language with several meanings that pushes and tests the boundaries of the law.”
Kramer said even banning the party would not solve the deeper social forces behind its rise. “Democracy cannot and should not ban frustration, anger or radical political opinions,” he said. “You have to act against an organization that works against the Constitution and the democratic order, but that will not address the social problem it represents. We have to ask why 40% do support it. That question should have been asked 10 years ago. If there is a ban in order to protect our democracy, the real challenge will begin the day after.”
Kramer has previously said he would consider leaving if the AfD came to power. He is now more cautious, but says the concern remains. “I still work in Thuringia, but of course my family and I are taking precautions for the possibility that a far-right party forms a government in a German state.”
Asked what it would mean if roughly 40% of voters backed the AfD but people nevertheless celebrated because it failed to win an outright majority, Kramer said the result would be deeply ambiguous. “First of all, it means that the majority, 60%, did not vote for the party,” he said. “But I hope people will be shocked and understand the danger our democracy is in and what needs to be done. It would be a very ambivalent moment. It would show how far the political center of gravity has shifted and how much our standard for political stability has been lowered.”
Kramer also rejected attempts to rank the threats facing German Jews today, whether from the far right or from the convergence of parts of the far left and Islamist movements since October 7. “I would take that argument seriously,” he said. “Last year there were 8,725 antisemitic incidents, more than three times the number in 2022, and 68% were classified as Israel-related antisemitism. That is a physical, immediate and visible problem that threatens Jewish life every day.”
The figures correspond with the 2025 annual report by Germany’s RIAS antisemitism monitoring organization.
“But far-right rule is dangerous in a different way, through appointments, budget priorities, education and memory culture,” Kramer said. “This is a party where many far-right extremists and antisemites have found a home. Jews today do not have the luxury of choosing whom to fear. The authorities have not helped them on this point. They have left that field open to Alternative as well.”
For Kramer, Saxony-Anhalt could serve as a preview of what lies ahead for Germany. “It is certainly a warning of what could happen,” he said. “This is a party that was once on the fringes of German politics, and today, without substantially changing its platform, it can govern.”
He said he sees three possible consequences. “The first is that people get used to it and understand that if it gets numbers like these, it has to be taken into account, and then the psychological barrier breaks. The second is that the eastern states become a laboratory where we can see how Alternative functions in government. And the third is what we are seeing now: parties band together simply to keep it out. That was possible when it was at 10%. When it reaches 25%, 35% or more, you cannot freeze it out forever.”
‘If I leave Germany, it will be for the same reason I left the Soviet Union’
In Halle, where a neo-Nazi gunman tried to storm the synagogue on Yom Kippur in October 2019 and murdered two people after failing to enter, the election is being watched particularly closely. Max Privorozki, chairman of the city’s Jewish community, said the past seven years have left little room for optimism.
“What happened on October 7 overshadowed even the attack on the synagogue on Yom Kippur,” he said. “Everything that has happened to us since leaves us little room for optimism, especially antisemitism and the connection between the far left and radical Islam.”
He said the rise of populist and extremist parties is not accidental. “There is disappointment here with the policies of the authorities in Germany and the European Union,” he said. “Disappointment with current politics causes people to look for alternatives, sometimes simply for the sake of an alternative. People do not always ask whether these parties are actually capable of solving the problems. I hope we manage to hit the brakes before it is too late.”
Despite the concerns, Privorozki insisted that Halle’s Jewish community has no intention of disappearing. “Whatever happens, Jewish life in Halle and Saxony-Anhalt will continue,” he said. “We have had problems in the past and dealt with them. There is no discussion of leaving.”
Then he added: “I left the Soviet Union because I did not want to continue living in a totalitarian state. If one day I leave Halle and Germany, it will be for the same reason I left the Soviet Union 37 years ago.”
Polls close at 6 p.m. local time, with initial results expected immediately afterward. Germany will then learn whether Saxony-Anhalt has simply become another powerful AfD stronghold, or whether it has broken the final postwar barrier preventing a far-right party from governing a German state.

Kintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘Style as well as substance’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

Amid all the bunting and hoopla of the platinum jubilee back in 2022, you may well have missed that Colchester, Britain’s oldest recorded settlement, got an upgrade from town to city status. And, as we all know, no true city is complete without at least one fancy restaurant that serves the likes of duck liver mousse on lattice tuiles. Well, in Colchester, Kintsu takes that slot.
Or at least it did until May 2025, when chef Paul Wendholt abruptly shut up shop, citing financial pressures. The name Kintsu plays on the term kintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold, silver or platinum or, more commonly, of embracing imperfection and making something pleasing out of bad luck. So it’s rather fitting that Wendholt, a two-time winner of the Essex Chef of the Year gong, managed to reopen Kintsu just four months later, and a year on is now offering eight courses, plus a few extras, for £90 a head in a Grade II-listed building, albeit one that’s down a back lane beside a multi-storey NCP car park. The setting will win no beauty contests, but when a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him. Come for the secure parking, stay for the treacle-cured Dingley Dell pork from nearby Suffolk and the Colchester cherries with amaretto.
Even the very idea of a tasting menu will deter some customers: too faffy, too fiddly. But here, from the first warm-up snack – whipped Montgomery cheddar in a fluted tartlet casing under a blanket of crunchy yeast and yet more cheese – even the hardest of the “I just want me dinner” brigade might find their hearts softening. This is followed by that duck liver mousse-topped tuile with glossy, amber beads of onion gel piped on top and a fat, postage stamp-sized chunk of bread pudding piled with ricotta, lemon, and raw peas and shoots. Style as well as substance.
Hunks of warm sourdough arrive, clearly fresh from the oven and reminding you how sweet and fragrant sourdough can be, especially when it’s spread with glorious Fen Farm butter. A plague upon all that hard, spongy nonsense served up and down the land as a plinth for scrambled eggs. While we work our way through these opening snacks, Lionel Richie’s Dancing on the Ceiling plays in the background, and the bread turns up to Shattered Dreams by Johnny Hates Jazz. By the time the Braxted tomatoes arrive, we are deep into Living in a Box territory, which feels about right for a Saturday lunchtime in a listed barn. Why can’t all restaurants play mid-1980s chart music?
Those first course tomatoes are a rhapsody of very good fruit arranged strategically on silky whipped pecorino with a wicked green basil oil. It is 1pm on a Saturday and we are on one of only two tables occupied. The minimal staff – two in the kitchen and one on the floor – couldn’t be lovelier, ferrying thick, chunky and squat Cornish crab tarts that look almost like mince pies. There’s lots of brown meat layered under the white, and very good, crunchy pastry. This is good, thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty rather than flippant. I wish more people were here to taste it, but they are probably all at a bottomless brunch somewhere, eating ethylene-ripened avocado mush on fumaric acid-injected bread that tastes of old flip-flops. More fool them.
  We, meanwhile, are having wild Suffolk bass, its skin all crisp and blistered, cooked precisely and served on a foamed sauce flecked with chives and beads of orange oil. Next up, that treacle-cured pork, which is hot, juicy, pitch-black around the edges, and comes layered with sweet raw and cooked apple. At this point, a third booking arrives, which is great for Kintsu but curtails my enthusiastic crooning along to The Closest Thing to Heaven by the Kane Gang. The strongest course comes next in the form of Herdwick lamb, and features a moist, well-seasoned medallion with a dark, rich jus, tiny nests of shredded turnip, and yet more lamb, roasted, pulled and compacted on to a metal skewer, and topped with cream and shredded mint.
A pre-pudding of yoghurt, raspberry and lemon resets the mouth. Then an inventive dessert of Colchester cherries, both cooked and preserved, and served on something biscuity, something creamy and something with a whiff of amaretto. It doesn’t look like much on the plate – a collapsed Jenga of dessert ideas – but it is utterly fabulous. We pay the bill over slices of homemade fig-leaf fudge that I would happily hand out in boxes at Christmas. Or eat alone on the sofa.
Kintsu is a huge example of a small regional indie doing its very best in rather weird times. Use these places or lose them. Right now, Kintsu is open: beautifully restored, with shimmers of gold.
- 
  Kintsu 11a North Hill, Colchester, Essex, 01206 574361. Open lunch Fri & Sat, noon-1.30pm (last orders); dinner Weds-Sat, 6.30-8pm (8.30pm Fri & Sat; last orders). Tasting menus only, five courses for £65 or eight for £90, both plus drinks and service

Memory of water: the women reshaping Venice – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

Venice is a city of tradition and projection, a place feeding the imagination of millions of people arriving from elsewhere. The “impossible city”, suspended on water, often appears unchanged, fixed in time. Yet, like the water that carries it, the city is in constant, subtle transformation.
We often speak of Venice as if it were immobile. We call it timeless, suspended outside history, untouched by change. But Venice is changing. It is fragile, exposed, under pressure. On one side, rising sea levels and increasingly unpredictable tides are reshaping the lagoon and threatening a delicate equilibrium. On the other, mass tourism continues to transform the city from within. Homes become short-term rentals, local businesses give way to visitor-oriented commerce, and residents leave the historic centre in steadily increasing numbers. The spaces left empty by those who move away are often filled by tourism itself, both a cause and a consequence of this transformation.
Yet beyond the dominant narratives of overtourism and climate breakdown, another, quieter transformation is taking place. Venice lies on contradictions – appearance and structure, illusion and rootedness. One of these tensions emerges in the role of women in shaping the city’s identity. While many Venetian traditions are historically grounded in women’s labour, from lace-making to textile work and other forms of craftsmanship, women have long been excluded from what in Venice constitutes public space: water.
In Venice, water functions as the street. The city is crossed by about 150 navigable canals, which remain its main routes for movement, work and social exchange. For centuries, these waterways have been spaces governed by explicit rules and implicit codes that largely excluded women. As in many other cities where women have historically been marginalised from the street, in Venice they have been marginalised from the water. From navigating boats, from professions such as gondoliera and sandolista, from boatbuilding and competitive rowing. Today, these boundaries are beginning to shift.
The journalist Anna Toniolo has lived with Venice her entire life, having been born and raised only a few kilometres from the city. This project grew from years of observing Venice and from a shared awareness, with photographer Daniela Sala, that some of the city’s most vital spaces remain inaccessible to women – not through formal prohibition, but through traditions deeply embedded in everyday life. Between November 2025 and March 2026, they spent weeks documenting the experiences of women whose work and lives are closely connected to the lagoon, through field reporting, interviews and observation, seeking stories that challenge the dominant image of Venice.
The stories gathered in this project reveal how women are reclaiming space precisely through tradition, carrying forward skills and professions that have long defined Venetian identity while simultaneously reshaping them.
In 2010, Giorgia Boscolo became the first woman to obtain a gondolier licence, breaking a centuries-old barrier and opening the way for others. Today, women practising the profession are still few. According to fellow gondoliers, those actively working can be counted on the fingers of two hands, although more women have passed the qualification exam in recent years. There are about 440 licensed gondoliers in Venice, alongside approximately 200 substitutes – qualified gondoliers who have passed the exam but do not yet hold their own licence.
A similar profession is that of the sandolista, who rows a sandolo, a traditional flat-bottomed Venetian boat once widely used for everyday transport across the lagoon. Today, there are only about 20 sandolisti left, and just one of them is a woman: Chiara Curto.
In the city’s remaining squeri – the traditional boatyards where wooden boats are built and repaired – Silvia Scaramuzza is the only female maestra d’ascia, or master boatbuilder. Other women are creating new paths into these spaces.
In 2020, Marta Canino founded “Fie a Manetta”, a name that roughly translates as “Girls at Full Speed”, while also evoking the image of women taking the helm. It is the first, and still the only, motorboat navigation school in Venice run by women and open to everyone.
The idea grew from the awareness that navigation remains a predominantly male environment. “Girls, we need to start recognising each other and giving social value and political weight to our role in this city,” Canino said.
Slowly, and often without proclamation, women are entering and inhabiting Venice’s public spaces through practice. Their presence does not simply occupy the water, but begins to redefine it.

‘Britain’s Yellowstone’: restoration project aims to take the greed out of land acquisition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:57 UTC
14:00:57 KST

It is difficult to find the most remote place in England. There is no public transport, no roads and no sign of any human habitation. Online route finders mistakenly direct cars up a grassy track. But miles along gravel forest roads in the far north of Northumberland is the largest contiguous rewilding site under single ownership in the country.
The vast glacial bowl of 7,500-acre Emblehope Moor has been bought for £8.5m by Restore, a nature restoration company that works with landowners across Britain.
The aim is to bring golden eagles, curlews, black grouse and beavers back to the moor which in former guises was a traditional grouse shooting and sheep farming estate and a dog-training ground.
But the restoration project, which is still seeking to raise £4m to fund its 20-year scheme, also has a unique proposition: after delivering new biodiversity and abundance alongside financial returns for investors and repaying the crucial £4.5m Triodos Bank loan that enabled the purchase, it will hand over the site to local community or charitable ownership.
“We want to prove that the bank is paid back, investors get their two-times return but we don’t need to become the next for ever laird,” said Benedict Macdonald, an environmental writer and the founder and director of Restore. “We’re keen to leave a well-funded community project for the future. It’s not an aggressive land-holding model; it’s both a capitalist and community model and I want it to become the national model for the uplands – we’ve got to take the greed out of it for it to work.”
The environmentalist Ben Goldsmith hails the burgeoning mosaic of increasingly wild estates in Northumberland as Britain’s Yellowstone.
Close to Emblehope in the north of Northumberland is Rothbury, the largest estate to come on the market for 30 years, which the Wildlife Trusts are seeking to buy with an unprecedented £30m fundraising appeal that is nearing its target.
Other private estates in the area, including 12,000-acre College Valley and 4,000-acre Hepple Wilds, are accelerating nature restoration while the vast 148,000-acre Kielder Forest is increasingly managed by Forestry England for biodiversity.
“We’re not the size of Yellowstone but we’re in England’s largest wild landscape by a long factor,” said Macdonald.
Emblehope, a site of special scientific interest (SSSI) which was managed for biodiversity by former owners the Royal Kennel Club for a number of years, already has exciting numbers of raptors, including merlin and prospecting golden eagles. The site’s streams still have trout and salmon, and there are red squirrels and pine martens in the area.
But Restore’s first tasks will be to return water to desiccated peat moorland and remove swaths of non-native sitka spruce.
A hidden network of land drains have left what should be water-soaked peatland completely parched. Patches of sphagnum moss that are usually water-filled sponges even in summer are dry. Modelling suggests Emblehope’s rewetted peat could store an additional 100,000 cubic metres of water, equivalent to about 40 Olympic swimming pools.
“It’s going to be a massive exercise to identify the exits of water from the land,” said Macdonald.
In the future, they will call on beavers to help hold back more water. There are promising patches of birch and willow growing beside one stream – beaver food – but Macdonald has witnessed beavers making dams out of heather on even more treeless moors in Norway and is confident they will thrive.
Before that, there is a more urgent task for the ponies that are to be introduced on to the site.
The cattle- and sheep-grazing on the estate’s moorland was reduced by the previous owners on the advice of conservationists but Macdonald is alarmed by dry “thatch” beneath the thick tussocks of moorland grass. “It’s quite dangerous from a fire point of view,” he said. His priority is to get Exmoor ponies on to the site, because they will eat down the grassy thatch and reduce the fire risk.
Opening up the site to more diverse grazing animals will reduce aggressive grass species and increase the diversity of the sward. The grass is also currently too thick and long for curlew chicks to survive and find food, and so other species will benefit from the grazing animals.
Destined for the chop are dense sitka plantations, which harbour little life and raise predation to unnaturally high levels because goshawks lurk in them.
On Emblehope, the removal of the trees will hit a few species, such as long-eared owls and crossbills. But these will remain in the wider landscape because there are huge tracts of plantation forestry across neighbouring Kielder.
Restore plans to leave patches of a few older trees but admits the problem with retaining any sitka – and the problem with its Forestry England neighbours – are what Macdonald calls the “little shitkas”, the baby trees that pop up all over the wilding moors from wind-blown seed.
The solution is to plant broadleaved screens around the edge of the site to stop wind-blown sitka seed.
While Restore’s promotional videos have tantalised people with glimpses of lynx, Macdonald is wary of being seen to endorse moves to bring back the lost predator, which many rewilders view as an ideal solution to Britain’s overpopulation of wild deer. While a survey suggests 72% of local people are in favour of reintroducing lynx, many sheep farmers in the area are vehemently opposed to an animal that could make their working lives harder.
“We have no funded plans for lynx, and we have no wish to be in the reintroduction party,” said Macdonald, although he conceded “the economic argument [in favour] is compelling”. Research to be published next year will quantify the potential tourism bonanza to Northumberland.
Although there are proposals to release lynx into surrounding Kielder, one was blocked by Natural England and a second, the Wildlife Trusts-backed Missing Lynx project, is still consulting. Emblehope is unlikely to be a key habitat for the forest-dwelling animal.
Despite Restore’s wilding manifesto, it is retaining the estate’s farmer and gamekeeper.
“What surprises me is how surprised people are that we’ve retained staff who know so much about the land,” said Macdonald. “The farmer is a real student of the history of grazing here and he’s very open-minded. The gamekeeper has been looking after some of Britain’s highest densities of birds of prey. These guys work 18-hour days, they live and breathe the area.”
Restore will fund the transformation of Emblehope via conventional income from forestry (removing the sitkas) and cattle, sheep and, in the future, education and carefully limited eco-tourism – as well as government environmental land management payments. But it expects most of its income to come from natural capital payments.
These include carbon credits for the sequestration in restored blanket bog and “30x30 Restore units” whereby corporations pay for the restoration of 30-metre by 30-metre patches of habitat. Restore’s vision is that corporations pay not for biodiversity outcomes but for conservation action on the land which provides more wildlife. Macdonald said: “It’s perfectly natural for large corporates to sponsor big sporting events across the world. In nature, in England, this is a big event.”

Travellers to EU face renewed queues as border-check flexibility rules expire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Travellers to the EU could face renewed border queues as flexibility measures for the bloc’s entry-exit system officially come to an end – although numerous sources have indicated that some member states will not enforce biometric checks.
Airlines last week called on the European Commission to extend discretionary powers to pause EES controls when necessary until the end of 2026, with the deadline for “flexibility” passing on 6 September.
Peak holiday season has not resulted in a repeat of the long queues seen at some European airports in early summer, which at worst led to numerous passengers missing flights. But the aviation and travel industry believes further chaos was averted only through relaxation of the rules demanding biometric information, including fingerprinting of non-EU-citizens.
While Brussels has not extended the discretionary period, it appears that cross-Channel travellers to France will not face changes next week because of technical problems with the EES software commissioned by French authorities.
The fingerprinting kiosks expensively procured by Eurotunnel, Port of Dover and Eurostar at London St Pancras are still not operational. Dover said it was not expecting any changes next week, with car drivers yet to be subject to EES checks.
A Eurotunnel spokesperson said it was “awaiting confirmation from the French authorities on the timing of this next phase” but was “ready to implement full biometric checks as soon as formal clearance is granted”.
A Eurostar spokesperson said: “The phased rollout of EES continues. EES enrolments will continue to be completed manually by border officers.”
A senior airline source said that while they would be monitoring closely, they did not expect to see full enforcement at the busiest European airports. Border officials in main foreign tourist destinations, most notably Greece, appeared to have unofficially exempted UK passengers from EES checks to avoid queues. The source said they expected the practice to continue.
Luke Petherbridge, the director of public affairs at the UK travel industry trade body Abta, said it was continuing to push the European Commission to allow discretionary suspension of border checks beyond September, “recognising that there is still some way to go until EES is fully and consistently operational across all participating countries”.
The airlines trade body Iata has called for an official extension, saying last week that EES-related delays had resulted in people missing flights and connections.
Thomas Reynaert, the head of external affairs at Iata, said: “These are real impacts being felt by passengers. It gives Europe a bad reputation. When systems fail, passengers lose the trust in the system and when people are late, airlines pay a high cost.”
The European Commission declined to provide further comment. A spokesperson said early last week: “We are in close and constructive contact with those few member states where some adjustments are needed at certain border crossing points.
“And during an additional period of operational adjustment that is needed at these few operational border crossing points, the commission stands ready to provide additional support to these member states.”
